# Abstract

# This dissertation focuses on the role of neoliberal beliefs in perceptions of and women’s

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment. My primary research sought to answer the question:

# What is the role of neoliberal beliefs in people’s perceptions of and experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment among women and how are systems of power, privilege, and oppression integral to

# these perceptions and lived experiences?

# In Study 1 (N=426), in an online survey of U.S. adults I analyzed the potential role of

# other social beliefs and participant identity in the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs; and I

# analyzed the role of neoliberal beliefs in perceptions of women’s experiences of sexual assault,

# sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility. We found support for our first hypothesis that

# higher participant endorsement of economic system justification, belief in a just world, racism,

# sexism, and classism predicted higher neoliberal belief endorsement. For our second hypothesis,

# we found partial support that some more historically and currently privileged groups endorsed

# neoliberal beliefs at higher rates (men, politically conservative participants, White conservative

# participants compared to women, politically Democrat, and White Democrat individuals

# respectively). There was also an interaction between participant race and social class in

# neoliberal belief endorsement. Specifically, among White participants as social class increased

# so did neoliberal belief endorsement but among Black participants as social class increased,

# neoliberal belief endorsement decreased. Lastly, we found support for our final hypothesis

# showing higher neoliberal belief endorsement was associated with greater acceptance of sexual

# assault, sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility myths.

# 

# xvii

# In Study 2 (N=445), I employed an experimental online survey of U.S. adults to

# understand how neoliberal beliefs and perceptions of women’s sexual assault might vary as a

# function of stereotypes about marginalized groups of women. Supporting expectations,

# participants were more likely to blame Black women and women stereotyped as members of the

# “undeserving” poor (e.g., those who rely on government assistance and are not seen as honest

# and hardworking) for sexual assault compared to White and “deserving” poor women

# respectively. Additionally, partially supporting our expectations, higher participant blame toward

# Black women for sexual assault was mediated by perceptions that Black women were less

# valuable; further, this finding was mediated by stronger participant neoliberal belief

# endorsement. Similarly, higher participant blame toward the “undeserving” poor woman was

# mediated by perceptions of her oversexualization, and this relation was stronger among

# participants higher in neoliberal belief endorsement.

# In Study 3, I sought to understand the role of neoliberal beliefs in policies and practices

# that add constraints to lower-income women contributing to increased vulnerability to

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment based on their housing and workplace precarity. I

# inductively analyzed 22 interviews with Black and White women living and working in more

# (e.g., living in motels out of necessity and lack of access to permanent housing) or less

# precarious situations (e.g., living in government-funded housing) in Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor,

# MI. Participants described their workplace and housing experiences of mistreatment in terms of

# five themes: bureaucracy, safety/violence, space issues, and mistreatment, and neoliberal

# beliefs. Through these women’s reflections on their daily lives, they importantly demonstrate that

# 

# xviii

# research in areas of marginalized women’s mistreatment requires a deeply thoughtful approach

# to understanding the ways in which neoliberal policy and other influencers at the structural level

# implicate their individual experiences in day-to-day life.

# 

# Chapter 1: Introduction

# How do we decide who deserves certain goods, outcomes, and experiences in society?

# People generally have their own opinions about this, and researchers have also spent a great deal

# of time examining this question (Jones & Harris, 1967; Kelley, 1967; Kelley & Michela, 1980).

# The idea of individualism or individual control is central to the idea of who is seen as deserving

# or undeserving of certain resources or outcomes, including who is to blame for gender-based

# mistreatment. The significance of individualism has been a defining feature of the United States

# since its inception and is linked with a prominent ideology known as neoliberalism (Harvey,

# 2005; Feagin, 1972). Further, researchers have found evidence for the relation between

# individualism and individual control in people’s perceptions about who deserves resources in

# times of economic need, of human rights violations, and of gender-based victimization (Bullock,

# 1999; Bullock, Williams, Limbert, 2003; Drolet, et al., 2016; Feagin, 1972; Lott & Bullock,

# 2001; Staerklé & Clémence, 2004; Stringer, 2014).

# When people make judgments about a woman’s culpability for her own gender-based

# mistreatment, they often rely on perceptions of what the woman did in the situation and her

# personal character, including perceived sexual availability and conscientiousness or

# responsibility (Abrams et al., 2003; Burt, 1980; Du Mont et al., 2003; Dyar, et al., 2021;

# Eigenberg & Garland, 2008; Forbes et al., 2004; Grubb & Harrower, 2008; Howard, 1984;

# Kamke, et al., 2023; Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a; Koss, 1985, 2011; Lonsway & Fitzgerald, 1994;

# Luginbuhl & Mullin, 1981; Romero-Sánchez, et al., 2018; Ryan, 1976; Stormo et al., 1997;

# 

# 2

# Stuart, et al., 2019; Suarez & Gadalla, 2010; Workman & Freeburg, 1999). Importantly then,

# observers’ perceptions of a woman’s level of control in a situation based on her actions,

# inactions, and individual character attributes helps them decide about the level of blame that can

# be attributed to her. However, we know that when people make decisions about a woman’s

# blame for these experiences, they are often influenced by other characteristics not related to the

# specific situation at hand or are even created by the observer to help them maintain the

# perspective that the world is a just place where people generally get what they deserve (Lerner,

# 1980). Creating a story that affirms the world is just can help people make sense of deleterious

# events through what researchers discuss as “system justification” (Jost & Banaji, 1994; Jost, et

# al., 2004; Jost & Hunyady, 2005). Further, those who are more likely to believe that the world is

# truly a just place have also been shown to blame women more for their experiences of sexual

# assault (Culda, et al., 2018; Grubb & Harrower, 2008; Hammond, et al., 2011; Hayes, et al.,

# 2013; Lonsway & Fitzgerald, 1994; Vonderhaar & Carmody, 2015).

# The significance of individualism and belief in individual control in explaining outcomes

# in life has been a defining feature of the culture of the United States since its inception; more

# recently it has been linked with a prominent ideology known as neoliberalism (Harvey, 2005;

# Feagin, 1972), described in the next section. Neoliberal beliefs have been shown to predict

# people’s endorsements of just world beliefs, perhaps helping explain why people rely on the

# belief that the world is generally a place where people get what they deserve (Bay-Cheng, et al.,

# 2015). Therefore, if we are thinking about how people decide what others deserve in life,

# 

# 3

# including in women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment, neoliberal beliefs might be an

# important concept to consider in our research.

# Neoliberalism and Neoliberal Beliefs

# The concept of neoliberalism varies in its focus and definition across disciplines, public

# discourse, culture, and more (Beattie, et al., 2019). However, for the purpose of the current

# research, I will draw on theorists such as David Harvey, Wendy Brown, and from researchers

# from psychology who discuss neoliberal beliefs and their impact on the individual. I will start

# with a brief history of neoliberalism, then will discuss the centrality of individualism in

# neoliberal beliefs and its role in perpetuating capitalism, and finally will outline an opposing

# position to neoliberal beliefs in the context of women’s experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment.

# An Introduction to the Concept of Neoliberalism

# Neoliberalism was originally proposed as an economic ideology in the 1930s and was

# strongly influenced by classic ideas of liberalism (Harvey, 2005). Neoliberalism is associated

# with free-market capitalism, a somewhat hands-off government, and notions that individuals can

# succeed or fail based on their own skills and hard work, competition, and personal

# responsibility/wherewithal (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey, 2005). Neoliberal ideology

# discounts systemic inequality and thus seeks to limit government interference in social concerns

# such as civil rights, welfarism, and other forms of institutional and structural forms of

# discrimination that those who endorse neoliberal beliefs see as irrelevant to individual success,

# which is integral to the goals of capitalism including “wage reductions, increased unemployment,

# 

# 4

# and part-time labor without benefits” (Arfken, 2018, p. 685; Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey,

# 2005; Perez & Salter, 2019; Son Hing, 2013). A neoliberal resurgence has been linked with

# prominent leaders during the 1970s and 80s such as Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan, and

# to policies like The Personal Responsibility and Work Reconciliation Act that sought to limit

# government interference in these issues (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey, 2005). Since the

# resurgence in the 1970s, the effects of neoliberal ideology can be seen in the globalized valuing

# of wealth and economic growth, while ignoring the structural discrimination and violence that

# are integral to and exacerbated by this monetary growth; rather, the ideology’s view of individual

# actors remains the key figure in making assessments of responsibility for life outcomes (Perez &

# Salter, 2019).

# The Role of Individualism

# The belief that individual control is what separates those who succeed and those who fail

# is a central idea in neoliberalism and is rooted in the belief that the world is fair and just (Bay-

# Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey, 2005; Perez & Slater, 2019; Son Hing, 2013). As Son Hing (2013)

# described:

# “…within social contexts marked by group inequality and a history of capitalism, explicit

# prejudice and neoliberal economic beliefs should be linked because they are part of a

# cluster of ideologies that serves to legitimize a hierarchical status quo” (Son Hing, 2013,

# p. 165).

# According to this logic, if we operated in a truly fair and free market capitalist society, a

# person’s life circumstances are completely up to them; they could accomplish whatever they

# 

# 5

# wanted if they only worked hard enough. Economic mobility would abound. However, as is

# pointed out in the book, Deaths of Despair, that is not the state of contemporary American

# capitalism (Case & Deaton, 2020). Rather, the original conditions that made the colonization of

# this land possible have continuously been reproduced through our reliance on and exploitation of

# cheap labor and laborers who are disproportionately represented by Indigenous People and

# People of Color (Bruyneel, 2020). This is exemplified by Segalo and Fine who state, “colonial

# legacies continue to influence modes of production, knowledge systems, wealth distribution, and

# movement of people and resources between borders” (Segalo & Fine, 2020, p. 5).

# Further, research has documented the trend that people are more likely to be plagued by

# intergenerational economic confinement than to be upwardly mobile (Case & Deaton, 2020).

# Even though many Americans acknowledge vast disparities in economic wealth, people still

# generally believe that we live in a truly fair and free market capitalist society where individual

# control is emphasized in economic outcomes (Bullock, 2013; Feagin, 1972; Jost, et al., 2015).

# Further, even those who belong to disadvantaged economic groups often endorse these ideas

# (Jost et al., 2015). Research helps explain the endorsement of these beliefs and the lack of class

# consciousness among groups that are negatively affected by them as strategies of self-protection

# (Feagin, 1972; Jost & Banaji, 1994; Larrain, 1983; Liu, et al., 2011; Marx & Engels, 1998).

# These neoliberal ideas appeal to people because they appear to be consistent with principles of

# dignity, individual freedom, and control (Harvey, 2005); therefore, many cling to these ideals

# despite their absence in their lives. Further, neoliberalism has been linked to increased economic

# 

# 6

# disparities in the U.S. and across the globe through globalization and capitalist economies

# (Bettache & Chiu, 2019; Manne & McKnight, 2010).

# Psychological research has been criticized for reproducing neoliberal ideology through its

# focus on human processes that are often decontextualized from socio-historical factors that shape

# such outcomes and focus on individual factors to explain behavior and personality (Adams, et

# al., 2019; Bettache & Chiu, 2019; Gjorgjioska & Tomicic, 2019). Importantly, while

# neoliberalism is an economic ideology affecting policy and practice at the systems level, moving

# from these broad societal notions of neoliberalism to individuals, we see evidence for these

# systems’ influence on people’s perceptions of the world around them (Bettache & Chiu, 2019;

# Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Kashima, 2019).

# Crucially, psychological researchers Bay-Cheng and colleagues (2015) created the

# Neoliberal Beliefs Inventory to capture individual endorsements of neoliberal ideology that

# measures central neoliberal beliefs about systemic inequality, competition, personal

# responsibility, and the role of government in individual matters. In creating this scale, these

# researchers documented that those who endorse just world beliefs are also more likely to endorse

# neoliberal ideology (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015). Specifically, through the belief that these systems

# are fair (even when they are not), some people—even those most oppressed by the systems

# themselves-- excuse and even rationalize the many injustices that the system itself creates, thus

# allowing the individual to believe the world is fair and just (Jost & Banaji, 1994; Lerner, 1980).

# Consequently, while neoliberalism in general is concerned with economic policies and practices

# 

# 7

# at the system level, these ideas have implications that produce a host of individual-level

# outcomes, including individual behaviors, beliefs, and interactions between people.

# Neoliberal Beliefs and Gender-Based Mistreatment

# Researchers have additionally demonstrated that despite the seemingly positive

# perspective that neoliberal beliefs offer (e.g., that anything is possible if you work hard enough),

# the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs is associated with less collective action for women, lower

# consciousness of sexism, lower endorsement of feminist beliefs, more acceptance of rape myth

# ideology, and the endorsement of racist ideology (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Son Hing, et al.,

# 2013). Further, as previously discussed, the narrative of individual actions and character as the

# focus for blame in women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment has long been established

# by researchers. Thus, individuals’ endorsement of neoliberal ideas in the U.S. at the system level

# appears to be important to the way people view individual-level experiences in the world around

# them ranging from the allocation of resources to gender-based mistreatment. As Harvey (2005)

# states, under neoliberalism, “personal failure is generally attributed to personal failings, and the

# victim is all too often blamed” (p. 76).

# While any woman can experience gender-based mistreatment for any reason, based on

# the intersectional experiences of sexism, classism, and racism under neoliberalism, lower-income

# women, and Black women (of varying class backgrounds) are disproportionately susceptible to

# the negative outcomes resulting from neoliberalism. This includes experiences of sexual

# violence; when these experiences do happen, they are less likely to be taken seriously compared

# to other women (Cortina et al., 1998; Fessler, 2018; Foley et al., 1995; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982;

# 

# 8

# Kane, 2020; LaFree, et al., 1985; MacKinnon, 1979; Maryland Coalition Against Sexual Assault

# [Maryland Coalition Against Sexual Assault MCASA], n.d.). Perceptions of sexual availability

# and responsibility that researchers have found to be central in people’s tendency to blame women

# for experiences of gender-based mistreatment are also elements of common stereotypes

# associated with Black women and lower-income women specifically (Collins, 2000; Ferguson, et

# al., 2005; Grubb & Harrower, 2008; Howard, 1984; Koss, 2011; Loughnan, et al., 2013;

# Workman & Freeburg, 1999). These group-based stereotypes are associated with perceptions of

# individual failing like the rationale that is central to neoliberal beliefs about people’s general

# outcomes in life (Harvey, 2005). Further, ignorance of the ways that systemic systems of racism,

# classism, and sexism shape the lived experiences and outcomes of women’s gender-based

# mistreatment fits within a neoliberal framework of beliefs that is reflected in much of the

# research on Black and lower-income women’s experiences of violence (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015;

# Harvey, 2005; Son Hing, et al., 2013). While neoliberal beliefs themselves may not directly lead

# to increased violence among women, the endorsement of such beliefs can lead to support for

# policies that help continuously reproduce the conditions that maintain women in positions where

# they are more likely to experience gender-based mistreatment and for people to discount those

# experiences when they do happen.

# A goal of this project across three studies is to refrain from falling into the expected

# patterns of decontextualized psychological research (Adams, et al., 2019). Specifically, my

# research will be guided by decades of feminist and community psychologists’ arguments, as well

# as the analytical lens of epistemologies of ignorance, according to which we will be critical of

# 

# 9

# the way that often in psychological research actions and results of those actions are studied

# without the contextual social-historical consideration that are crucial to their undoing (Segalo &

# Fine, 2020). Some researchers have been asking the more difficult question of who is benefiting

# from the exploitation of others and are making analysis of power central to their psychological

# inquiry; I wish to follow in this direction (Bullock, 2013; Segalo & Fine, 2020). I will attempt to

# achieve this goal by centering intersectionality theory in the framing and interpretation of my

# research (Settles & Buchanan, 2014; Shields, 2008).

# Offering an opposing argument to neoliberalism, intersectionality theory proposes that

# systems of oppression such as racism, sexism, and classism lead to crucially different

# experiences, opportunities, and perspectives about others. While recognizing that individuals are

# not viewed in terms of single social positions, the primary focus of intersectionality attends to the

# ways in which overlapping power hierarchies affect individuals based on their different positions

# in those hierarchies (Collins, 2000; Collins & Bilge, 2016; Crenshaw, 1991; Crenshaw, 1989;

# hooks, 2000; Lorde, 1984; Moradi & Grzank, 2017; Yuval-Davis, 2006). Further, assumptions

# about membership in certain groups that are often visible to observers such as race, gender, age,

# and more can affect how individuals perceive others based on the socially constructed

# categorization of these identities (Settles & Buchanan, 2014). Specifically, research has

# suggested that people do indeed make qualitatively different assumptions about others based on

# people’s perceived membership in multiple groups; these perceptions are influenced by systems

# of privilege and oppression (Bavishi, et al., 2010; Lott & Saxon, 2002; Reid, 2010; Settles &

# Buchanan, 2014).

# 

# 10

# According to this theory, observers’ expectations about, and judgments of, women who

# experience mistreatment with different intersecting social identities (e.g., Black working-class

# women vs. White working-class women) are likely qualitatively different as a function of the

# mistreated women’s different social positions (Cole, 2009; Ghavami & Peplau, 2012). Thus, for

# example, White working-class women have access to some race-related privilege that Black

# working-class women do not; for that reason, they may be viewed differently by observers. In

# the same way, Black middle-class women have access to class privilege that their working-class

# counterparts do not (see Bowleg, 2008 for examples of race, sexuality, and gender; see also Cole,

# 2009; Collins, 2015).

# Given the pervasiveness of neoliberal beliefs in the context of the U.S., my specific hope

# in this dissertation is to draw attention to the circular way in which lower-income women are

# maintained in positions that make them disproportionately vulnerable to experiences of gender-

# based mistreatment through the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs via a lack of subsidized

# housing and a lack of formal and effective protection working in precarious and under-valued

# jobs, while also drawing attention to the attitudes that help inform such policy. As Angela Davis

# described the centrality of these beliefs in the experiences and perpetuation of violence against

# women, “As the violent face of sexism, the threat of rape will exist as long as capitalist society

# survives” (Davis, 1981, p. 45). While Davis discusses capitalism as central to the violence

# perpetuated against women and the focus in this dissertation is the role of neoliberal beliefs in

# this violence, it is important that I circle back to the relationship between individuals and

# structures. It can be argued that the resurgence of neoliberalism and the integration of neoliberal

# 

# 11

# beliefs into the very fiber of what it means to be a productive citizen has ensured a capitalist

# society that allows the pooling of wealth and resources among a select few at the exploitation of

# the masses (Marx, 2010/1867; Harvey, 2005). As Arfken (2018) states,

# “It is something of an oversimplification to view neoliberalism as an ultra-libertarian

# doctrine devoted to free-market ideology and averse to all forms of government

# intervention. In actual practice, neoliberalism has little aversion to strengthening national

# and international institutions as long as they foster forms of regulation and intervention

# that channel benefits and resources to a small cadre of people who remain committed to

# bringing nearly every aspect of human existence under capitalism (Arfken, 2018, p. 686).

# These ideas have led me to the following research questions for consideration: What is

# the role of neoliberal beliefs in other forms of gender-based mistreatment apart from sexual

# assault? How do neoliberal beliefs shape people’s perceptions of gender-based mistreatment

# among Black and White lower-income women? What is the role of neoliberal beliefs in helping

# to reproduce the conditions that keep lower-income women susceptible to high rates of gender-

# based mistreatment and how is this tied to their precarity of housing and work? In the first two

# studies I used surveys, one attitudinal and one experimental, to examine the relationship between

# neoliberal beliefs and other social attitudes, and to assess how holding neoliberal beliefs is

# associated with the general public’s tendency to blame different groups of poor women for their

# experiences of sexual assault. In Study 3 I used semi-structured interviews to directly assess both

# neoliberal beliefs and experiences of mistreatment among Black and White poor women, while

# considering the role of their housing and employment precarity. By considering the implications

# 

# 12

# of neoliberal beliefs for both a broad sample of U.S. citizens and for poor women themselves, I

# hope to shed light on their importance in maintaining poor women’s difficult position in U.S.

# society.

# 

# 

# 13

# Chapter 2: Neoliberal Beliefs and Gender-Based Mistreatment

# Researchers have begun to explore the importance of neoliberal beliefs in people’s

# perceptions of individual-level experiences. Given extant research that demonstrates the link

# between the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs and rape myth acceptance, a central goal of this

# study was to extend the literature in three ways using two online surveys. In the first survey, I

# explore the relationship between neoliberal beliefs and people’s perceptions of other types of

# gender-based mistreatment (sexual harassment and gender-based incivility). Since neoliberal

# beliefs are related to more sexist general ideas and less collective action for women, it seems

# likely that the endorsement of these beliefs would be associated with greater acceptance of other

# forms of gender-based mistreatment too. Additionally, in this first survey, I assess whether

# people’s endorsements of neoliberal beliefs differ based on their own positionality and

# relationship to power in the world by analyzing the role of various participant social identities in

# the likelihood of neoliberal endorsement. Lastly, while research supports that people who are

# more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs also have higher rates of rape myth acceptance toward

# women in general, I examine this in a second survey experiment that investigates the role of

# neoliberal beliefs in people’s perceptions of women who face the highest rates of sexual assault--

# lower-income Black and White women.

# Sexual Assault

# Researchers have demonstrated that individuals often blame women who have

# experienced sexual assault for their own mistreatment (Campbell, 2008; Janoff-Bulman et al.,

# 1985; Muehlenhard, 1988; Ryan, 1976; Van der Bruggen & Grubb, 2014). Research on people’s

# 

# 14

# perceptions of women’s experiences of sexual assault demonstrates the key role of personal

# responsibility (one key element of neoliberal ideology) in people’s judgments of how much

# women are to blame for the treatment they receive. Specifically, research has demonstrated that

# people rely on individual attributions about the situation and people in the situation to come to a

# conclusion about blame (Luginbuhl & Mulin, 1981; Ryan, 1976). They draw on characteristics

# and features of the incident such as perceptions of its severity, what the woman was wearing,

# whether the woman was intoxicated or not, how many previous sexual partners the woman had,

# whether she reported the attack, how much she resisted the attack, and whether or not she knew

# the person who attacked her (Fitzgerald, et al., 1995; Grubb & Harrower, 2008; Howard, 1984;

# Koss, 1985; Koss, 2011; Luginbuhl & Mulin, 1981; Stormo, et al.. 1997; Workman & Freeburg,

# 1999). Further, perceptions of sexual objectification have been shown to be central in people’s

# judgments of women’s experiences of sexual assault (Loughnan, et al., 2013).

# Sexual Harassment

# Similar to the literature on women’s experiences of sexual assault, facets of personal

# responsibility and sexual objectification are also central in people’s perceptions of women’s

# experiences of sexual harassment. For instance, researchers have demonstrated that women tend

# to be blamed more for their experiences of sexual harassment if they fail to report the experience,

# if the woman doesn’t label it as sexual harassment, and if the perceiver doesn’t see the

# harassment as severe (Fitzgerald et al., 1995; Klein et al., 2010; Lucarini et al., 2020; Marin &

# Guadagno, 1999). Further, as in people’s perceptions of women’s sexual assault, researchers

# have shown that if perceivers view the woman as more promiscuous or are primed with content

# 

# 15

# that sexually objectifies women in general, they are more likely to blame the woman for her

# harassment (Bernard, et al., 2018; Ferguson, et al., 2005).

# Incivility

# Incivility is defined as, “rude, condescending, and ostracizing acts that violate workplace

# norms of respect, but otherwise appear mundane” (Cortina, et al., 2017, p. 299). While research

# on incivility generally focuses on people’s experiences of it rather than others’ perceptions of it,

# Ali, and colleagues, (2015) found that those who were most concerned with the adequacy of their

# own abilities were more likely to attribute their own experiences of incivility to internal causes,

# thus justifying the incidents of incivility (Ali et al., 2015). Further, Kiebler and Stewart (2022a)

# showed that while people generally blame women for their experiences of all gender-based

# mistreatment (sexual assault, sexual harassment, and incivility), they attributed more blame to

# women who had experiences in which responsibility was most ambiguous (most for incivility,

# and then less for harassment and assault, generally).

# Given this literature, there is reason to believe that myths based on gender-based

# harassment and incivility might be affected by the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs as well.

# First, the literature on stereotypes of women blamed for sexual harassment focuses on personal

# responsibility, which is a central tenet of neoliberal ideology and is central in people’s myths

# about sexual harassment as well. Second, in the literature on incivility, researchers have

# demonstrated that incivility is “selective,” in that it allows discriminatory behavior via sexism

# and racism to be concealed through these “mundane” acts of mistreatment (Cortina, 2008;

# Cortina, et al., 2013). Because neoliberal ideology is said to be “meritocratic, post-feminist,

# 

# 16

# [and] post-racial,” just as uncivil acts are often perceived as small and detached from systemic

# workplace mistreatment, it seems likely that people who endorse neoliberal beliefs might also

# believe that uncivil treatment at work is not targeted or a big deal. Further, the literature on

# incivility supports the notion that people do make attributions (at least about themselves) about

# the cause of uncivil treatment in gender-linked ways.

# Perspective and Positionality

# Based on differential levels of access to privilege and oppression in relation to systems of

# oppression, people bring their own experiences to their perceptions of any situation. Therefore,

# another important goal of this study is to understand how individual differences might affect

# participant endorsement of neoliberal beliefs. Specifically, I will assess important participant

# characteristics (e.g., social class, race, gender, and political identity) that may be central to

# neoliberal belief endorsements as well as other prominent beliefs that have been shown to be

# linked with differential levels of neoliberal belief endorsement.

# Perspective

# Bay-Cheng and colleagues (2015) created the neoliberal belief inventory, and found that

# participant endorsement of racism, sexism, and just world beliefs were significantly related to

# their endorsement of neoliberal beliefs. Specifically, those who endorsed racism, sexism, and just

# world belief ideology were also more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs (Bay-Cheng, et al.,

# 2015). Given the above discussion of the central neoliberal beliefs that attribute outcomes in life

# to individual effort while also discounting the reality of structural inequality, these results are

# well founded. Specifically, theorists of neoliberalism suggest that individuals who endorse

# 

# 17

# neoliberal beliefs at high rates would believe that individual failings or hard work can be

# attributed to individual outcomes rather than systems of oppression like racism and sexism

# (which they would believe don’t exist in the first place) (Arfken, 2018, p. 685; Bay-Cheng, et al.,

# 2015; Harvey, 2005; Perez & Salter, 2019; Son Hing, 2013). Further, the focus on individual

# drive for individual outcomes supports the belief that the world is a just place where people

# generally get what they deserve.

# While Bay-Cheng and colleagues provide some evidence for important beliefs that

# influence people’s likelihood of endorsing neoliberal beliefs, I propose building on these

# findings to understand how people’s perceptions of classism and economic system justification

# might affect endorsements of neoliberal beliefs. Similar to the findings above, individuals who

# endorse neoliberal beliefs might also be likely to endorse classism and economic system

# justification as explanations for inequality based on class in order to maintain the illusion that the

# world is indeed a just and fair place. Further, given that individual effort is central to neoliberal

# beliefs, it seems plausible that those who endorse neoliberal beliefs at higher rates would be

# likely to discount classism as an important factor in individual economic outcomes and would

# likely endorse the economic system as just.

# Positionality

# The literature on gender-based mistreatment shows that individuals’ social identities—

# their positions in social hierarchies including gender, race, social class, and political identity--

# influences people’s perceptions of these experiences. For instance, as is already demonstrated

# clearly in the literature, the social identities of victims and perpetrators are important in people’s

# 

# 18

# understanding of their mistreatment, but so too are participants’ own identities (Donovan, 2007;

# George & Martínez, 2002; Wheeler & George, 2005). Additionally, though not without

# exceptions, men are generally more likely to blame women for experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment compared to women themselves (Pollard, 1992; Workman & Freeburg, 1999).

# Further, researchers have demonstrated that participants identifying as more politically

# conservative are considerably more likely to blame women for experiences of sexual assault

# compared to less conservative individuals (Rosewood & Hammond, 2023).

# While the literature on gender-based mistreatment shows extensive support for the

# importance of individual social identities in differences in perceptions of those experiences, the

# literature on neoliberal beliefs lacks an exploration into how these social identities might be

# underlying differences in these endorsements. The research by Bay-Cheng and colleagues (2015)

# was important to creating the neoliberal beliefs inventory as a crucial tool for psychological

# research; however, their sample did not allow us to understand how neoliberal beliefs might be

# different among many different groups of people. Results from their study did show that

# conservative political affiliation was linked with greater endorsement of neoliberal beliefs, but

# little else has been analyzed in terms of potential participant identity difference in endorsement

# based on sample limitations (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015).

# However, there is a body of literature that suggests the importance of identity in the

# likelihood of people making structural versus individualistic attributions for subjects like poverty

# that is important to consider. Although the research findings are mixed, individuals’ own racial

# and class identity seem to be important factors contributing to how people make attributions

# 

# 19

# (Bullock, 1999; Feagin, 1972; Young, 2004). Specifically, some research has demonstrated that

# individuals from lower-income backgrounds and those who identify as African American were

# more likely to make structural attributions for poverty, while people from higher-income

# backgrounds and those who identify as White were more likely to make individual attributions

# for poverty (Bullock, 1999; Feagin, 1972). Other research by Young (2004) documented ways in

# which similar groups have been less inclined to name structures as primary reasons for their

# situation in life. However, given the current emphasis on structural inequality in the workplace,

# people belonging to groups most affected by recent issues related to the “worker/job shortage”

# (e.g., low-wage workers) might be even more inclined to make structural attributions (e.g.,

# People of Color and lower wage workers) (Susik, 2021). Therefore, in addition to examining

# how the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs might lead to greater belief in gender-based

# mistreatment myths, I would like to understand how race, class, gender, and political identity

# together and individually might also contribute to differential endorsement of individualistic and

# structural attributions of gender-based mistreatment via the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs.

# Group-Based Stereotypes

# In addition to the ways the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs (that may differ based on an

# individual’s set of identities) might be intertwined with assumptions of individual control and

# resulting ideas of blame for other types of mistreatment, both the literature on neoliberalism and

# on gender-based mistreatment highlight the importance of group-based stereotypes in assessment

# of blame for gender-based mistreatment as well. This brings me to the final goal of this study: to

# 

# 20

# understand how neoliberal beliefs about individual control and personal responsibility might

# shape people’s perceptions of gender-based mistreatment regarding specific groups of women.

# While researchers have contributed greatly to understanding the tie between the macro-

# level ideology of neoliberalism and individual-level endorsements of neoliberalism and other

# beliefs, there has been little effort to understand how endorsement of neoliberal beliefs is related

# to group-based expectations and stereotypes. For instance, if neoliberal beliefs are an important

# predictor of rape myth acceptance, does this association hold true for all women? Or might this

# association be stronger for some women as a result of group-based stereotypes?

# As noted above, psychological researchers have generally provided evidence that when

# people make decisions about who deserves what, and in what contexts, they rely on individual

# characteristics and behavior (Lerner, 1980). These ideas are often linked to group-based

# stereotypes that attach certain characteristics and behavior, whether positive or negative, to

# certain groups of people (Crocker, et al., 1998; Goffman, 1963; Lerner, 1980; Feather, 1999;

# Feather, 2015; Reyna, et al., 2005). The literature on system justification and just world ideology

# (which we know are linked with the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs) specifically shows that

# people rely on stereotypes based on group membership to justify that group’s mistreatment

# (Lerner, 1980; Jost & Banaji, 1994).

# While any woman can experience gender-based mistreatment for any reason, lower-

# income women and Women of Color are disproportionately susceptible to experiences of sexual

# violence, and their experiences are less likely to be taken seriously compared to other women

# (Cortina, et al., 1998; Fessler, 2018; Foley, et al., 1995; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982; Kane, 2020;

# 

# 21

# LaFree, et al., 1985; MacKinnon, 1979; MCASA, n.d.). Further, research on gender-based

# mistreatment has documented ways in which group-based stereotypes that are seen to be

# controllable by the individual are used as justification for blame. In the literature on sexual

# assault, researchers have shown the importance of stereotypes related to both race and class in

# people’s level of blame attribution, with more blame attributed to poor women and Women of

# Color for the same experiences (Buchanan, et al., 2008; Donovan, 2007; Donovan & Williams,

# 2008; Dupuis & Clay, 2013; Foley, et al., 1995; George & Martínez, 2002; Gravelin, et al., 2019;

# Kane, 2020; LaFree, et al., 1985; Spencer, 2016).

# Respectability

# Researchers have demonstrated that lower-income women and Women of Color are more

# likely to be stereotyped in ways that coincide with characteristics that Americans use to justify

# these higher levels of blame toward women who have had these experiences. Specifically, these

# women are stereotyped as lacking in respectability. The concept of respectability stems

# originally from a strategy used by some Black U.S. and Caribbean individuals to maintain the

# perception that they were respectable individuals (that is, worthy of respect and consideration as

# full members of the community) despite negative assumptions and stereotypes rooted in systemic

# racism and colonialism (Crockett, 2017; Dazey, 2021). Perceptions of sexualization and

# conscientiousness have been shown to be linked with respectability; both are well-documented in

# the literature as central to people’s blame attribution for gender-based mistreatment as well

# (Feather, 2015; Harris, 2003; Heuer, et al., 2012; Mikula, 2003; Walker, et al., 2002). “To be

# seen as respectable is to be deserving of respect and having social value…” (Kiebler & Stewart,

# 

# 22

# 2023, p. 237). Therefore, to say someone is lacking in respectability would mean they are not

# deserving of respect based on assumptions of over-sexualization and lower conscientiousness

# (Skeggs, 1997).

# Stereotypes of Black Women. Stereotypes rooted in White supremacy and a history of

# enslavement and colonialism in the United States are still dominant in implicating the lives of

# Black women today (Collins, 1991; Jerald, et al., 2016; West, 2000). Stereotypes of

# hypersexuality (Jezebel stereotype) and aggressiveness (Sapphire stereotype) among Black

# women have long been juxtaposed to the expectations of White femininity (of women as docile,

# modest, and respectable), and have been used historically as validation for their enslavement,

# rape, and continued mistreatment (Anderson, et al., 2018; Collins, 1991; Collins, 2000;

# Rosenthal & Lobel, 2016).

# In the context of gender-based mistreatment, differential assumptions about respectability

# have been central in people’s attributions of blame toward Black women. Specifically, racism, a

# perceived lack of respectability, and hypersexualization (which is a facet of respectability) have

# all been documented as important predictors of people’s blame toward Black women in their

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment (Buchanan, et al., 2008; Donovan, 2007; Donovan &

# Williams, 2008; Dupuis & Clay, 2013; George & Martínez, 2002; Gravelin, et al., 2019).

# Stereotypes of Lower-Income Women. Although stereotypes about respectability have

# been a prominent issue contributing to higher levels of blame attribution of Black women for

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment, there are ways in which respectability surfaces as

# relevant to some groups of White women, if we also consider social class. While research to date

# 

# 23

# hasn’t explicitly named respectability as important in blame of White lower-income women,

# there are a few studies that point to its potential importance.

# In an experimental study, Spencer (2016) found that research participants were

# significantly more likely to blame low socioeconomic status (SES) women for experiences of

# sexual assault, and to perceive those women to be more promiscuous (presumably less

# respectable) compared to high-SES women. Further, Kiebler and Stewart (2022a) have shown

# that perceptions of a lack of respectability mediated the relationship between class and blame for

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment; lower-income women were blamed more than

# middle-class women across incidents of sexual assault, sexual harassment, and incivility. Kiebler

# & Stewart (2021b) also found that participants were more likely to pay attention to and comment

# on peripheral details of a woman’s life (e.g., her education and living situations) as opposed to

# her experience of sexual assault, if the woman was described as lower income rather than

# middle-class.

# Other studies have similarly confirmed that people are more likely to see lower-income

# women as less respectable (more sexualized and less responsible) than higher-income women

# (Bettie, 2000; Landrine, 1985; Lott & Saxon, 2002; Francombe-Webb & Silk, 2016). It is well

# documented in the literature on welfare that lower-income women (particularly lower-income

# Women of Color) are consistently portrayed as lacking in morals, over-sexualized and

# irresponsible, and these stereotypes have been used to justify slashing support and imposing

# more barriers to getting financial help (Brown- Iannuzzi, et al., 2017; Bullock, et al., 2001;

# 

# 24

# Clawson & Trice, 2000; Feagin, 1972; Hancock, 2004; Kelly, 2010; Masters, et al., 2014;

# Wilcox, et al., 1996).

# While strongly supporting the importance of considering stereotypes related to both race

# and class separately, the research outlined above has failed to consider the potential influence of

# overlapping systems of oppression that implicate the lives of these women who hold both

# marginalized raced and classed identities at once. Perceptions of race and class are often

# overlapping and conflated in the context of the U.S. and thus may influence people’s blame

# attribution in experiences of mistreatment. Specifically, people often assume that low-income

# women are Women of Color and Women of Color are low-income. Few studies have considered

# the significance of whether these group-based stereotypes are homogenously applied to all

# members of a group, and thus how they relate to blame. Neither have these studies contemplated

# the importance of individual beliefs about neoliberalism in accounting for blame.

# There has been little research on how both race and class matter to people’s perceptions

# of women’s mistreatment (Ghavami & Peplau, 2012). In U.S. culture, race and class are often

# conflated—with Whiteness assumed to be associated with middle-classness and Blackness

# assumed to be associated with working or lower-classness (Morales, 2014; Moss, 2003; Ostrove

# & Cole, 2003; Yuval-Davis, 2006). In addition, the current body of research has failed to

# consider within-group differences among lower-income and Black women, treating them as one

# homogenous group with equal experiences, often by comparing them to other dominant groups

# of women (e.g., Black to White women, poor to middle-class/rich women). Therefore, in the

# current study we aim to assess how perceptions of lower-income Black and White women--

# 

# 25

# based on the overlapping systems of oppression (classism, sexism, and racism) -- might lead to

# differential assessments of their mistreatment, and also and considering the importance of

# neoliberal beliefs in applications of stereotypes.

# Stereotypes of the “undeserving” poor. To extend the literature that provides support

# for the idea that neoliberal beliefs are central to people’s endorsement of rape myth acceptance,

# this study seeks to understand if these myths might influence blame more readily for certain

# groups of women. Further, while Black and lower-income women are more likely to experience

# sexual violence, they are often left out of psychological research or treated as homogenous

# groups to be compared to other dominant groups of people. Instead, I will assess how lower-

# income Black and White women are described in ways consistent with the “deserving” and

# “undeserving” poor might complicate our understanding. While the “deserving” poor are seen as

# being hard-working and responsible, the “undeserving” poor are stereotyped as being

# irresponsible, lazy, and hyper-sexual (hyper-fertile) (Allison, 1994; Feagin, 1972; Hartigan,

# 1997; Oorschot, 2000; Will, 1993). While these notions are related conceptually to respectability

# (so important in racist stereotypes), a distinct logic has developed to categorize some poor people

# (regardless of race) as virtuous and worthy of positive treatment and helpful policies, and others

# as not deserving of sympathy or assistance.

# Although race is often conflated with class in the context of the United States, with

# People of Color assumed to be poor and White people assumed not to be, we know that People

# of Color have actually been historically, and are currently, overrepresented in poverty because of

# continued racist policies and practices of oppression dating back to slavery (Dunbar, 1997; Moss,

# 

# 26

# 2003; McIntosh, et al., 2020). Further, in the literature that documents characteristics of the poor,

# these notions of deservingness are raced in a way that serves to maintain the economic

# exploitation and deprivation among People of Color via these stereotypes. Specifically, those

# generally depicted as members of the undeserving poor are People of Color or White individuals

# who belong to subgroups marked explicitly by their race in ways that signal their peripheral

# relationship to Whiteness as a dominant group (e.g., “White trash,” “hillbillies”) (Bérubé &

# Bérubé, 1997; Crockett, 2017; Hartigan, 1997). The construction of poor White people as not

# fully White is in line with Liu and colleagues’ (2011) concept of downward classism in their

# Modern Classism Theory, which suggests that individuals with higher perceived status are

# discriminatory towards those “below” them as a strategy to ensure their own economic needs are

# met (Liu, et al., 2011).

# Group-Based Motivations for Blame

# The way that people’s perceptions of individual control are influenced by group-based

# stereotypes is also relevant in people’s judgments of how deserving someone is of a particular

# outcome (Crocker, et al., 1998; Williams, 2009). Further, this has been shown to be true in the

# context of deserving one’s economic position in the world. People who are more likely to make

# structural attributions for poverty are also more likely to support policy that aids the poor, and

# those who are more likely to make individual attributions for poverty are more likely to see the

# poor as deserving their position in the world (Bullock & Lott, 2010b; Bullock, et al., 2003;

# Feagin, 1972; Weiner, 1995; Williams, 2009). Researchers have also documented that people

# making judgments about others often fall back on group-based stereotypes when assessing their

# 

# 27

# deservingness even in the context of human rights violations (Brown-Iannuzzi, et al., 2017;

# DeSante, 2013; Drolet, et al., 2016; Ellis & Faricy, 2019; Hancock, 2004; Hansen, 2019; Limbert

# & Bullock, 2005; Reyna, 2005; Staerklé & Clémence, 2004).

# Therefore, when considering the role of neoliberal beliefs in people’s perceptions of

# mistreatment toward certain groups of women, we can see how the key roles of beliefs about

# personal responsibility and individual control, and stereotypes about the respectability of women

# in these groups might lead us to similar findings as those documented for rape myth acceptance.

# Stereotypes have been shown to be a key link between perceptions of individual control and

# justification for their exploitation (Feagin, 1972; Jost, et al., 2015).

# Study 1

# Hypotheses

# Hypothesis 1a. I expect that participant endorsement of various social beliefs is

# associated with different levels of support for neoliberal beliefs. Consistent with previous

# research, participants who score higher on endorsement of racism, sexism, and belief in a just

# world will be significantly more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs (Bay-Cheng, 2015; Son

# Hing, et al., 2013). Further, participants who score higher on measures of economic system

# justification, and classism will also be significantly more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs.

# Hypothesis 1b. Although the literature on structural attributions is somewhat contested,

# given the current political climate and increased emphasis on structural inequality, I predict that

# the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs may be different for different groups defined by race, class,

# gender, and political identification. Specifically, I expect racially Black-identifying participants,

# Method

# Participants were recruited through Amazon’s Turk Prime Panels platform. Using Turk

# Prime Panels allowed me to stratify the sample by race to ensure adequate size of all groups.

# Ensuring this sample representation allowed us to look at important potential participant

# differences based on race in endorsement of neoliberal beliefs. Some research suggests that paid

# convenience samples from MTurk are as representative of results gathered from “high-quality

# commercial samples,” but I used additional strategies to ensure quality data which are outlined

# below (Thomas & Clifford, 2017). I conducted this first study to assess the relationship between

# various social attitudes and neoliberal beliefs, the role of participant identities in shaping

# endorsement of neoliberal beliefs, and the relationship between neoliberal beliefs and gender-

# based mistreatment myth acceptance.

# Sample. The sample consisted of 426 adults 18 years of age and older who currently

# reside in the United States. In addition to these restrictions, using Turk Prime Panels, I recruited

# equal numbers of Black- and White-identifying participants in order to test group-based

# differences on our outcome variable (Chandler, et al., 2019). Based on previous research that

# supports group-based differences in my primary measures, it is important to sample enough

# people from these groups (especially from sample sources that are usually highly skewed as

# White) to allow for these group-based analyses. Participants saw all measures in the survey.

# 

# 30

# Prior to collecting data, I used G\*Power to identify an adequate sample size to detect

# effects in my planned analyses. To detect a relatively small effect size (0.14 or larger) using a

# power of 0.80, I needed to collect data from at least 400 participants (Cohen, 1988; Erdfelder, et

# al., 1996). Because small effect sizes generally range from 0.10 - 0.25, collecting data from 400

# participants was predicted to allow me to detect a small effect well within this range.

# Participants. Participants were all asked to respond to a series of 12 demographic

# questions at the end of the survey related to gender, age, education, race/ethnicity, sexuality,

# socioeconomic resources currently and growing up, income currently and growing up, class

# identity, marital status, and political party identity.

# Participants averaged about 48 years old. In terms of gender identity, participants most

# frequently reported identifying as women (53.3%; N=227) followed by men (45.1%; N=192) and

# gender non-conforming, gender fluid, and/or gender variant (1.6%; N=7). High school graduate

# represented the most frequently reported highest education of participants (29.9%; N=127),

# followed by some college but no degree (21.2%; N=90), a bachelor’s degree (19.3%; N=82), an

# associate’s degree (10.1%; N=43), a master’s degree (8.0%; N=34), some high school but no

# diploma (5.2%; N=22), trade/technical/vocational training (4.5%; N=19), a PhD/law/medical

# degree (1.6%; N=7), and no school completed (0.2%; N=1). White-identifying participants

# comprised nearly half of the sample (48.4%; N=206) followed by Black/African American

# participants (47.2%; N=201), and multiracial/multiethnic participants that were not coded as

# White or Black/African American (4.5%; N=19). Most participants identified as heterosexual

# (89.9%; N=383) followed by bisexual (3.1%; N=13), lesbian (2.1%; N=9), gay (1.6%; N=7),

# 

# 31

# none of these categories (1.2%; N=5), pansexual (0.7%; N=3), asexual (0.7%; N=3), and bisexual

# and pansexual (0.2%; N=1). Most frequently, participants reported being married or in a

# domestic partnership (40.3%; N=170) compared to being single and never married (39.3%,

# N=166), divorced (10.6%; N=45), widowed (6.2%; N=26), and separated (3.6%; N=15).

# When asked about their socioeconomic status growing up, participants most frequently

# reported that they had enough to get by but no extras (43.4%; N=184), followed by more than

# enough to get by (22.9%; N=97), barely enough to get by (16.3%; N=69), very poor without

# enough to get by (7.5%; N=32), well off (7.3%; N=31), and very wealthy (2.6%; N=11).

# Participants also most frequently reported having enough to get by but no extras (43.2%; N=183)

# when asked about their current economic status. This was followed by more than enough to get

# by (22.2%; N=94), barely enough to get by (15.8%; N=67), very poor without enough to get by

# (8.7%; N=37), well off (8.0%; N=34), and very wealthy (2.1%, N=9).

# Growing up, participants most frequently reported their families earning yearly incomes

# of less than $15,000 (28.4%; N=119) followed by $25,001-$35,000 (16.9%; N=71), $35,001-

# $50,000 (15.0%; N=63), $50,001-$75,000 (14.8%; N=62), $15,001-$25,000 (13.8%; N=58),

# $75,001-$100,000 (5.3%; N=22), $100,001-$150,000 (3.1%; N=13), and more than $150,000

# (2.6%; N=11). For current income, participants most frequently reported earning yearly incomes

# of $50,001-$75,000 (18.2%; N=77), followed by less than $15,000 (17.7%; N=75), $25,001-

# $35,000 (15.3%; N=65), $35,001-$50,000 (14.9%; N=63), $15,001-$25,000 (13.2%; N=56),

# $75,001-$100,000 (10.1%; N=43), $100,001-$150,000 (6.8%; N=29), and more than $150,000

# (3.8%; N=16).

# *Measures*

# In the first study, participants were asked to respond to a series of scales assessing

# neoliberal belief endorsement, attitudes about various social issues, and then finally about sexual

# 

# 35

# assault, sexual harassment, and incivility myth acceptance scales. Some alphas of scales in the

# current study differed from the original published scales likely due to differences in the samples.

# Neoliberal beliefs. To measure neoliberal beliefs participants were be asked to respond

# to Bay-Cheng, Alizaga, & Zucker’s (2015) 26-item Neoliberal Beliefs Scale. This scale includes

# 4 subscales including, system inequality (e.g., “I think people imagine more barriers, such as

# discrimination, than actually exist”), competition (e.g., “People should be allowed to compete to

# ensure that the best person wins”), personal wherewithal (e.g., “Anyone who is willing to work

# hard can be successful in America”), and government interference (e.g., “A problem with

# government social programs is that they get in the way of personal freedom”). All items were

# presented on a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” with a

# “neither agree nor disagree” item in the middle. In the development of this scale, it has

# demonstrated high internal consistency (a = .91-.95 across 4 studies). In the current study, the

# reliability for this scale was high, a = .90. I treated this as one scale without assessing sub-scale

# differences. See Appendix B for more details.

# Sexism. Attitudes about sexism were assessed using the 15-item Ambivalent Sexism

# Inventory by Glick & Fiske (1996). An example of these items is “Women seek special favors

# under guise of equality.” All items were presented on a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from

# “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” with a “neither agree nor disagree” item in the middle.

# Research on the development of this scale has reflected high reliability (a = .83-.92 across 6

# studies). In the current study, reliability was a = .81. See Appendix C for more details.

# 

# 36

# Racism. Racist attitudes were assessed using the 8-item, Symbolic Racism 2000 Scale

# (Henry & Sears, 2002). An example of these items is “Over the past few years, Black people

# have gotten more economically than they deserve.” In this version, all items were presented on a

# 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” with a “neither agree

# nor disagree” item in the middle. Reliability for this scale ranges from a = .60-.85 depending on

# the racial demographics of the participant answering. The reliability in the current study was a =

# .67. See Appendix D for more details.

# Classism. Participant perspectives on attributions for poverty (or classism) were assessed

# using Bullock’s (1999) 16-item Revised Attributions for Poverty Questionnaire (originally based

# on Furnham, 1985) (a = .84). In the current study, the reliability was a = .69. An example of

# these items is “Poverty is caused by lack of motivation and laziness among the poor.” All items

# were asked on a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” with a

# “neither agree nor disagree” item in the middle. See Appendix E for more details.

# Economic system justification. Perceptions of the current economic system in the U.S.

# were assessed using the 17-item Economic System Justification Scale by Jost & Thompson

# (2000) presented on a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”

# with a “neither agree nor disagree” item in the middle. An example of these items is “There will

# always be poor people, because there will never be enough jobs for everybody.” Reliability for

# this scale in its original use was a = .73. In the current study, reliability was a little lower a = .66

# than in previous studies. See Appendix F for more details.

# 

# 37

# Belief in a just world. Participants were asked to respond to 8 items that assess their

# beliefs in a just world using the Just World Ideology Scale (Lucas, et al., 2007). An example of

# these items is “I feel that people generally earn the rewards and punishments that they get in this

# world.” Reliability for this scale ranged from .88-.92 across subscales. In the current study,

# reliability was a = .69. I treated this as one scale without assessing sub-scale differences. All

# items were asked on a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree”

# with a “neither agree nor disagree” item in the middle. See Appendix G for more details.

# Gender-based mistreatment myth endorsement. To assess myth endorsement for

# sexual assault, sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility, participants were asked to

# respond to a series of parallel items from three scales assessing these beliefs. Participants were

# asked to respond to the 20-item, short-form version of the Illinois Rape Myth Acceptance Scale

# which had high reliability (a = .92) (e.g., “If a woman is willing to ‘‘make out’’ with a guy, then

# it’s no big deal if he goes a little further and has sex”), and the 20-item Illinois Sexual

# Harassment Acceptance Scale (a = .94) (e.g., “If a woman is sexually harassed, she must have

# done something to invite it") (Lonsway, et al., 2008; Payne, et al., 1999). Gender-based incivility

# myths were assessed using newly created 36 items based on those from the Sexual Harassment

# Myth Acceptance Scale and from expert input. An example of these items is “Women who claim

# to be treated in condescending ways at work are often being dramatic”. All items were asked on

# a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” with a “neither agree

# nor disagree” item in the middle. Reliability for this new scale was a = .77. See Appendices H-J

# for more details.

# 

# 38

# To test the validity of the newly created gender-based incivility myth scale, I submitted

# the 36 items to an exploratory (principal components, PCA) factor analysis. With the goal of data

# reduction, I used varimax rotation. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin Measure of Sampling Adequacy

# was sufficient (.920) with measures above .70 being considered adequate. Bartlett’s Test of

# Sphericity was also considered sufficient (it was significant; p < .001). Results produced

# communalities that ranged from 0.50– 0.75. Following Hinkin’s (1998) suggestion of retaining

# items at or above the .40 criterion level, we were able to retain all 36 items in our measure. The

# initial analysis yielded an eight-factor solution explaining a total of 63.6% of the total variance.

# Following the first factor, each subsequent factor only explained less than 10% of the variance.

# Given the goal of data reduction in the creation of our scale and in creating clear factors to retain

# with the strongest loading items that are reflective of incivility theory used in creating our items,

# we then proceeded to reduce the number of factors in our scale. To do so, we compared all

# possible factor solutions in order to decide best fit based on representativeness of the components

# of incivility determined when creating initial items (denial and justification of rude behavior,

# condescension, ostracization, and gender-harassment) (Cortina, 2008; Cortina, et al., 2013;

# Cortina, et al., 2017). We used Hinkin’s (1998) recommendation to retain items that load about

# twice as strong on one factor compared to all others to choose items to retain. There was one

# instance in which an item loaded slightly less than twice as strong on the chosen factor compared

# to all others. We ended up with three potential factors. Please see Table 2 for more details on

# these factor loadings and Figure 2 for details on the initial scree plot. However, because again,

# our goal was data reduction and creating a parsimonious, unidimensional scale, we conducted

# 

# 39

# bivariate correlations between the three potential factors and also conducted scale reliability by

# calculating Cronbach’s alpha. These findings indicated that the three subfactors were somewhat

# distinct and not highly and consistently correlated (any factors that were significantly correlated

# had a Pearson Correlation Coefficient of less than .3) and that two of the three potential factors

# did not statistically hang together in a sufficiently reliable way (factor two, a = .331; factor three,

# a = -.255). This left us with one factor explaining a majority of the variance, that had clear

# theoretical cohesion, and were representative of the above components we thought integral to

# incivility experiences.

# Following the recommendations above, from the initial PCA, we removed 27 items and

# were left with 9. We reran the PCA with varimax rotation on the remaining 16 items. The

# Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin Measure of Sampling Adequacy was again sufficient (.935) and Bartlett’s

# Test of Sphericity was also considered sufficient (it was significant; p < .001). Results produced

# communalities that ranged from 0.475– 0.690. Following Hinkin’s (1998) suggestion of retaining

# items at or above the .40 criterion level, we were able to retain all 9 of the remaining items. This

# second analysis yielded a one-factor solution explaining a total of 62.8% of the total variance.

# The reliability for this scale was strong (a = .925). This reduced scale was used in all subsequent

# analyses assessing gender-based incivility myth acceptance.

# Demographic Variables. Among the participant demographic variables used in the

# primary analyses for this study include gender, race, political identity, and social class. Please

# see Appendix K for full question details.

# Participants were asked to respond to the following about gender question: “Which of the

# following best describes your gender identity?” Response options included: woman, man,

# gender-nonconforming, gender fluid, gender queer, gender variant, agender, bigender, or none

# of these categories describe me with a fill-in option. Based on the small number of individuals

# with certain gender identities in our sample, participant gender responses that were coded outside

# of the “man” or “woman” categories were re-coded as missing (N=5). For our analyses, women

# were coded as zero and men as one.

# 

# 45

# Regarding racial and ethnic identity, participants were asked to respond to the question:

# “Which of the following racial/ethnic categories describes you the best?” Response options

# included: Asian/Asian American/Pacific Islander, Black/African American, Hispanic/Latinx,

# Middle Eastern, Native American/American Indian, White, Multiracial/Multiethnic with a fill-in

# option, and none of these categories describe me with a fill-in option. Participant responses were

# recoded to fit into the binary variable of either White or Black/African American. Those who

# selected racial/ethnic identities that fit neither of these categories were recoded as missing

# (N=14). Since participants were able to select more than one identity response, those who

# selected Black/African American, and any other identity were recoded as just Black/African

# American for the purposes of the current study’s analyses (N=9). There was never a case where a

# participant identified as both White and Black/African American in the current data set.

# Participants who identified as White and another racial/ethnic identity were recoded as missing

# (N=9).

# For participant political identity, we asked the question: “If you could select one political

# party that best represents your political views, which would it be?” Response options included:

# Democratic Party, Republican Party, Constitution Party, Libertarian Party, Green Party, Tea

# Party, Independent, or other with a fill-in option. To create a binary variable to include in my

# regression analysis, Democratic-identifying participants were coded as zero; participants who

# identified as Republican, Constitution, or Tea Party members were coded as 1, to represent those

# politically more conservative participants. Libertarian, and Independent members were coded as

# missing (N=96). No participants identified as members of the Green Party.

# 

# 46

# Participant social class identity was measured across 5 variables assessing current income

# and resources, income and resources growing up, and class identity. We asked participants about

# their income in two questions: (1) “What is your current yearly household income?” and (2) “To

# the best of your knowledge, what was your family's yearly household income when you were

# growing up?” Response options included: less than 15k, $15,001-25k, $25,001-35k, $35,001-

# 50k, $50,001-75k, $75,001-100k, or $100,001-150k, $150k+. We also asked two questions about

# their resources: (1) “How would you describe your current economic resources?” and (2) “How

# would you describe your economic resources when you were growing up?” Response options

# included: very poor; not enough to get by; barely had [have] enough to get by; had [have]

# enough to get by, but no extras; had [have] more than enough to get by; well off; very wealthy;

# or prefer not to answer (coded as missing). Finally, we asked participants to identify their own

# social class standing: “How would you describe your social class?” Possible response options

# included: working-class, lower middle-class, middle-class, upper middle-class, upper-class, or

# other with a fill-in option.

# Given that social class is a complex concept to measure and the documented

# shortcomings of individual items meant to capture social class that really only capture one

# component in a mosaic that makes up one’s class position, from these variables, I created a

# composite participant class identity variable combining the 5 variables assessing social class

# (Diemer, et al., 2012). I created this composite variable by first creating a z-score for each

# variable. Creating z-scores for each variable allows us to combine variables that were measured

# in different ways (e.g., social class identity included options like “working-class” and our income

# 

# 47

# variables included options like $35,001-$50k) to create one variable that spans all five of our

# class indicators from the survey. Next, I was able to add the variable scores together for each

# participant and divide by five (which was the total number of z-scored class-related variables) to

# get individual class composite scores for each participant. Higher scores on the newly created

# class composite variable indicated higher resourced class positions.

# Results

# Preliminary Analyses. Following the collection of the data, I ran a few preliminary

# analyses to ensure quality and complete data. First, I tested the completion and accuracy of three

# attention checks that were placed at three different locations throughout the survey. I planned to

# drop participant responses from our final analyses if they did not complete all three attention

# checks and if any one or more were answered incorrectly. No participants were dropped due to

# failure of attention checks. Additionally, I assessed participant response homogeneity by

# conducting a string analysis in Excel on each of the scales in the survey. This allowed me to

# determine whether participants responded to all scale items in the same way (which would be

# unlikely in scales where there are reverse-coded items). No participants were dropped for

# homogeneous data responses because none had consistently homogeneous responses to a given

# scale or across multiple scales.

# Additionally, I computed bivariate correlations among all primary variables included in

# our analyses to assess the intercorrelation among each pair of measures. All variables (economic

# system justification, just world beliefs, sexism, classism, neoliberal beliefs, sexual assault myths,

# sexual harassment myths, and gender-based incivility myths) were positively and significantly

# 

# 48

# correlated with one another, p < .001. Most correlations between variables had a weak to

# moderate strength relation with one another (a Pearson’s correlation coefficient, or R-value of 0

# to -/+ 0.6) (Akoglu, 2018). Sexual harassment myth acceptance and sexual assault myth

# acceptance were the only variables that had a strong intercorrelation (0.77). Considering these

# preliminary findings that economic system justification, belief in a just world, sexism, classism,

# and neoliberal beliefs were weakly or moderately correlated, it seemed statistically appropriate to

# include these variables in one regression to assess our first hypothesis. Secondly, while sexual

# assault and sexual harassment myths were moderately strongly correlated, all myth variables

# were weakly correlated with neoliberal beliefs and therefore it seemed statistically appropriate to

# include each of the myths in a separate regression where neoliberal beliefs were expected to

# predict their endorsement in our third hypothesis.
