# Discussion

# Summary. This first study demonstrated the importance of neoliberal beliefs in people’s

# perceptions of women’s experiences of sexual harassment and gender-based incivility, while also

# confirming their centrality in people’s perceptions of women’s sexual assault where higher

# gender-based mistreatment myth acceptance in all instances was associated with higher

# neoliberal belief endorsement. Importantly, the results also supported the prediction that higher

# classist beliefs and economic system justification endorsement are associated with higher

# neoliberal belief endorsement. This replicates previous research showing that higher

# endorsements of racism and belief in a just world predict higher endorsement of neoliberal

# beliefs. Finally, the current study revealed the significance of participant identity in the

# endorsement of neoliberal beliefs.

# Detailed Discussion. In testing the first hypothesis, I expected, based on the research by

# Bay-Cheng and colleagues (2015) that participant beliefs about sexism, racism, and just world

# ideology would be important to their level of neoliberal belief endorsement. Additionally, I

# predicted that beliefs about classism and economic system justification would also be associated

# with their endorsement of neoliberal beliefs. Supporting this hypothesis, I found that participants

# 

# 55

# who endorsed sexism, racism, belief in a just world, classism, and economic system justification

# at higher levels were also significantly more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs. This is

# consistent with the neoliberal ideology that Wendy Brown discusses, according to which

# neoliberalism is concerned with more than economic policies and practices but rather extends to

# all realms of relations among individuals (Brown, 2003). Specifically, Brown states:

# “…neo-liberalism is not simply a set of economic policies; it is not only about facilitating

# free trade, maximizing corporate profits, and challenging welfarism. Rather, neo-

# liberalism carries a social analysis which, when deployed as a form of governmentality,

# reaches from the soul of the citizen-subject to education policy to practices of empire.

# Neo-liberal rationality, while foregrounding the market, is not only or even primarily

# focused on the economy; rather it involved extending and disseminating market values to

# all institutions and social action, even as the market itself remains a distinctive player”

# (Brown, 2003, p. 4).

# Every aspect of the human condition, emotion, and relationality under neoliberalism is

# reconfigured in terms of “market rationality” in which “neoliberalism produces rational actors

# and imposes market rationale for decision-making in all spheres” (Bettache & Chiu, 2019;

# Brown, 2003, p. 5; Teo, 2018). We see this clearly in this set of results where there is a

# relationship between neoliberal beliefs and other individual-level beliefs about fairness, equality,

# opportunity based on race and class.

# Further, as neoliberal theorists discuss, while neoliberal ideology generally includes the

# belief that systemic-level forms of oppression (e.g., sexism, racism, classism, and more) don’t

# 

# 56

# exist, we see in the current study that in fact those “rational actors” (e.g., individuals who

# endorse neoliberal beliefs at high rates) that are produced from neoliberal practices and policies

# are more likely to endorse beliefs that directly reinforce classist and racist ideas about the world

# and other people (Brown, 2003; Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey, 2005). They are also more

# likely to believe the world is a just and fair place, thus reinforcing the idea of meritocracy and

# the importance of competition in being successful. Combining ideas that we exist in a society

# where racism, sexism, classism and other systemic-level forms of privilege and oppression don’t

# exist helps support the reproduction of classist and racist stereotypes that justify the continued

# exploitation and oppression of these groups (Bullock & Lott, 2010a; Bullock, et al., 2008; Bay-

# Cheng, et al., 2015; Becker, et al., 2021; Collins, 2000; Goudarzi, et al., 2020; Lott & Bullock,

# 2001).

# Those who support neoliberal beliefs are deeply invested in ideas of individual-level

# control and freedom, with people envisioned to be successful (or not) as a result of their own

# work and effort and with government interference in this normal process discouraged (Bay-

# Cheng, at al., 2015; Harvey, 2005). However, findings from the current study show the central

# role that beliefs that help perpetuate group-based inequality (e.g., racism, classism, belief in a

# just world, and economic system justification) are associated with endorsement of neoliberal

# beliefs. Thus, despite the attractive claims of equal opportunity and the warnings of government

# interference that neoliberal thinkers espouse, they often perpetuate stereotypes that help maintain

# structural inequality based on racist and classist beliefs. Further, belief in a just world and

# economic system justification --two beliefs closely tied to neoliberalism-- help perpetuate

# 

# 57

# ignorance of the ways in which structural-level systems contribute to the continued exploitation

# of these same groups.

# Hypothesis 1b. Given our commitment to considering the ways that power and privilege

# affect how and what people experience, how they are treated, and how they interpret the world

# around them, we included an analysis exploring the likelihood of endorsing neoliberal beliefs

# based on our measurement of various participant identities. It is crucial to further emphasize that

# often analyses that claim the use of intersectionality lack a fully intersectional approach,

# including a discussion of the ways in which structural-level systems of power and privilege

# based on historical and contemporary political, economic, and colonial policies and practices

# operate in the lived experiences of individuals (Crenshaw, 1991; Crenshaw, 1989; Cho, et al.,

# 2013; Cole, 2009; Davis, 2006; Moradi & Grzanka, 2017; Warner, et al., 2016). Therefore, while

# a quantitative analysis challenges our ability to attend to these important considerations that

# intersectionality points to, it is essential that the context in which we discuss our findings based

# on “identity” does not stop with noting them, but rather contends with structural influences by

# asking the question: “what role does inequality play” in these differences? (Cole, 2009 p. 173).

# Thus, it is important to ask why differences in findings based on identity exist. Intersectionality

# theory compels us to emphasize the context in which differences transpire and to challenge the

# very structures that work to replicate inequality.

# The current study extends the literature on neoliberal beliefs to demonstrate the

# importance of participant identity in these endorsements. We tested differences in participant

# identity based on gender, race, political identity, social class, and each of their interactions.

# 

# 58

# Specifically, men, more conservative, more conservative White, and higher-class White

# participants were more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs. However, the results showed no

# statistically significant differences in the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs by social class or race

# alone, or in any of the other interactions tested.

# As mentioned in detail above, the importance of these differences is not clear without a

# focus on why they exist. While we predicted, based on previous research showing mixed findings

# for structural attributions, that lower-income individuals might be less likely to endorse these

# beliefs based on general devaluation in society and the current emphasis on structural inequality

# in workplace compensation as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic, social class alone was not a

# sole predictor (Bullock, 1999; Feagin, 1972; Young, 2004). Instead, within class, relationships to

# power and privilege based on racial identity appear to create more nuanced associations with

# neoliberal belief endorsement (as we found in the interaction between class and race). The

# current study only provided a first glance at the ways in which class is important to neoliberal

# beliefs. Given that there are many more nuanced stereotypes about the poor based on other

# relations to power, looking at social class alone as a predictor of neoliberal beliefs is not enough.

# Further, since neoliberal beliefs bring ideas about who deserves what into view, future

# researchers might more closely focus on ideas about deservingness based on within- class

# stereotypes (e.g., ideas about the “deserving” and “underserving” poor) in order to understand

# how the subtleties of class in relation to other forms of privilege and power might influence

# one’s endorsement of neoliberal ideology (Allison, 1994; Hartigan, 1997; Oorschot, 2000;

# Streinzer & Tošić, 2022; Tihelková, 2015; Will, 1993; Zatz, 2012).

# 

# 59

# As discussed in relation to findings from hypothesis 1a, despite neoliberalism’s central

# claim of a commitment to equality, those who were most likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs

# were also most likely to endorse racist, classist, economic system justifying, and just world

# ideology. In hypothesis 1b, we found that some groups who have been historically and presently

# more privileged (e.g., men, higher-class White participants) were more likely to endorse

# neoliberal beliefs that continue to ignore structural-level, group-based inequality central to

# experiences and mistreatment These beliefs are being perpetuated by those with more power in

# the U.S., thus giving credence to beliefs that ignore the reproduction of harm as a result of

# classist, racist, colonialist (…) practices and policies (Applebaum, 2008). While these

# individuals may not all directly benefit from the perpetuation of these ideas (e.g., low-income

# White individuals within the category of White found here), it is important for future researchers

# to examine potential complexities within these groups to gain a deeper understanding of how

# neoliberal beliefs are being taken up by people with various relations to power and privilege

# Hypothesis 1c. For our final hypothesis, I tested the relationship between neoliberal

# beliefs and myths about sexual assault, sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility. Previous

# research demonstrated the link between neoliberal beliefs and rape myth acceptance (Bay-Cheng,

# et al., 2015). Likewise, I found again that people who were more likely to endorse neoliberal

# beliefs were also significantly more likely to hold myths about sexual assault. Extending this

# literature, I additionally found that higher endorsement of neoliberal beliefs was also

# significantly related to higher endorsement of sexual harassment and gender-based incivility

# myth acceptance.

# 

# 60

# In the literature on sexual assault, sexual harassment, and incivility, aspects of a woman’s

# character and behavior have been shown to influence how people interpret their mistreatment

# and violence (Bernard, et al., 2018; Buchanan, et al., 2008; Cortina, 2008; Cortina, et al., 2013;

# Donovan, 2007; Dupuis & Clay, 2013; Ferguson, et al., 2005; Fitzgerald, et al., 1995; Foley, et

# al., 1995; George & Martínez, 2002; Gravelin, et al., 2019; Kane, 2020; Kiebler & Stewart,

# 2022a; Klein, et al., 2010; Koss, 1995; LaFree, et al., 1985; Lucarini, et al., 2020; Luginbuhl &

# Mullin, 1981; Marin & Guadagno, 1999; Pollard, 1992; Ryan, 1976; Spencer, 2016; Stormo, et

# al., 1997; Workman & Freeberg, 1999). In addition to the large literature on individual aspects of

# blame in gender-based mistreatment, sexual assault, harassment, and incivility, researchers have

# documented that those who are more likely to believe that the world is just are also more likely

# to blame individuals, report experiences less, and justify experiences of sexual assault, sexual

# harassment and in some instances, incivility (De Judicibus & McCabe, 2001; Dorit & Itzkovich,

# 2015; Kleinke & Meyer, 1990; Stömwall, et al. 2013). This line of research is crucial to

# psychological inquiry in people’s perceptions of women’s mistreatment because it creates a

# bridge between individuals and societal-level ideas about the world. It is not only beliefs about

# individual women actors that influence people’s beliefs about their mistreatment, but rather those

# beliefs are linked to a person’s broader ideas about our world that appear, on the surface, to have

# nothing to do with a given situation of gender-based mistreatment being judged. Further, it is

# likely that broader societal-level beliefs, like whether one sees the world as just, influence the

# ways that individuals rationalize individual-level experience to align with their schema of the

# world (Kelley & Michela, 1980).

# 

# 61

# While individuals believing the world is just might lead them to believe women get what

# they deserve, these findings don’t quite help us understand why individuals believe the world is

# just in the first place, and why then that belief might influence people’s perceptions of women’s

# mistreatment. In the current study, neoliberal beliefs seem to be central to people’s endorsement

# that the world is a just and rational place. The current study notably replicated the connection

# between just world beliefs and neoliberal beliefs (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015). Additionally, I found

# a relation between neoliberal beliefs and perceptions of three different types of gender-based

# mistreatment, while also showing how the perceiver’s positionality and relationship to privilege

# and power is important in shaping their likelihood of endorsing neoliberal beliefs that fuel a

# negative view of women’s experiences of mistreatment.

# As discussed in the introduction, Angela Davis made the evocative statement that

# capitalism, which is inherently fueled and built upon racist and classist ideology, is an integral

# driving force perpetuating the continuation of women’s sexual assault (Davis, 1981). This

# specific discussion of the entwined nature of capitalism and the devouring of life and labor and

# bodies at the primary expense of People of Color is what moved me to the questions posed in this

# dissertation. The accumulation and pooling of wealth through capitalist, neoliberal means among

# White, upper-class men in the U.S. has been a process supported by institutionalized racism

# through which the accumulation of all things not previously measured in economic domains

# becomes available to these men for possession (Brown, 2003; Davis, 1981).

# From this first study, we can see some of the key elements at work in generating

# women’s gender-based mistreatment experiences, and how they reflect the claims expressed by

# 

# 62

# Davis (1981) and Brown (2003). First, Wendy Brown suggests that neoliberal ideology produces

# “rational actors” who see all experience through a neoliberal lens. As a reminder, this is not an

# accidental outcome of neoliberal economic policies and practices but rather is an integral and

# strategic move by those pushing for and benefiting from a neoliberal world (Brown, 2003). In

# reframing all human interaction, emotion, and relationality as “a calculus of utility, benefit, or

# satisfaction against a micro-economic grid of scarcity, supply and demand, and moral value-

# neutrality” every human experience is reconfigured into economic rationality (Brown, 2003, p.

# 5). With this reconfiguration and in championing competition and meritocracy as core aspects of

# success, while denying the existence of systemic oppression, neoliberal ideology works to the

# benefit of a capitalist regime. Brown (2003) emphasizes,

# “If Marcuse worried about the loss of a dialectical opposition within capitalism when ‘it

# delivers goods,’ that is, when by mid-twentieth century, a relatively complacent middle

# class had taken the place of the hard-laboring impoverished masses Marx depicted as the

# negating contradiction to the concentrated wealth of capital, neo-liberalism entails the

# erosion of oppositional political, moral, or subjective claims located outside capitalist

# rationality but inside liberal democratic society, that is, the erosion of institutions, venues,

# and values organized by non-market rationalities in democracies” (Brown, 2003, p. 10).

# With this in mind, results from the current study highlight one way in which human experience

# of violence and mistreatment is reconfigured through a neoliberal and capitalist lens. While it

# might appear that capitalism and neoliberalism have almost nothing to do with attitudes toward

# gender-based mistreatment, this study supports a relation between these beliefs. Specifically,

# 

# 63

# individuals who espoused neoliberal beliefs at higher rates were significantly more likely to

# support rape myths, sexual harassment myths, and gender-based incivility myths in women’s

# experiences of violence and mistreatment. Women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment,

# understood through a neoliberal frame, are critiqued and analyzed in which people weigh the

# value and truth of women’s actions. Violence is assessed rather than abhorred through neoliberal

# framing.

# Secondly, Brown (2003) claims that neoliberalism reconfigures every aspect of our world

# into neoliberal terms of capitalist value and the clear connection we see in the current study

# between the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs and gender-based mistreatment myth acceptance.

# Thus, capitalism is central to the continuation of violence against women. As Angela Davis

# (1981) claims “[a]s the violent face of sexism, the threat of rape will exist as long as capitalist

# society survives” (Davis, 1981, p. 45).

# More specifically, this economic and interpersonal violence and exploitation has deep

# roots in the history of slavery in the U.S., as well as in the reproduction of the economic

# exploitation of Black people and other People of Color at the benefit of colonizers and their

# legacies. As Davis discussed, rape laws were first introduced to protect people in the upper-class

# and were not concerned with what happened to Black women (Davis, 1981). Rather, those of the

# upper classes, while their women were protected by such laws, under “one of the salient

# historical features of racism… the assumption that White men—…those who are economically

# powerful—possess an incontestable right of access to black women’s bodies” was and remains

# 

# 64

# prominent (Davis, 1981, p. 40). During the Reconstruction era, new modes of maintaining cheap

# exploited labor emerged as rights for Black Americans expanded.

# “These were the circumstances which spawned the myth of the black rapist, for the rape

# charge turned out to be the most powerful of the several attempts to justify the institution

# of lynching. Lynching, in turn, complemented by the systemic rape of black women,

# became an essential ingredient of the strategy of terror which guaranteed the over-

# exploitation of black labor…” (Davis, 1981, p. 42).

# It is through these histories that we see the stark centrality of capitalism and the resulting pooling

# of economic and non-economic resources among colonizers and their legacies in slavery, and the

# crucially important role that violence against women had and continues to have in maintaining

# economic prosperity among the wealthy while virtually eliminating critiques of economic

# structural oppression among the poor under current neoliberal practices, policies, and ideology.

# As Davis discusses,

# “But if the hidden basis of the license to rape black women is economic power, then it

# must be the class structure of capitalist society which harbors the incentive to rape. It

# seems, in fact, that men of the capitalist class and their middle-class partners are immune

# to prosecution because they commit their sexual assaults with the same unchallenged

# authority that legitimizes their daily assaults on the labor and dignity of working people”

# (Davis, 1981, p. 43).

# A discussion of neoliberal beliefs in the absence of this history of capitalism falls short of

# fully understanding how and why it has become this unquestionable championing of capitalism

# 

# 65

# at work in all relations in the current world. Given the ways in which capitalism is fundamentally

# intertwined with racism and the U.S. history of slavery, in the next study I turn to assess the

# ways that neoliberal beliefs affect people’s specific perceptions of low-income women’s

# experiences of sexual assault, while looking at how racial identity also complicates the role of

# neoliberal beliefs. Although the overall findings from the first study support the importance of

# neoliberal beliefs in people’s perceptions of women’s gender-based mistreatment in general, the

# second study seeks to understand more nuanced ways in which neoliberal beliefs might be at

# work in the experiences of sexual assault among women who are most at risk and who are

# stereotyped as illegitimate as victims of sexual assault (Fessler, 2018; Foley, et al., 1995; Gruber

# & Bjorn, 1982; Kane, 2020; LaFree, et al., 1985; MCASA, n.d.). Further, in the final study of my

# dissertation, I will explore the ways in which precarity of housing and work, arguably resulting

# from neoliberal ideology and policies, make it extremely difficult for low-income women to

# escape gender-based violence experiences.

# Limitations and Future Research Directions

# While this study makes important contributions to the psychological literature, there are

# areas of limitations that should be considered in future endeavors contributing to this area of

# research.

# Sample. I first want to take very seriously critiques about the sample used in this study

# which comes from Amazon’s Turk Prime Panels (Cloud Research). Although some research

# suggests that online convenience samples can be as reliable as other sources of collecting data if

# 

# 66

# appropriate steps are taken to ensure reliable data (Clifford, et al., 2015; Smith, et al., 2016), they

# have their drawbacks.

# First, and very seriously, one of the central goals of this dissertation is to understand how

# neoliberal beliefs are integral to the continuation of women’s violence and mistreatment. The

# sample chosen and used in this study, as well as the second, are not fully aligned with this goal.

# Not only were online convenience samples chosen for these studies, but specifically samples

# drawn from Amazon. Participants of online surveys, especially through major platforms such as

# Amazon, are often compensated very little for their time (Williamson, 2016). One study found

# that many older and younger MTurk workers used money made from completing surveys to help

# make ends meet, highlighting that many of the workers used in survey research on these

# platforms already belong to disproportionately economically oppressed groups (Williamson,

# 2016). Additionally, in interviews with MTurk workers, one woman commented that she has

# completed over 8,000 surveys and generally completes surveys for about 8 hours a day but only

# makes about $100 a month from Amazon to help supplement her already unacceptably low

# monthly food stamp stipend of $189 per month (Williamson, 2016).

# Additionally, on Turk Prime Panels, as a researcher, I was not able to set the amount paid

# to each participant through the Turk Prime platform even if I wanted to pay them more. In fact, I

# couldn’t even get a clear understanding of their compensation at all. When I inquired about how

# much participants were paid for participation in our survey, a Turk Prime (Cloud Research)

# consultant responded:

# 

# 67

# …we cannot quantify the amount each participant receives for a Prime Panels study

# because each survey platform used with Prime Panels has its own method of

# compensation and participants can therefore be compensated in a variety of ways

# depending on the payment method they choose. These options can include gift cards,

# cash, rewards points, and donations to charities chosen by participants. It is hard to

# make a 1:1 comparison or even monetize these earnings since some participants may

# receive something like 50,000 points for their participation on their platform and others

# may have their participation be donated to charity.

# It is important to note that online samples can be useful in protecting the identity of

# vulnerable participants, decreasing the time it takes to complete a questionnaire, and making it

# easier to collect data from “hard to reach” populations (McInroy, 2016). However, we are often

# implicated in the very systems we are trying to critique and expose, and we should, as

# researchers and individuals trying to dismantle systems of oppression through the work that we

# do, be cognizant of the ways in which we might be reproducing harm to groups we claim to care

# for. We must come up with more ethical ways of conducting research. We must continuously

# consider the nature of the work that we do and the implications that has on our ability to meet

# our goals especially among anti-capitalist researchers in the academy.

# Method. In addition to concerns presented related to the study’s sample, there are

# methodological considerations for future research as well.

# 

# 68

# First, the current study is only a one-study design. Although this study does replicate

# some findings from previous research, future studies should work on the replication of the

# findings presented here (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015).

# Second, in terms of sampling decisions, I only collected data from participants who

# identified as racially Black or White. As outlined in the introduction and discussion, the research

# on making structural attributions has been mixed (Bullock, 1999; Feagin, 1972; Young, 2004).

# Therefore, the current study sought to focus on just these two groups to ensure quality attention

# could be given to understanding the ways in which beliefs might be shaped by relations with

# power and privilege associated with these specific racial positionalities and because these groups

# most aligned with perceptions about individuals in the second study. Regardless, what is

# important to note is that future research must attend to differences in beliefs and attributions

# among other groups, while keeping central in their analyses how power is at play in influencing

# these perceptions.

# Third, in terms of method, I employed a survey design to understand the relationship

# between neoliberal beliefs and other perceptions. Future research designs should consider these

# beliefs and their relationships in the context of real-world settings. Specifically, I found that

# neoliberal beliefs predict rape myth, sexual harassment myth, and gender-based incivility myth

# acceptance. Future research needs to further explore how these beliefs might manifest in real-

# world settings that attempt to understand influencers of women’s mistreatment. In study 2 of the

# dissertation, I attempt to extend this research into a real-world setting using a vignette approach

# about lower-income women’s experiences of sexual assault.

# 

# 69

# Fourth, I created a new measure of gender-based incivility myths. While I tested the new

# measure using an EFA prior to using it in the full sample, future research should further validate

# this scale. Additionally, the measure of the neoliberal beliefs in this study mirrors very closely

# tenets of capitalist ideology. Although capitalism is an economic system, the current study

# focused on individual-level beliefs that may be important in structural-level economic realities

# such as capitalism. Future research should explore more directly how beliefs about neoliberalism

# support capitalism and its functioning and how then, capitalism is a central part of the way we

# relate to others and the world around us.

# Lastly, it may seem ironic or even misplaced to have a measure of so-called neoliberal

# beliefs, since all beliefs we hold could be considered neoliberal given that we arguably live in a

# neoliberal era. Our findings support previous research showing that despite living in a neoliberal

# era, there is indeed variability in the ways in which individuals are choosing to relate to

# neoliberal beliefs (Beattie, et al., 2019).

# Analyses. We did not collect information on the experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment among participants themselves – experiences that could potentially affect their

# endorsements of myths related to these experiences. However, the research findings on prior

# victimization are somewhat mixed with some research showing that rape myth endorsements do

# not differ between those who report past experiences of sexual assault and those who have not

# (e.g., Carmody & Washington, 2001; Grandgenett, et al., 2022; Mason, et al., 2004; Weiss,

# 2009) and other research finding that victims of sexual assault have lower endorsements of rape

# myths; this lower endorsement was sometimes contingent on other factors like whether the

# 

# 70

# victim reported the incident to police (e.g., Baugher, et al., 2010; Egan & Wilson, 2012;

# Vonderhaar & Carmody, 2015).

# Study 2

# Hypotheses

# Hypothesis 1. In the survey-embedded experiment, based on the literature supporting the

# importance of stereotypes related to respectability for Black and lower-income women, I expect

# to find main effects of both race and class with Black and undeserving poor women blamed more

# than White and deserving poor women respectively.

# Hypothesis 2. Additionally, I expect that participants will be more likely to blame Black

# women for their experiences of assault compared with White women, and for this relation to be

# mediated by lower endorsements of respectability (responsibility and sexualization) and lower

# perceptions of Black women’s general value. I also expect this relation to be moderated by

# participants’ endorsement of neoliberal beliefs, with those who are more likely to endorse

# neoliberalism also more likely to endorse stereotypes about Black women, thus leading to greater

# blame for their sexual assault. See Figure 4 for a visual representation of these predicted

# relations.

# Hypothesis 3. Finally, I expect that participants will also be more likely to blame

# undeserving poor women for their experiences of assault compared with deserving poor women

# respectively. Moreover, this relation will be mediated by lower endorsements of respectability

# (responsibility and sexualization) and lower perceptions of their general value. I also expect this

# relation to be moderated by participants’ endorsement of neoliberal beliefs, with those who are

# more likely to endorse neoliberalism also more likely to endorse stereotypes about undeserving

# poor women, thus leading to greater blame for their sexual assault. See Figure 3 for a visual

# representation of these predicted relations.

# Method

# As in Study 1, participants were recruited through Amazon’s Turk Prime Panels platform.

# This survey included a survey experimental procedure to assess the role of participant

# endorsement of neoliberal beliefs and likelihood to blame lower-income Black and White

# or undeserving poor)

# Figure 4: Study 2 Hypothesis 2a Model

# 72

# women for their experiences of sexual assault. Participants were asked to read one of four

# randomly assigned identical vignettes about a woman who had been sexually assaulted; her

# social class (undeserving or deserving poor) and racial identity (Black or White) was

# manipulated. Her social class was manipulated by using stereotypic descriptors that characterize

# these two groups in terms of the woman’s education (GED or dropped out of high school), living

# situation (in subsidized housing or a decent apartment for the money she makes), and how other

# people in her life describe her (lazy and always looks messy, or hardworking and honest). Race

# was manipulated by simply identifying in the text that she is racially Black or White and by

# changing her name (Keisha or Kathy). The vignettes have been used in a previous study where

# researchers found that participants were significantly more likely to identify the undeserving

# poor as “not hardworking” and as “someone who doesn’t try her hardest in life” compared to the

# deserving poor (Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a). Please see Appendix A for a full sample of these

# vignettes.

# Sample. Prior to collecting data, I used G\*Power to determine an adequate sample size to

# detect effects in my planned analyses. To detect a relatively small effect size (0.14 or larger)

# using a power of 0.80, I needed to collect data from at least 400 participants (Cohen, 1988;

# Erdfelder, et al., 1996). The sample in the second survey consisted of 445 adults 18 years of age

# or older who currently reside in the U.S. Fifteen participants were removed for having open-

# ended responses that didn’t make sense (e.g., “Okay okay we’ll talk soon love you mama mama

# mommy daddy love daddy bye”), and twelve were removed as a result of our string analyses

# 

# 73

# where these participants responded uniformly to some or all survey items in a scale, leaving us

# with a final sample of 418 people.

# gender identity, participants most frequently reported identifying as women (61.5%; N=257)

# followed by men (36.4%; N=152) and gender non-conforming, gender fluid, and/or gender

# variant (2.2%; N=9). High school graduate represented the most frequently reported highest

# N=3). White identifying participants comprised a majority of the sample (72.2%; N=299)

# followed by Black/African American participants (18.1%; N=75), Hispanic/Latinx participants

# (4.1%; N=17), Asian/Asian American/Pacific Islander participants (1.9%; N=8), Native

# American/American Indian participants (1.7%; N=7), Middle Eastern participants (0.7%; N=3),

# multiracial/multiethnic participants (0.7%; N=3), Indian/West Indian (0.5%, N=2). Most

# participants identified as heterosexual (86.5%; N=359) followed by bisexual (5.3%; N=22), gay

# N=6), and bisexual and asexual (0.2%; N=1). Most frequently, participants reported being

# Measures

# All items discussed below were presented to participants after they read the vignette

# about the woman’s experience of sexual assault.

# Blame. Participants were asked 6 questions regarding how much they blamed the woman

# for her experience of sexual assault based on Schult & Schneider’s (1991) Rape Questionnaire

# was used (α = 0.73) (Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a). An example of these items is, “Keisha/Kathy’s

# behavior contributed to what happened in the scenario.” All items were asked on a 5-point Likert

# Scale ranging from “strongly agree” to “strong disagree.” Please see Appendix L for more

# details.

# Respectability. Respectability was measured by separately assessing participant

# perceptions of sexualization and responsibility of the woman in the vignette. Participant

# perceptions of sexualization of the woman in the vignette were assessed using 8 items (α = 0.65)

# such as, “Keisha/Kathy doesn’t come across as very interested in sex in her everyday life.”

# Participant perceptions of the responsibility or conscientiousness of the woman in the vignette

# was assessed using 8 items (α = 0.86) such as, “In her everyday life, Keisha/Kathy is not a

# dependable person.” Both sets of items have been previously used in a study assessing

# participant perceptions of respectability (Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a). All items were asked on a 5-

# point Likert Scale ranging from “strongly agree” to “strongly disagree.” Please see Appendix M

# for more details.

# Value as a person. Participants were asked to respond to 10 items that aimed to assess

# their perceptions of the woman’s value from the vignette (a = .76). These items were adapted

# 

# 79

# from Rosenberg’s (1965) self-esteem scale. An example of these items is, “Keisha/Kathy is a

# person of worth, at least on an equal plane with others.” All items have been adapted to reflect

# participant perceptions about the specific scenario they are asked to read about and will be asked

# on a 5-point Likert-Scale ranging from “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” with a “neither

# agree nor disagree” item in the middle. See Appendix N for more details.

# Neoliberal Beliefs. Neoliberal beliefs were measured using the same 26-item Neoliberal

# Beliefs Scale from Bay-Cheng and colleagues (2015) (a = .83) that was used in Study 1.

# Demographic Variables. Participants were additionally asked to respond to the same 12

# questions related to demographic information as in the first survey. All variables were assessed

# by asking participants the same question with the same possible responses and coding of the

# variable as was described in detail in Study 1. Please see Appendix K for a full list of questions.

# Pilot Assessment

# To test various components of our experiment prior to running it with a full sample, we

# conducted a pilot study with 285 undergraduate Introduction to Psychology students through the

# university’s subject pool platform. Specifically, we were interested in testing the validity of our

# race and deservingness manipulations.

# Race Manipulation. In our study, we wanted to test for potential differences in blame

# attribution toward a woman in the vignette based on her racial identity. Apart from manipulating

# the woman’s specified race by telling participants in the vignette that she was either Black or

# White, we also manipulated her name as either Kathy or Keisha. Further, in our pilot assessment,

# we included a condition where the race of the woman was not specified and we provided a name

# 

# 80

# that had been rated as race neutral: Madison (https://cdn.sisense.com/wp-content/uploads/What-

# Baby-Names-Tell-Us-About-Ethnic-and-Gender-Trends.pdf). The perpetrator’s name in all

# vignettes was chosen in a similar way to reflect a generally accepted race-neutral name: Jayden

# (https://cdn.sisense.com/wp-content/uploads/What-Baby-Names-Tell-Us-About-Ethnic-and-

# Gender-Trends.pdf).

# Following the vignette, participants were asked “What was the race of the woman in the

# previous scenario?” To test whether the manipulation of the woman’s racial identity was being

# correctly understood by participants, I ran a chi-square analysis to see whether participants who

# read about the Black woman were more likely to identify her as Black, and if those who read

# about the White woman were also more likely to identify her as White in our manipulation check

# question. Supporting the manipulation of race, the chi-square analysis was significant, indicating

# differences in reporting the racial identity of the woman based on the vignette that participants

# read X2(10, N = 283) = 237.16, p = <.001 with a moderate effect size estimated using Cramer’s V

# = .65 (values closer to 1 indicate large effect sizes) (Cohen, 1988). Given that there were more

# than 2 groups in our chi-square analysis, I analyzed the adjusted standardized residuals to

# understand where the significant differences were in our results. Generally, values greater than

# 1.96 reflect p-values of less than .05. Participants who read about the Black woman were

# significantly more likely to identify her as Black (z = 14.2) compared to Asian/Asian

# American/Pacific Islander (z = -1.0), Hispanic/Latinx (z = -1.2), White (z = -7.7), other (z = -0.7),

# and no race mentioned (z = -5.3). Those who read about the White woman were significantly

# more likely to also identify her as White (z = 8.1) compared to American/Pacific Islander (z =

# 

# 81

# 0.5), Hispanic/Latinx (z = 1.2), Black (z = -7.4), other (z = -0.7), and no race mentioned (z = -

# 1.1). Lastly, participants who were assigned to read the vignette where no racial identity was

# specified were significantly more likely to report that no race was mentioned (z = 6.3) compared

# to American/Pacific Islander (z = 0.5), Hispanic/Latinx (z = .00), Black (z = -6.7), White (z = -

# 0.4), and other (z = 1.4).

# Additionally, I ran an ANOVA to test for potential differences in likelihood of blaming

# the woman in the vignette based on the three race conditions. Results indicated that there were

# no differences in blame attribution toward the woman in the vignette based on racial identity

# (F(2, 284) = 0.17, p = .984). Primarily, I was concerned with ensuring that there were no

# significant differences in the main outcome variable of blame between participants who read the

# condition where race was not specified and participants who read conditions where race was

# specifically stated.

# Deservingness Manipulation. The deservingness manipulation was assessed by asking

# participants to respond to two questions: “Would you describe the woman from the previous

# scenario as hard-working?” and “Would you describe the woman from the previous scenario as

# someone who doesn’t try her hardest in life?” Participants who read an undeserving poor

# vignette were significantly more likely to describe the woman as not hard-working X2(1, N =

# 284) = 93.97, p = <.001, Cramer’s V = .58. Further, participants were significantly less likely to

# describe the woman as someone who tries her hardest in life if they read about an undeserving

# poor woman X2(1, N = 284) = 25.74, p = <.001, Cramer’s V = .30. Based on these results, as well

# 

# 82

# as results from a previous study, the manipulation of the deserving and undeserving poor

# conditions appear to be strong (Kiebler & Stewart, 2023).

# Results

# SPSS version 27.0 was used to conduct all preliminary and primary analyses in our study.

# For all analyses an alpha of .05 was used to assess significance with values less than this

# threshold considered to be statistically noteworthy. Hayes Process Macro Model 7 was used to

# conduct our moderated mediation analysis (Hayes, 2013).

# Preliminary Analyses. Identical preliminary analyses were conducted as were completed

# for the first survey, regarding attention checks and string analyses to check for response

# homogeneity. As mentioned above, 15 participants were removed from the original sample for

# having open-ended questions that were unclear, and another 12 were removed following string

# analyses assessing homogeneity of responses to questions. The final sample consisted of 418

# participants.

# I also tested the adequacy of our manipulations using our manipulation check questions

# (See Appendix O for question details). First, I conducted a chi-square analysis to assess the race

# manipulation used in the vignette. As in the pilot, our manipulation of race was supported X2(5,

# N = 417) = 184.03, p = <.001, Cramer’s V = .66. Since there were more than two groups in the

# chi-square analysis, I again analyzed the adjusted standardized residuals to understand where the

# significant differences were. Participants who read about the Black woman were significantly

# more likely to identify her as Black (z = 12.5) compared to Asian/Asian American/Pacific

# Islander (z = -2.4), Hispanic/Latinx (z = 0.2), White (z = -9.3), no race mentioned (z = -0.7), and

# 

# 83

# other (z = -5.1). Those who read about the White woman were significantly more likely to also

# identify her as White (z = 9.3) compared to American/Pacific Islander (z = -2.4), Hispanic/Latinx

# (z = -0.2), Black (z = -12.5), nom race mentioned (z = 5.1), and other (z = 0.7).

# Additionally, I conducted another chi-square analysis to assess the accuracy with which

# participants perceived the deservingness manipulation (the woman being described as either a

# member of the deserving or undeserving poor). Results supported that participants who read

# about the undeserving poor woman were significantly more likely to identify her as not hard-

# working, X2(1, N = 418) = 81.53, p = <.001, Cramer’s V = .44. Additionally, participants who

# read about the undeserving poor woman were less likely to report that she is someone who tries

# her hardest in life, X2(1, N = 418) = 37.03, p = <.001, Cramer’s V = .30.
