# Discussion

# Summary. Results for this second study supported previous research emphasizing the

# importance of including both race- and class-based analyses in research on perceptions and

# judgments of women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment, as both were found to be

# important predictors of participants likelihood to blame. Notably, this study additionally makes

# 

# 89

# important contributions to psychological research that includes analyses that take into

# consideration the socio-historical context in which we exist. Specifically, the inclusion of the

# role of neoliberal beliefs in participant perceptions of women’s sexual assault is a contribution to

# our psychological understanding of the ways that world views that may not seem prominent to

# these perceptions have a prominent role in shaping them.

# Discussion

# Supporting the first hypothesis, I found that participants were significantly more likely to

# blame women stereotyped as belonging to the undeserving poor and Black lower-income women

# for their experiences of sexual assault compared to the deserving poor and White women,

# respectively. However, results did not indicate support for an interaction between race and

# deservingness as affecting participant blame attribution. Despite some previous research finding

# no main effect of race or class-based deservingness in participant blame attribution, we still

# hypothesized that we might see main effects for both groups of women.

# Specifically, there is a rich body of research and history that supports greater perceived

# blame attribution toward Women of Color and limited consequences for those who enact such

# violence toward them (Buchanan et al., 2008; Donovan, 2007; Donovan & Williams, 2008;

# Dupuis & Clay, 2013; George & Martínez, 2002; Gravelin et al., 2019; Roberts, 1997; White,

# 1985). Further, research on people’s perceptions of lower-income women’s experiences of

# gender-based mistreatment, while consistent in terms of higher tendency to blame tends to vary

# in other important aspects such as stereotype content or the inclusion of the woman’s race in the

# study (Spencer, 2016; Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a; Kiebler & Stewart, 2022b; Kiebler & Stewart,

# 

# 90

# 2023).

# Finally, there is little research that has considered the potential effects of both race and

# class of a woman on people’s perceptions of their sexual assault. Studies including both

# demonstrate the necessity of including both in our understanding of people’s perceptions of these

# women’s experiences of violence but have typically not found strong support for intersectional

# understanding of these women’s mistreatment among observers (Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a;

# Kiebler & Stewart, 2022b; Kiebler & Stewart, 2023). We know that Women of Color and lower-

# income women experience higher rates of gender-based mistreatment and that people tend to

# blame these women more for their experiences. However, researchers often do not include an

# analysis of both race and class in single studies. Given the tendency for people to conflate race

# and class in the U. S., this previous research suggests that this conflation may be one explanation

# for the lack of intersectional findings in this line of research (Kiebler & Stewart, 2022a; Moss,

# 2003; Ostrove & Cole, 2003; Yuval-Davis, 2006). Specifically, these researchers would argue

# that the lack of intersectional findings is not reason to exclude intersectional approaches to future

# research. Rather, more research should be conducted to understand how perceptions of race and

# class in experimental surveys might be conflated within participant imagination in a vignette

# design.

# Partially supporting the second hypothesis, I found that participants were significantly

# more likely to blame Black women for their sexual assault, and this relation was mediated by

# participant perceptions that Black women are less valuable in general compared to White

# women. Further, this relation was strongest among participants who endorse neoliberal beliefs at

# 

# 91

# high rates. One previous study by Kiebler & Stewart (2023) found that participants were

# significantly more likely to blame White lower-income women for experiences of sexual assault

# compared to Black lower-income women, and this relationship was mediated by perceptions of

# these women’s lack of value and irresponsibility. While this previous finding is important to

# consider in the context of these findings, the current study additionally takes into consideration

# the role of participant neoliberal belief endorsement in the overall relation with blame attribution.

# While we had anticipated that all three stereotypes would help explain higher blame

# attribution toward Black women based on the literature, the finding that participants were

# significantly more likely to see Black women as less valuable compared to White women is not

# surprising when considering the additional measure of participant neoliberal belief endorsement.

# Using the stereotype content model, psychological researchers have demonstrated that

# discrimination among People of Color and low-income individuals partially stems from people’s

# ratings of them as low on measures of competence and warmth (Fiske, 2015; Fiske, 2018; Fiske,

# et al., 2002). Further, Black women, their work, and contributions are often not valued and are

# seen as invisible in formal institutions (Settles, et al., 2019; Settles, et al., 2021; Settles, 2022;

# Thomas & Hill, 2022). Finally, neoliberal beliefs, which are an addition in the current study, can

# also help explain this finding. Specifically, the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs is associated

# with a disregard for systems of oppression like racism and classism (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015;

# Harvey, 2005). Therefore, individuals who strongly endorse neoliberal beliefs at high rates are

# likely to attribute economic and other failings in life to individual lack of effort rather than

# historically rooted colonialism, racism, and other oppressions (Arfken, 2018; Bay-Cheng, et al.,

# 

# 92

# 2015; Bullock, 2013; Feagin, 1972; Harvey, 2005; Jost, et al., 2015; Perez & Salter, 2019; Son

# Hing, 2013).

# Partially supporting the third hypothesis, and replicating previous research findings, I

# found that participants were significantly more likely to blame women stereotyped as members

# of the undeserving poor for sexual assault, and this relation was mediated by participant

# perceptions that these women were oversexualized, irresponsible, and less valuable compared to

# the women described to be members of the deserving poor (Kiebler & Stewart, 2023). However,

# participant neoliberal belief endorsement only moderated the relation where sexualization was

# found to mediate participant blame toward the undeserving poor women. Specifically, as

# outlined above, participants were significantly more likely to blame the undeserving poor women

# for sexual assault and this relation was mediated by perceptions of her oversexualization. This

# pattern was strongest as participant neoliberal belief endorsement strengthened too.

# Based on previous research, it seems clear that stereotypes about the undeserving poor as

# being over-sexualized consistently relate to people’s perceptions of these women’s gender-based

# mistreatment (Kiebler & Stewart, 2023). In the current study, when considering participant

# neoliberal beliefs, again, stereotypes about undeserving poor women as over-sexualized were

# found to be especially salient in judgments about their mistreatment. The addition of neoliberal

# beliefs into the current study help strengthen our understanding of what factors drive the

# relationship of blame toward lower-income women in their experiences of sexual assault.

# While researchers have demonstrated that people generally blame women for experiences

# of mistreatment based on the actions or lack of action the woman took in the scenario and based

# 

# 93

# on her personal character attributes, the current study replicates some previous research detailing

# the importance of stereotypes about historically marginalized groups of women in these

# perceptions. Specifically, participants were more likely to blame Black women for their sexual

# assault if they perceived them as less valuable than White women. Additionally, participants

# were more likely to blame women stereotyped as the undeserving poor based if they viewed

# them as oversexualized. These are invented characteristics of these women based on historically

# rooted, overlapping racist and classist stereotypes.

# Building from research by Bay-Cheng and colleagues (2015), the current study takes

# their finding that higher endorsements of neoliberal beliefs predict higher endorsements of rape

# myth acceptance and applies it to real-life scenarios. While I found that these beliefs hold up in

# perceptions of blame for women’s mistreatment, this study demonstrates their specific centrality

# in perceptions of sexual assault among women who already face the effects of neoliberal policy

# in other realms of life too. Lower-income women and Black women are more likely to

# experience sexual assault in their lifetimes, and they are often not seen as legitimate victims

# (Cortina et al., 1998; Fessler, 2018; Foley et al., 1995; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982; Kane, 2020;

# LaFree, et al., 1985; MacKinnon, 1979; Maryland Coalition Against Sexual Assault [Maryland

# Coalition Against Sexual Assault MCASA], n.d.). This study shows the role of neoliberal beliefs

# in this process of discounting these women’s experience of gendered violence. Just as they are

# not seen as legitimate victims of capitalist exploitation via slashing of welfare protections, they

# also are not seen as legitimate victims of gender-based violence.

# 

# 94

# Thinking back to the introduction, people who endorse neoliberal beliefs generally

# support limiting government interference in social concerns due to the central neoliberal belief

# that individual success and failure is within the control of the individual (Harvey, 2005). While

# these individuals discount the reality of structural inequality that plays a dominant role in the

# success and failure of individuals, I proposed the use of intersectional theory as an alternative

# framework to neoliberalism’s neutrality in life outcomes (Arfken, 2018; Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015;

# Harvey, 2005; Perez & Salter, 2019; Son Hing, 2013). Intersectionality theory helps us

# understand the current study’s pattern of findings where racism, classism, and sexism

# differentially play a role in stereotype application which results in blame for economically and

# racially marginalized women in their experiences of sexual assault (Bavishi, et al., 2010; Collins,

# 2000; Cole, 2009; Collins & Bilge, 2016; Crenshaw, 1991; Crenshaw, 1989; Ghavami & Peplau,

# 2012; hooks, 2000; Lorde, 1984; Lott & Saxon, 2002; Moradi & Grzank, 2017; Reid, 2010;

# Settles & Buchanan, 2014; Yuval-Davis, 2006).

# So, while neoliberal beliefs may offer the illusion of individual agency and control in life,

# the findings from this study provide a deeper understanding of the ways that these beliefs

# operate. Specifically, among individuals who endorse neoliberal beliefs at higher rates, the role

# of stereotypes in blame attribution for these marginalized women is strengthened. Therefore,

# despite the ignorance of structural inequality that is central to neoliberal beliefs, we see that

# individuals who place greater emphasis on neoliberalism rely more on stereotypes in making

# assessments about blame for the sexual assault of Black women and lower-income women.

# These stereotypes, which have been used as the justification for the continuous economic

# 

# 95

# oppression of Black women and lower-income women, help suggest that the neutrality that

# neoliberal beliefs are said to imply is an illusion. In fact, those holding neoliberal beliefs are

# particularly influenced by preconceived stereotypes about groups of women when it comes to

# making judgments about their culpability in experiences of sexual assault.

# The focus on individual actors in all outcomes in life provides some belief in individual

# control which is psychologically important. However, ignorance of the role of power and

# oppression in these processes helps perpetuate inequality that is rooted in systemic racism,

# sexism, classism, and more. In fact, it could be argued that this process of getting individuals to

# buy into the belief that we have complete control over our lives through the resurgence of

# neoliberalism is an integral mechanism supporting capitalism.

# Limitations and Future Directions

# While the current study makes important contributions to the literature, there are some

# limitations that should be noted. Many of the limitations outlined in the first survey are important

# to consider in the current study as well. Specifically, this study also has limitations regarding the

# sample and my role in the reproduction of neoliberalism, the one-study design, our measure of

# supposed neoliberal beliefs, and our lack of consideration of participant experiences of gender-

# based mistreatment.

# Similar to our first survey, the current study used an online convenience sample of

# participants to collect data from individuals who are paid very little for their work, while large

# corporations benefit greatly as a result of this exploited labor. The central goal of this dissertation

# concerns critiques of neoliberalism. While platforms that allow for the collection of convenience

# 

# 96

# samples create opportunities for people to engage in research of interest and for researchers to

# understand beliefs and attitudes among the larger population (particularly about neoliberal

# beliefs in this study), the continued use of these platforms without critique for their treatment of

# participants only works to cover up the often, neoliberal implications of psychological research

# and data collection more specifically.

# Again, the current study is a one-study design. This study, like the first, replicates some

# findings from previous research however, future work should consider the replication of the new

# inclusion of the importance of neoliberal beliefs in participant perceptions of these women’s

# experiences of sexual assault (Kiebler & Stewart, 2023). We additionally did not collect

# information on experiences of sexual assault among our participants in this study. As outlined in

# the limitations of the first study, the research concerning the effect of previous victimization on

# perceptions of other people’s experiences of victimization are mixed. Despite this, it could be

# important for future researchers to take this into consideration when analyzing people’s

# perceptions of women’s mistreatment.

# Finally, the current study considers only one type of sexual assault scenario: one where

# the woman knows the perpetrator. There is some research to support the importance of

# considering the type of relationship with the perpetrator in people’s judgments about a woman’s

# culpability for gender-based mistreatment and therefore, future researchers might increase the

# variation in vignettes to include different type of victim-perpetrator relationships and interactions

# (Abrams et al., 2003; Black & McCloskey, 2013; Gravelin et al., 2019; Persson & Dhingra,

# 2021; Suarez & Gadalla, 2010).

# 

# 97

# Chapter 3: Housing and Work Precarity: Lower-Income Women’s Perceptions of their

# own Mistreatment

# As outlined in Studies 1 and 2, the concept of deservingness has been extensively studied

# in psychological research and has been discussed in relation to similar concepts such as fairness,

# justice, relative deprivation, and entitlement (Feather, 1999; Feather, 2015; Hareli, 1999; Reyna,

# et al., 2005). Lerner’s (1980) just world theory describes deservingness as people’s beliefs that

# the world is generally just and is a place where people typically are deserving of their own life

# outcomes (Lerner, 1980). These judgments can be used to decide what others deserve but have

# also been used to reflect on what the self deserves, which is the focus of Study 3 (Heuer, et al.,

# 2012; McClelland, 2010).

# The goal of Studies 1 and 2 was to understand how the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs

# might be linked to ideas about what low-income women and Black deserve; specifically, how

# much they are viewed as deserving blame for their experiences of gender-based mistreatment. In

# Study 3, the goal is to extend this literature by looking at how policy and ideas shaped by

# neoliberal beliefs might affect women’s own experiences of gender-based mistreatment and their

# interpretation of it as well. Specifically, policies that makes it difficult to obtain scarce

# government funded housing, and policies that maintains an abundance of cheap labor, are

# primarily rooted in ideas of neoliberalism that justify the deservingness of some over others.

# Therefore, the goal of Study 3 is to ask the question: how do ideas of deservingness rooted in

# neoliberalism shape the lives and experiences of violence among low-income women depending

# on their access to stability in housing and work? Additionally, in Study 3, I seek to understand

# 

# 98

# how neoliberal beliefs may be present among these women themselves, thus shaping their

# perspectives on their own lives, other women’s lives similar to and different from themselves,

# and their experiences of mistreatment in the workplace and more generally.

# Precarious Housing

# The “feminization of homelessness” is a term used by researchers to demonstrate the

# effects that policies and practices endorsed at the national, state, and local levels contribute to the

# disproportionate rates of homelessness among women in general, and the even higher rates

# among Women of Color (Bullock, et al., 2020; Bullock, 2013). Living in poverty alone has been

# linked with increased risk of experiences of sexual violence (MacKinnon, 1979; Maryland

# Coalition Against Sexual Assault [MCASA]).

# Further, researchers have demonstrated that not only does living in poverty contribute to

# the likelihood of having these experiences, but it also contributes to how women themselves

# understand these experiences. Research by Bay-Cheng and Bruns (2016) explored the ways

# young women make sense of their experiences of consensual unwanted sexual experiences. They

# found that low-income women who were not students were less likely to discuss their

# experiences of unwanted sexual experiences as completely harmless. Instead, they expressed

# reasons for consenting to this treatment for various reasons, one of which was the need for

# continued economic support from the person who treated them this way. Another study by

# Bullock and colleagues (2020) highlighted the necessity of women (especially Women of Color)

# in precarious housing situations to accept violence from partners to shield themselves from

# further economic vulnerability or vulnerability from interacting with the police. Finally, another

# 

# 99

# account highlighted in Edin & Shaefer’s (2015) book about those living among the $2-a-day

# poor, documented similar situations, in which young girls and women weigh the risks and

# benefits of permitting unwanted sexual violations that are influenced by their classed positions

# and both hunger and the need for cash to pay bills that the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance

# Program (SNAP) did not cover (e.g., electricity, etc.).

# This small body of research highlights how systemic economic vulnerability creates

# conditions that put poor women at exceptional risk of gender-based mistreatment and violence.

# However, researchers who have greatly contributed to our understanding of how housing

# precarity and living in poverty contributes to women’s likelihood of experiencing gender-based

# mistreatment as well as how these women make sense of those experiences, have thus far failed

# to consider women in poverty as a heterogenous group. Specifically, as Bullock (2013) outlines

# in Women and Poverty: An Ongoing Crisis,

# “Homelessness exists when people lack safe, stable, and appropriate places to live.

# Sheltered and unsheltered people are homeless. People living doubled up or in

# overcrowded living situations or motels due to inadequate economic resources are

# included in this definition, as are those living in tents, or other temporary enclosures” (p.

# 11).

# However, these various experiences of housing precarity may bring with them differing levels of

# precarity and these may affect women’s experiences of violence and their interpretation of those

# experiences. Specifically, women living in government subsidized housing may be more

# protected in certain ways from experiences of violence based on more stability in housing

# 

# 100

# compared to women living in motels where the certainty of housing is often unclear day to day.

# Women living in motels who participated in our interviews were not living there out of choice.

# All women in those positions mentioned pursuing housing through government assistance but

# had been unsuccessful either in obtaining funding for housing or were on a waitlist to do so.

# These motels were far from luxury but were rather the only affordable option the women could

# secure without stable income or credit required to rent housing in the area. Further, while many

# of these women would attempt to scrape enough money together to be able to stay overnight in a

# local motel, all of them described going nights without housing or sleeping in their car. Some

# also mentioned local organizations would occasionally pay for their accommodations at a motel

# for a few nights, but this was not a common occurrence. For many, the budget motels in the area

# afforded houseless women the ability to keep a roof over their head for a few nights given that

# local shelters often operated in a rotating manner, meaning that people could not stay there

# indefinitely but would have to cycle out to allow other people a chance to stay there.

# In this Study, I will explore the ways that housing precarity might be linked to women

# being more likely to experience gender-based mistreatment, aiming to understand the ways that

# the women make sense of their experiences of mistreatment based on their access to stable

# housing (Bay-Cheng & Bruns, 2016). Specifically, I will interview women living in motels and

# women living in HUD apartments. Living in HUD housing offers significantly more stability for

# those who can gain access to this very limited program, while living in a motel offers little in the

# way of stability, with women often having to move their things out each day (unless paying a

# weekly rate that many can’t afford to do), and to pay nightly for a place to sleep. HUD housing

# 

# 101

# locations are government-owned dwellings that offer rent to occupants at a lower price. This is in

# comparison to other low-income housing programs like Section 8 housing, which is a voucher

# program that allows people to find privately owned apartments

# (https://www.hud.gov/topics/rental\_assistance). Participants in both programs face significantly

# lower rates of housing instability compared to those who cannot access these programs (Edin &

# Shaefer, 2015). Moreover, women often live in all of these kinds of housing at different times.

# Precarious Work

# In addition to contributing to ideas about who is deserving of government-funded

# housing, neoliberal policy in the U.S. also helps maintain a constant demand for cheap and

# exploited labor, with poor women continuously stuck in low wage work where they can’t make

# ends meet either on or off government assistance (Edin & Lein, 1997; Feagin, 1972). For

# example, the 1996 welfare reform shifting from Aid to Families with Dependent Children

# (AFDC) to Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), had the goal of “ending welfare

# as we know it,” which was seemingly successful at getting people off the welfare rolls. However,

# it has arguably contributed to “diminishing the quality of the average low wage job in America”

# by flooding the market with too many low-wage workers, which in turn allowed employers to cut

# benefits, hours, and pay because they could simply replace employees more readily (Edin &

# Schaefer, 2015, p. 61).

# Many women who have cycled between being primarily on government assistance or

# working in low wage jobs choose to go back to government assistance due to the added burden

# of costs while working (no time to work for cash in the informal labor sector, travel costs to and

# 

# 102

# from work, cost of care for children, etc.)—or at least they did in 1997 (Edin & Lein, 1997).

# Today, more people are in the workforce, and few (2 out of 100 Americans) receive cash aid,

# both due to increased stigma and policies like the 1996 Welfare Reform Act that have pushed

# people into the workforce or at least off welfare rolls (Edin & Schaefer, 2015). However, due to

# policies like those adopted in 1996, low-wage workers again saturate the workforce, helping to

# create poor work conditions among the lowest level of workers who are deemed completely

# dispensable.

# Women working in low-wage jobs, especially those in service positions that are growing

# faster than manufacturing jobs, report high rates of gender-based mistreatment (Edin & Schaefer,

# 2015; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982). Further, they report tolerating experiences of sexual harassment

# and other forms of mistreatment, because their income depends on tips (Messing, 2014).

# Customers may feel that they can take advantage of those serving them because of the power

# imbalance defined by service jobs themselves. The low incomes associated with these jobs force

# jobholders to rely heavily on tips from their customers, leaving those serving largely at the mercy

# of those being served. It is this economic dependency and structural relation that makes women

# in low-wage jobs particularly vulnerable to mistreatment by customers as well as others in the

# workplace.

# Additionally, people in the U.S. are increasingly earning money for work in the informal

# economy (Aptone, 1997). The informal economy has been defined as “the production of, or trade

# in, goods and services – that occur outside the purview of the state but are otherwise legal” (from

# Aptone (1997), based on the work of Castells and Portes (1989, p. 18)). Women who are still

# 

# 103

# receiving cash-based forms of government assistance, as well as those living among the $2 a day

# poor who are not receiving cash assistance, many of whom live in precarious housing situations

# of various degrees, report working in the informal economy as an additional or alternative means

# of earning an income to help make ends meet (Edin & Lein, 1997; Edin & Schaefer, 2015).

# However, there has been little research to understand how women working in these service

# positions informally might be further susceptible to experiences of mistreatment based on

# increased vulnerability, as a result of not being formally tied to the business for which they work.

# In this study, I will explore how various levels and combinations of precarity in housing

# and work make women vulnerable to gender-based mistreatment. I note that these different

# levels refer to the women’s particular work and/or housing situation at the time I interviewed

# them. In fact, many of them worked and were housed in all of the kinds of settings I’ve outlined,

# at one time or another. Another goal of this study is to examine how women make attributions

# about their own mistreatment, while considering potential differences in attributions based on

# differential experiences of housing and employment precarity. Women working in more

# precarious jobs might be less likely to attribute their experiences of gender-based mistreatment to

# their own actions, and more to their need to endure these experiences given their economic

# vulnerability and the level of power already embedded in their jobs (Messing, 2014). Further,

# women living in precarious housing might similarly attribute their experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment to their need to achieve economic stability (Bay-Cheng & Bruns, 2016; Bullock, et

# al., 2020; Edin & Schaefer, 2015). I aim to understand how women facing differential levels of

# precarity in housing and employment might interpret their experiences similarly and differently.

# 

# 104

# Those who have adopted ideas of neoliberalism may blame themselves more and be less likely to

# make structural attributions for their experiences of mistreatment.

# In addition to considering how precarity in housing and employment affects women’s

# perceptions of their mistreatment and position in life, a final goal of this study is to explore how

# different features of identity might be important predictors of women making structural

# attributions. Additionally, research has documented that many positional and identity-related

# factors contribute to people’s attributions for poverty (either structural or individualistic).

# Research by Bullock (1999) supports the importance of class identity in people’s likelihood of

# making attributions for poverty, with lower-income individuals more likely to make structural

# attributions and middle-class individuals more likely to make individual attributions for poverty.

# Further, race has also been found an important consideration in attributions for poverty.

# Specifically, Feagin’s study in 1972 documented those African American and low-income

# individuals, as compared to higher-income and White individuals, were more likely to attribute

# poverty to structural inequalities. However, other researchers have documented ways in which

# similar groups have been less inclined to name structures as primary reasons for their situation in

# life (Young, 2004).

# While the literature is somewhat mixed regarding the likelihood of people making

# structural or individualistic attributions based on race, the recent prominence of the “job/worker

# shortage” might complicate people’s perceptions further. Specifically, the abundance of coverage

# on these recent issues could bring new light to the structural inequalities that contribute to them,

# 

# 105

# or it could create deeper rifts among groups of people based on the idea that some people “just

# don’t want to work” (Susik, 2021).

# Additionally, literature on the White working-class suggests that status as a member of

# the “deserving” or “undeserving” poor might also influence their perspectives on the level of

# individual control people have for their life circumstances. Specifically, those who belong to the

# deserving poor might believe in and endorse the very systems that are responsible for their

# exploitation, due to the status they gain through their downward comparisons to the undeserving

# poor (Bérubé & Bérubé, 1997; Crockett, 2017; Hartigan, 1997).

# Methods

# Interviews

# All interviews were conducted with current residents of Ypsilanti and Ann Arbor,

# Michigan. Based on the most recent Census data from 2021 (United States Census Bureau, n.d.),

# the proportion of people living in poverty in the city of Ypsilanti is nearly two and a half times

# the proportion of people living in poverty at the state level (31.6% compared to 13% at the state

# level). Further, compared to other surrounding cities, Ypsilanti is more densely populated with

# People of Color, specifically underrepresented minorities (URM) (28.2% Black or African

# American; 4.6% Hispanic or Latino]; and 64.9% White, not Hispanic or Latino). Based on this

# information, women were recruited primarily in Ypsilanti to begin with and then recruiting

# strategies shifted based on some participant feedback about where low-income women stay in

# the area.

# 

# 106

# I invited a fellow graduate student to help me conduct these interviews. The question of

# matching interviewer and interviewee race-ethnicity is a complicated one. Some feminist

# researchers believe that reflecting on one’s own identity is enough to do justice to the issue of

# how our own positionality affects our research, the people, and communities we engage with

# during the process of research, and how our research gets taken up. Other scholars endorse a

# more holistic process of reflection and action regarding reflexivity (Ramazanoglu & Holland,

# 2002; McClelland, 2017; Whitson, 2016). For this project, given the sensitivity of entering

# communities and asking them to share pieces of their lives with us, I thought it important to find

# a fellow graduate student who identifies as a Woman of Color to conduct the interviews with the

# participants who also identified as Women of Color. While there are still differences in terms of

# power always present within the work that we do, given educational differences between

# interviewers and interviewees, my hope was that some of the obstacles to communication that

# might exist if I were to conduct all the interviews myself could be mitigated.

# Recruitment

# A total of 22 women participated in one-hour interviews (N=9 living in precarious

# housing [motels]; N=13 living in less precarious housing [HUD apartments]) about their

# experiences living and working in more or less precarious situations (See Appendix P for a

# sample of the interview protocol). Prior to being formally invited to participate in our interviews,

# flyers were placed near and in selected motels and HUD apartment buildings where women

# could be pre-screened for their experiences working in the precarious work positions (See

# Appendix Q for the full pre-screening survey; See Appendix R for detailed recruiting location

# 

# 107

# information). I proposed sampling primarily based on housing because it is more feasible to

# locate women in particular housing than those working in formal and informal jobs. While we

# did sample based on current housing (either women living in HUD apartments or in motels),

# most women had experience with more and less precarious housing or homelessness (92.3%).

# Further, I expected that many of those living in precarious housing would also have experiences

# with both precarious formal and informal work, which turned out to be accurate (82.5% of the

# women reported experience with both formal and informal work). Interviews were semi-

# structured, allowing for some variation in follow-up questions with the goal of hitting on each

# central question in the interview protocol.

# Recruitment fliers included both a quick response (QR) code that participants could scan

# with the camera of their cell phones to take the pre-screening survey and also included a

# telephone number to call or text which was connected to my phone but used an alternative phone

# number via an app called Talkatone for the pre-screening survey. I provided the telephone option

# for participants who might not have access to internet data on their cell phone. Each time

# participants called to conduct the pre-screening survey, I would open the pre-screening link on

# my phone, read all questions to them and fill it out as we went. They then would be instantly

# notified if they qualified for the interview, and we would schedule a time and place to meet.

# Interviews took place at various locations depending on the preference of the participant

# and the comfortability of the researcher conducting the interview. Interview settings included the

# participant’s home, and various parks (Prospect Park, Ann Arbor Skate Park, Waterworks Park;

# and Nancy Park). Upon completion of the interview, participants were paid $40 in cash.

# 

# 108

# The following long-term stay motels were targeted: Your Motel, Harmony House Motel,

# and Victory Inn. Both Your Motel and Harmony House Motel are located along Michigan Ave.

# in Ypsilanti, Michigan. Victory Inn is in Ann Arbor on Washtenaw Ave. Originally targeted

# were Your Motel and Harmony House Motel. Following some interviews, I found that some

# women were currently or had previously stayed at Victory Inn in Ann Arbor. Given I was still

# recruiting women for interviews, I left fliers in the lobby of Victory Inn after gaining this

# knowledge.

# Additionally, I was able to gain access to one HUD apartment building in Ypsilanti

# (Chidester Place). With permission of the management, I was able to leave a stack of fliers in the

# laundry room located on each floor of the building and to leave a flier on each individual unit’s

# door. In addition, I left fliers at close bus stops and businesses as well (Please see Appendix Q

# for detailed recruiting location information). This apartment complex has ~151 rentable units.

# Given that this was a HUD apartment building, it offered a certain level of stability in housing

# (as opposed to the long-term stay motels) while maintaining similar economic precarity among

# our entire targeted sample (Apartments.com, n.d.).

# Participant care considerations. Given the potentially sensitive and upsetting nature of

# some of the questions in Study 3, I compiled a list of community-based resources that could be

# of use to these women that they may or may not already be aware of including sliding scale

# mental health resources, food banks, other healthcare resources, childcare, and more. Please see

# Appendix S for more details.

# 

# 109

# Sample

# A little less than half of the participants (41%; N=9) recruited currently lived in

# precarious housing (long-term stay motels). The other half (59%; N=13) of the participants were

# currently living in less precarious housing (HUD apartments) but were also low-income and

# lived in the same cities (Ann Arbor and Ypsilanti).

# All interview participants identified as women and as being born in the U.S. Ages of

# women interviewed ranged from 20-83 years old with an average of 48 years (9.1%, N=2 did not

# respond to the question regarding their age). About one third (31.8%; N =7) of the women

# identified as Women of Color (Black [N=4; 18.2%], Native American [N=2; 9.1%], or Mexican

# and White [N=1; 4.5%]), while the other two thirds of the sample identified as White (68.2%;

# N=15).

# About one third of the women reported they had finished high school or obtained a GED

# (31.8%; N=7); 27.3% didn’t finish high school (N=6); 18.2% had completed some college but no

# degree (N=4); 9.1% each had obtained an associate’s or bachelor’s degree (N=2 each); and 4.5%

# had obtained a master’s degree (N=1).

# Most women reported having children (72.7%; N=16) while 27.3% did not (N=6).

# Among women who had kids, more than half (68.7%; N=11) of the women reported their kids

# didn’t currently live with them (9.1% each (N=2 each) either reported their kids lived with them

# or that some of their kids lived with them; and 4.5% (N=1) didn’t respond). Half (50%; N=11) of

# the women indicated they were currently in a relationship and half were not. Among those who

# reported having a partner currently, 45.5% (N=5) indicated that their partner currently lives with

# 

# 110

# them while the rest did not. Finally, more than half (68.2%; N=15) reported that they have family

# that lives nearby while 31.8% (N=7) did not.

# Research Questions

# While the analysis of data for this study is largely inductive, there is some guiding

# literature that can support some expectations regarding these women’s experiences and their own

# interpretation of them as well. Specifically, poor White women might be more likely than poor

# Black women to see their position as fitting within the framework of neoliberalism. Based on Jim

# Crow ideology that positioned poor White individuals as more valuable than all Black

# individuals in the country, these lingering ideas might be influential in the ideas of poor White

# individuals regarding their position in life and their ability to change their circumstances because

# buying into this system has been historically beneficial to them (symbolically, not in actuality)

# (hooks, 2000). This may impact how these women see their experiences of sexual violence as

# well, considering potential connections to the results from Studies 1 and 2 related to the

# endorsement of neoliberalism and blame toward poor women for their experiences of sexual

# violence. I expect Black women to be less likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs, and therefore not

# to see their life circumstances and experiences of sexual violence as their own fault.

# Those living in more secure housing might be more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs as

# a way of separating themselves as inherently better from those who have even less (Allison,

# 1994; Hartigan, 1997; Oorschot, 2000). However, these women might also have experiences

# living in more precarious housing, so we might expect to see that race is a more important

# contributing factor to perceptions of blame than current housing.

# 

# 111

# Finally, women living in more precarious housing situations might be more likely to

# experience mistreatment compared to those in more stable housing (e.g., HUD housing) due to

# certain protections afforded by stable housing to women in those situations (Bullock, 2013).

# Importantly, I expect that neoliberal beliefs will be a factor in the perpetuation of these women’s

# experiences of mistreatment based on the precarity of their housing. For example, neoliberal

# beliefs and policies are likely to leave more women in more precarious housing, thus

# contributing to their mistreatment experiences.

# Analysis Plan

# Methodology. As a feminist psychologist, it is important to situate the way in which I

# think knowledge is produced and can be gained about other people and their experiences. The

# methodology guiding the research methods and analysis in this study aligns most closely with the

# critical-ideological epistemological position. While critical theories are not uniformly defined,

# there are central tenets that underly this perspective. Specifically, “criticalists advocate a reality

# that is constructed within a social-historical context” and “... criticalists conceptualize reality and

# events within power relations and they use their research to emancipate oppressed groups”

# (Ponterotto, 2005, p. 130). It is also important to identify one’s epistemological perspective

# because it will determine the questions we ask, how we collect data, and what we think research

# can actually tell us as a field and as a society (Braun & Clarke, 2020; Ponterotto, 2005). My

# research is primarily guided by intersectional, structural, and critical-ideological epistemological

# frameworks. Specifically, I draw on historical and systemic factors such as neoliberalism,

# capitalism, racism, sexism, classism, and more in guiding the questions I ask and in framing and

# 

# 112

# interpreting findings. Further, I invoke an intersectional approach to this work in that I do not see

# nor interpret these underlying historical and systemic factors as disconnected. Rather, they help

# construct our current reality in ways that compound one another in disparate ways across time.

# Methods. Using this epistemological position as a framework to guide the questions and

# analysis in this Study, I operate from the perspective that every participant has a reality that we

# can try to understand by interacting with them, while recognizing that people’s reality is shaped

# by our social-historical context. While this ontological framework generally seeks to understand

# unique experiences which all are seen as valid without numerical frequency, I am also concerned

# in this study with patterns of experiences across groups of people and how we can use these

# patterns to speak to policy and practice needed for these women.

# To analyze interview data collected from participants, one of the co-chairs of my

# dissertation and I made use of a codebook, coding reliability and reflexive thematic analysis

# (Braun & Clarke, 2020; Guest, et al., 2012). Specifically, using a reflexive thematic analysis

# approach, I followed Braun & Clarke’s (2020) suggestion for generating themes which includes:

# “familiarization; coding; generating initial themes; reviewing and developing themes; refining,

# defining and naming themes; writing up” (Braun & Clarke, 2020, p. 39). The steps followed in

# reflexive thematic analysis allowed us to move from semantic coding that stuck close to what

# participants said to explore the latent content of responses across and within participant

# responses that helped move us into the realm of analysis (Ryan & Bernard, 2003; Braun, et al.,

# 2018). Latent content analysis via the deeper development of our themes provides the necessary

# tools to meet the goals of our ontological perspective—that social-historical context matters and

# 

# 113

# thus shapes the way people see and interpret their worlds. Further, central to the critical-

# ideological perspective is the assumption that the subjectivity of the researcher(s) is not

# controllable, but rather, should be utilized as an integral part of reflection in the process of data

# analysis to understand how data and the analysis of those data might be affected (Braun &

# Clarke, 2020; Wilkinson & Kitzinger, 2013).

# We followed an inductive (or data-driven) content analysis approach to initially

# organizing participant responses; meaning, initial codes were developed based on surface-level

# understanding of participant responses to questions. These codes included: experiences of

# mistreatment related to housing; experiences of mistreatment related to work; beliefs about what

# people deserve (including the participants themselves); and desires and hopes in life as well as

# what participants think stands in their way of achieving them.

# A total of 592 participant responses were extracted from interviews that fit these broad

# categories. Following this, we worked together to create themes that went beyond initial codes to

# capture more nuanced understanding of the data within and across categorical codes. While there

# were many more themes to be explored, the scope of this project warranted some boundaries

# around participant responses. Specifically, we chose to focus on issues related to work and

# housing that concerned mistreatment, given the centrality of mistreatment and violence

# experiences among low-income women that guides this dissertation. Based on the initial, broad

# categorization of women’s responses, we again familiarized ourselves with participant responses

# within each of these categorizations. We each took notes on responses to each of the four

# original categories and we met to discuss the similarities and dissimilarities for the ways we were

# 

# 114

# organizing the data. Based on this meeting, I then developed our initial codebook which

# consisted of 11 themes. We reviewed the codebook together and adjusted based on our

# familiarizations with participant responses. The final list of 9 themes relevant to mistreatment

# related to housing and work included: bureaucracy, issues with the space itself, hard work for

# little payoff, bad leadership/customers, violence, safety, discrimination, mental health, and

# neoliberal beliefs. Bureaucracy and issues with the space itself specifically pertained to

# participant responses about housing, and hard work for little payoff was related to responses

# about work experiences. All other themes spanned across work and housing experiences among

# these women.

# Finally, once themes were developed, named, and defined in our codebook (before

# writing up results), we assessed our agreement, or reliability, in coding participant responses. We

# did this by coding 10-12 passages at a time, calculating our percent category agreement (Holsti

# index), adjusting the theme definitions in our codebook as needed for clarity, and re-coding until

# reaching an appropriate level of reliability (80% or higher) (Boyatzis, 1998; Holsti, 1969;

# McHugh, 2012). Our first round of coding 12 participant passages yielded a 76.9% agreement.

# We discussed disagreements and made changes in the codebook to help both coders understand

# how to apply the codes to the text. Once 90% agreement was reached, I coded all remaining

# participant responses and re-checked our reliability after all data were coded (Boyatzis, 1998). A

# total of 369 participant responses were coded for our 9 themes.

# Using a mix of both reflexive thematic analysis and coding reliability thematic

# approaches to analyzing our interview data allows for reflexivity about the role of the researcher

# 

# 115

# in the process of data interpretation and provides a numerical representation for the coding

# reliability between two psychological researchers studying and deeply immersed in the interview

# data. While this reliability is only representative of two specific people’s ability to code similarly

# and cannot be interpreted as suggesting “objectivity” about participant responses, it provides

# some evidence that overlapping interpretations of these data was accomplished, and that

# evidence can be important for other researchers’ interpretation of our findings (Braun & Clarke,

# 2020).

# Responses to the questions were coded for as many themes as occurred within the

# response; thus, the themes are not mutually exclusive. On average, each response was coded for

# about one theme. While we originally started with 9 themes, we removed 3 from our analysis due

# to low frequency of response. Specifically, we calculated the frequency of each theme being

# reported by these women across 354 excerpts. Themes reported in 10% or fewer of the responses

# were dropped. These themes included: mental health and hard work for little payoff. We then

# decided to combine the themes of violence and safety as well as bad leaders/bad customers and

# discrimination concerns and experiences, in order to reflect on these qualitatively overlapping

# experiences and fears among the women.

# The five themes that we were left with, in order of frequency of presence in women’s

# reflections were: bureaucracy (86.4%; N=19), safety/violence (86.4%; N=19), mistreatment

# (86.4%; N=19), space issues (68.2%; N=15), and neoliberal beliefs (86.4%; N=19). Note that

# all the themes were mentioned by most of the women. Participant response lengths averaged

# about 147 words per response. The themes, along with examples, appear in Table 13.

# 

# 116

# Frequencies related to each of the themes can be found in Table 14.

# Table 13: Study 3 Theme Definitions and Examples

# Bureaucracy

# Definition

# This theme includes comments that reference issues

# navigating, or concerns related to bureaucracy (e.g., housing,

# workplace, governmental, etc.) that can include comments that

# reflect issues or concerns related to bureaucracy within their

# specific housing unit (e.g., with management policies),

# concerning the state/federal level related to their housing with

# state or federal entities (e.g., navigating Section 8

# requirements), concerning the community level related to their

# housing on the community level (e.g., limited organizational

# resources), alluding to potential for being penalized because

# certain behaviors aren’t allowed (e.g., saving) while on

# government assistance, and more.

# Examples

# I: And do you feel like in general your current housing

# situation meets your basic needs, if at all? P: it does meet my

# basic needs. I mean I’ve got shelter, you know I've got heat.

# I've got air, you know I just don't need the constant bullying

# Results and Preliminary Discussion

# Bureaucracy

# This theme includes comments that reference issues navigating, or concerns related to,

# bureaucracy (e.g., housing, workplace, governmental, etc.); these may be comments describing

# issues or concerns related to bureaucracy within their specific housing unit (e.g., with

# management policies), concerning the state/federal level related to their housing with state or

# federal entities (e.g., navigating Section 8 requirements), concerning the community level related

# to their housing on the community level (e.g., limited organizational resources), alluding to

# potential for being penalized because certain behaviors aren’t allowed (e.g., saving) while on

# government assistance, and more. Among the women we interviewed, while the specific

# bureaucratic demands differed depending on the institution and what women needed, women

# across housing and work situations reported difficulties navigating and interacting with

# government and local housing bureaucracy related to finding and maintaining stable housing,

# and with bureaucracy at work that set up environments that often made these women fearful of

# losing their job.

# In the interviews, women often discussed government bureaucracy and policy that limited

# their ability to secure and maintain stable housing. For instance, women discussed stringent

# income cutoffs for acquiring government funded housing, short time periods to find housing that

# will accept your housing voucher before you lose it (90 days), long waitlists and lotteries to even

# get on a waitlist to get a housing voucher, having to spend all of one’s assets before Social

# Security benefits are activated, finding housing in an area that the Section 8 office will approve

# 

# 123

# and then the specific housing passing inspection, COVID-19 causing issues in obtaining

# assistance due to limited appointments and appointment type (in person/virtual), losing benefits

# when trying to work, and rehabilitative services that help them find work not helping them find

# work that matches their skills and interests. Women also mentioned other barriers to maintaining

# housing or other benefits of governmental policies. One woman mentioned she lost her food

# stamp card and couldn’t access her funds until the new card came in the mail. Another woman

# mentioned that laws about where homeless individuals can sleep or have temporary shelters have

# caused her to lose everything she owned when someone called the police on them for their

# temporary shelter set up.

# Example: “The waiting lists are really long. Uhm. And even getting on a waiting list is

# lottery” (woman living in a HUD apartment).

# Apart from government policies that limited these women’s ability to find and maintain

# stable housing, housing bureaucracy also provided a different set of barriers. For instance,

# women mentioned it was hard to find a place that would accept their Section 8 voucher due to

# stereotypes about those who get this kind of assistance; and poor rental history, criminal record,

# and past evictions affecting approval once they do find a place that will accept the voucher.

# Women living in both types of housing at the time of our interviews faced bureaucratic

# barriers related to those in charge of those establishments. Specifically, women living in HUD

# apartments mentioned bureaucracy affecting their housing experience such as: fear of getting

# written up for supposedly violating a rule (three write ups can lead to eviction), unequal

# expectations of adherence to the rules among tenants by management, being told they have to

# 

# 124

# pay for anything that breaks in their apartment, rent increases each year when disability

# increases, limits on people visiting them or staying with them, and a need for a firmer anti-

# harassment policy. Additionally, a few women mentioned that management accidentally evicted

# the wrong person before and threw out all their belongings.

# Example: “Well, supposedly three write ups could equal eviction. But there are people

# with folder after folder of 20 years of write ups that never been evicted or anything. But

# other people have been evicted so I guess it depend on the severity of the problem”

# (woman living in HUD apartment).

# Women living in motels at the time of the interview mentioned motel bureaucracy

# affecting their housing experience such as: increases in nightly prices without increases in the

# accommodations themselves, a lack of WIFI, no microwaves in rooms, an extra charge for using

# a credit card, the need for an ID card to stay in one of the cheaper motels, and the fact that it

# costs them about $2,000 a month to stay in the motel.

# Example: “Yeah and I’m like man I gotta pay this much money from this damn Your

# Motel and y’all don’t even got a microwave in here no more. Just a refrigerator and just

# the TV and your bed. I mean you guys need upgrade on your towels and your rags if

# you’re gonna charge people that much money. Exactly and the blankets. Like y’all need

# to, you need new carpet in this damn place… And then, if you use a credit card, they

# charge you five dollars extra which I think is bullshit. So, I’m I’m paying for another

# night and I’m giving you a credit card and you’re telling me I gotta pay 65 dollas?”

# (woman living in a motel).

# Safety/Violence

# Frequency and Definition. Most women in the interviews made comments that were

# coded for safety/violence. This theme included comments that reflected women’s concerns,

# fears, or vigilance about their safety and experiences of violence as they relate to their housing or

# work situations. This could include (but was not limited to) sexual harassment, experiences of

# violence, shootings, yelling, fighting, sexual assault, stalking, being “picked up” while walking

# down the street, aggression, etc. Comments could also include avoidance actions (e.g., staying

# inside to keep their family safe), vigilance about safety (e.g., being aware of one’s surroundings),

# or fears about safety (e.g., generally feeling unsafe in their environment). While violence often

# included elements of mistreatment, the theme of violence was coded to reflect their experience if

# it also included the elements of the safety/violence theme.

# Similarities in safety/violence. Women in the two housing settings shared some

# commonalities in the types of fears and experiences of violence in relation to their housing.

# Apart from general concerns about their safety where they live women regardless of their type of

# housing, also discussed experiences and fears of sexual assault and sexual harassment. Related to

# these fears and experiences of assault and harassment they discussed men following them back to

# their room or apartment; fears of having to use the communal shower area in their motel that also

# housed the only washer/dryer that was accessible through the women’s bathroom; not wearing

# “nice” clothes for fear of people who live in their building harassing them; and being careful

# 

# 127

# about what they talk about and how they talk to other people, especially men because they didn’t

# want to come across as too friendly for fear of sending the wrong message and experiences of

# harassment or worse.

# Example: “But what happened to me there [at their old HUD apartment in the area] is

# a man tried to rape me, one of my neighbors and uh I ended up pressing charges on him

# and… they gave him two years probation. And then he came back to the same apartment,

# on the floor I live[d] on, that he lived on and was able to go back. And that's where I

# cracked. I lost it. I got raped way back in the 90s by about 10 guys and it was bad. And

# when he grabbed me, that whole thing flooded back immediately, and I was in complete

# terror, I mean it was just really bad. I like my apartment [but] when they let him stay, I

# said I can't handle this, and he came up dead about two weeks after I left. I ended up

# being out of a place for almost two years [staying with family/homeless]. It was bad,

# really bad. I shouldn't have just walked away, but I did. I didn't see any other way at that

# time… this lady over here at Clark tower she tried to mess me over and stop me from

# getting in here, because she was mad that I left and. You know I didn't do anything

# wrong; it was it was her not taking care of that situation with that guy and I just cracked,

# I mean I left. I I’d paid my rent every single day up to that day” (woman living in a HUD

# apartment).

# In this excerpt one of the women currently living in a government subsidized apartment

# reflected on her experience living in a different HUD apartment building. A man attempted to

# rape her that lived on her floor and was then allowed to return to her same floor after being

# 

# 128

# released on probation. Despite the extreme difficulty that many of these women across housing

# type discussed in obtaining government funded housing accommodations (getting off the waitlist

# and then into a lottery where you still must randomly be selected), this woman left that apartment

# to go and live with her sister down south. That didn’t work out and she shortly found herself

# back in Michigan and homeless for over a year before securing her spot in the current HUD

# apartment. Additionally, because she left her previous funded apartment situation abruptly, the

# manager at her old apartment building tried to convince the manager of her current building not

# to approve her for an apartment. What is important for this and many of the other examples of

# experiences and fears of sexual assault and harassment regardless of the type of housing these

# women were in, is that particularities of the precarity of this housing either specifically

# contribute to their experiences of mistreatment through the lack of protection related to their

# housing, or they leave women more susceptible to further housing insecurity as in the case of this

# woman. Other concerns were common among the women we interviewed: concerns about theft

# of their belongings and their food; fears about people using drugs who live near them (one

# woman was newly recovering from a drug addiction so this environment was particularly

# challenging for her); fears of threats from management (either in the apartment building or in the

# motel they were staying in); and fear of befriending others in their building/motel.

# Finally, the women, were concerned about reporting their experiences of violence and

# mistreatment to the management of their housing or to a formal institution like the police,

# regardless of their current housing situation. Specifically, women did not view management as a

# useful source to report to and feared reporting to the police (e.g., one woman discussed her fear

# and anxiety of the police coming around any time because she was currently on probation and

# the risk of getting in trouble could jeopardize this status).

# Example: “I just feel like I need to say out of it and just try to keep me and my family as

# safe as possible” (woman living in a motel).

# Differences in safety/violence. Women’s concerns and experiences related to safety and

# violence differed in some ways in terms of what they focused on depending on the type of

# housing they were in. Specifically, women living in HUD housing at the time of the interview

# focused on interpersonal factors as central to their concerns and experiences of violence and

# safety related to their housing. Specifically, these interpersonal factors often focused on

# strategies of protection such as concealing information about themselves and being hyperaware

# 

# 130

# of their surroundings. For instance, women discussed having to interact frequently with people

# who harassed them or they feared would harass them in their building in order to access building

# resources (e.g., food pantry); fears about people knowing which apartment they live in or what

# car they drive; avoiding using the stairs in their building because they don’t have cameras like

# the elevators do; trying to protect other women in their building from mistreatment, and how

# high up from the ground floor they live.

# Example: “Which is why I don't let people in my apartment and I, I made the mistake

# that one time of letting one person in and they're like… Now, now, like all the people I'm

# really not sure I want to know where I live, know where I live. And people will chime in

# too. Like if you're in line at food gathers and you say oh, I live, you know someone asked

# you where you live, and you say I live on the second floor… and they say oh where? Or

# what number? And I say, oh I’m near the laundry. And they’re so they’re like, okay so

# this guy showed up at my door. Like four times in one day because I talked to him in line

# at food gatherer. So, it's very like you know gossipy and… Creepy” (woman living in a

# HUD apartment).

# Among women living in motels at the time of the interview, concerns and experiences

# related to their housing also included interpersonal factors, but ones that were often more public

# in nature; moreover, the women reporting these were less focused on strategies for protecting

# themselves. Specifically, they expressed fears of mistreatment using public transportation,

# solicitation for sex while simply walking down the street to get to where they need to go,

# concerns about the fact that prostitution occurs where they live, and taking turns sleeping due to

# 

# 131

# fears of people breaking in. Therefore, while those who had been able to secure government

# funded housing had interpersonal fears about those that lived in their building, those currently

# living in motels had broader interpersonal concerns and experiences that involved more diffuse

# anxiety about other people. Women currently living in motels talked less about strategies to

# protect themselves from these interpersonal experiences or fears relative to those in government

# funded housing at the time of the interview.

# Example: “It’s like psychologically I feel like I'm having to go in through a war zone to

# get to a meeting [drug recovery meeting]. Uh, I had a guy try to pick me up as I'm

# Finally, many of the fears and experiences of violence related to the motel housing were

# expressed in terms of survival concerns. These included concerns about how the women were

# generally going to make it from day to day. For example, women expressed fears about not

# having a place to sleep that night, about where their next meal will come from (if it comes at all),

# Example: “I’m shattered. I'm scared. I don't like having that feeling of okay, am I going

# Mistreatment

# This theme consisted of women’s specific experiences with people (e.g., bosses,

# customers, management, people who live in their apartment/motel, other people they work with)

# who had mistreated them (e.g., getting written up for drinking water in front of a customer,

# homeowner hovering and critiquing while they clean, getting fined at work, getting written up

# for an unclear apartment, etc.), or with people who were described by the person as overbearing,

# unpleasant, unqualified, or incompetent. This could include experiences of discrimination from

# leaders, bosses, management (at work or in their housing), colleagues, customers, or people they

# live nearby. Most of the women described experiences with mistreatment.

# Across housing type, women mentioned experiences of discrimination based on gender

# presentation, physical ability status, socioeconomic status (e.g., when trying to find housing), and

# mental health status, and also discussed experiences of harassment from people who manage

# 

# 133

# their housing and people who live in the same building. As a result of this mistreatment and

# discrimination, some women discussed avoiding building resources in order to prevent further

# harassment.

# Space Issues

# Women commented about issues associated with their living space in terms of physical

# features (e.g., small, or dirty), or the absence of features available to them (e.g., no way to heat

# food up). Over two-thirds of the women interviewed noted concerns related to their housing

# space.

# Women currently living in a HUD apartment made comments concerning their general

# discontent with the environment. Specifically, they mentioned that the apartment is too small,

# that it is noisy (e.g., they often hear other people, washers/dryers, the freeway), that they’ve

# encountered mice, that the mail area is unsecure, the neighborhood is not wheelchair accessible,

# and there aren’t enough activities for children in the neighborhood.

# Example: “Probably 20 years ago. Honestly, they started taking things away and not

# really brining anything back for the kids. I mean this park, this park is nice, and we do

# have quite a few parks in Ypsilanti but not like if you go to the apartment complexes out

# here, there’s no playgrounds for the kids in the apartment complexes. You have to leave

# 

# 136

# the area where you live to go to the park. So, yeah definitely could have more activities

# for the kids” (woman living in HUD apartment).

# They also mentioned things in their living space that negatively affect their health such as people

# smoking in the building, people having pets in the building (they have allergies), and not being

# able to control the temperature of their apartment year-round (e.g., the heat and air conditioning

# is set to come on at certain times of the year regardless of the temperature outside).

# Example: “Well with me what the issue is right now is that they won't turn the air

# have a solid answer and uhm, and it's like I have to deal with that, because the heat

# makes me sick really sick” (woman living in HUD apartment).

# bathroom when I need to… Uhm, not having a bunch of people, you know, having all of

# us having to stay in in the same room (I: In one room, yeah). Oh man. And uh, yeah. And

# I’m by myself. I mean you know I it's nice because I only have to deal with myself. I don't

# have to deal with… everybody else, yes” (woman living in HUD apartment).

#
