# 139

# Neoliberal Beliefs

# Participant comments often reflected neoliberal beliefs. These included their own ideas

# and their perceptions of other people’s ideas related to educational attainment, work ethic,

# individualism/personal responsibility for life circumstances, being grateful for the bare minimum

# (e.g., housing—even if it’s awful, etc.), and the tension between wanting to help people and not

# feeling like you can because of constraints (e.g., an “us” against everyone else mentality). Most

# of the women expressed neoliberal beliefs in their interviews either about themselves and their

# own experiences or perceptions of those experiences or about other people.

# Women offered a lot of insight into their experiences, perceptions, and hopes related to

# work. At the same time, many of their comments about work, regardless of their housing or work

# precarity status, reflected neoliberal beliefs about prioritizing hard work and feeling that one’s

# value in life stems from work contributions. Specifically, women talked about not feeling as

# good as other people when they aren’t working, about not feeling productive enough when they

# do work (even though they mentioned they were working as fast as they could), and about

# wanting to go back to work (regardless of health status). Their comments emphasize the

# centrality of work as integral to their feelings of worth in life.

# Example: I: what do you hope for yourself for the future? Participant (P): That my

# lungs, my health gets better so I can go back to work. I: Yeah. No, but for anything else?

# Just to go back to work? P: Well, to go back to work, and be there for my kids and my

# grandbabies. (woman living in a motel)

# 

# 140

# In the example above, it is clear that above anything else, this woman desires to go back to work.

# Even thoughts about her family come second to this when asked about her hope for her future.

# This is despite the fact that her doctor has told her she can’t work because of health issues

# (difficulty breathing) that likely are a result of previous jobs (breathing in chemicals at cleaning

# jobs).

# Example: “P: Yeah, it's just just being able to depend on having a check coming in. And

# then the way that you feel when you’re working. You always feel better about yourself…I

# just know that when I don't that I don't feel as good of as a person as anybody else that

# does…” (woman living in HUD apartment).

# Similarly, the woman above discusses that she misses working and having a consistent income,

# and the feeling that you get when working. She doesn’t feel as good as anyone else who is

# working, despite the fact that her health limits her ability to work.

# Women in informal work positions mentioned that in those positions their work and skills

# are often devalued in the way that people treat them, and they are compensated little for their

# time and work. They additionally discuss that in informal positions they are not protected in the

# same ways they are in formal positions. For example, there can often be a lack of consistency in

# how much and how often they are compensated, their bosses can cut their hours with little notice,

# and people expect a lot more for very little pay.

# Example: “For instance, there was a woman in this Church I was going to at the time

# and I uh I needed help, I needed to earn some extra money. And so, they set me up with

# this lady who needed help. And so, I get over to her house it's a complete disaster it's a

# 

# 141

# great big place in Canton and they have money. She's paying me 10 bucks an hour. And I

# mean she wanted blood… I was, I was sick before I even get done doing the first half of

# the house. I had worked myself sick and then she's following me around like wanting me

# do this, wanting me to do that, wanting me to this… And then she's rolling behind me,

# looking at what I’ve done and that's taking me twice as long and I’m like I ain’t doing

# this again… I did it one more time and that was it. She got blood for that money”

# (woman living in HUD apartment).

# The belief that certain work is less valuable (e.g., through lower pay and more expectation of

# output) contributes to the acceptance of the exploitation of this type of labor. Based on neoliberal

# beliefs, one is responsible for their own position and outcomes in life. It is up to you whether you

# succeed or fail depending on how hard you want to work. We can see these beliefs playing out in

# the lived experiences of these women in positions where they are especially vulnerable to

# mistreatment and being devalued in informal work positions.

# Neoliberal beliefs were also present in their perceptions of others and of themselves.

# Specifically, women, across housing and workplace situations, evoked stereotypes about others

# that mirrored neoliberal beliefs when considering why people are without work and what others

# are deserving of. For instance, they reflected that some people just don’t want to work because

# they’re lazy or because of COVID, that family examples of using government assistance set

# them up to do the same as adults, and that people only deserve and are entitled to the very basics

# in life.

# 

# 142

# Example: “Well, I think there's plenty of jobs, but people are not willing to work. They

# want to get paid for doing nothing, sitting on their butts and, no that’s not the way I feel

# it should work. If you want money in your pocket, I think you should do the work that you

# are getting paid to do. You know, and and I think right now, there’s plenty of jobs. But

# there’s people out there saying, oh I got disabilities, I got this that. Well, you have to be

# proven by a doctor to have that disability in order to get it, okay. But the the there’s other

# people that don’t want to work. And I think them kind of people are just lazy” (woman

# living in a HUD apartment).

# Additionally, women, again regardless of housing and workplace precarity, often solely blamed

# themselves and their own decisions for their position in life. They believe that other people are

# deserving of things, but not them. They very often blamed themselves for their position in life

# based on their education level (e.g., that they never finished school), their health, or criminal

# background. Many expressed that they wanted to pursue education when they couuld.

# Example: “Uh… I don’t know. I don’t know what it is… I feel like I’ve not done

# enough… like in my life like I’ll I’ll be 39 this year. And like I feel just like I’ve not done

# enough. So, that’s like what where schooling and stuff comes in like…” (woman living in

# a motel).

# Women also expressed some interpersonal concerns, regardless of their housing and

# workplace settings, that reflected neoliberal beliefs. Specifically, they noted that they often felt

# like they couldn’t befriend other people in a similar position as them because they worried they

# 

# 143

# would get taken advantage of, and that they didn’t trust people enough to give them money in

# times of need because they worried people would spend it on drugs or other non-necessities.

# Example: “I don’t understand why why I gotta be giving people money at the uh

# intersection like what the hell? But people gotta want good for theyself. I can’t just want

# good for everybody. You have to want it. It have to be in you. You have to, I have to see

# you want it too” (woman living in a HUD apartment).

# In this interpersonal vein, women also frequently expressed a general scarcity mindset that really

# seemed to drive a wedge between people in and outside of workplace settings. For example, they

# felt that they didn’t get enough money to live on government assistance because there isn’t

# enough to go around; they mentioned they had to exhaust all other resources before being able to

# get help from local agencies; that in the workplace people wouldn’t speak out about mistreatment

# for fear of rocking the boat and ending up in trouble themselves; and that they felt responsible

# for the benefits of their fellow employees based on the way the reward system was set up to

# depend on the success of all for everyone’s bonus.

# Example: “I was at work, and I had gotten in trouble because I bent over to pick

# something up and threw my back out… They did an investigation cuz they said I had

# caused an accident… that was another reason why I quit was because uhm they lost their

# bonus. The whole building lost their bonus because of me. And they told them that. And

# everybody was like you should quit, we don't like you here. Why did you report that you

# had hurt. You're not supposed to report that you got hurt. Now we've lost our bonus”

# (woman living in a HUD apartment).

# 

# 144

# Women in the interviews across housing and workplace experiences also mentioned

# some barriers external to themselves and their own actions that they saw as prominent to their

# position in life. For example, they pointed out that people don’t get paid enough, that there are

# barriers that limit them from being able to access housing even with government assistance (e.g.,

# work status and credit checks for housing even with a Section 8 voucher), and the catch 22 of

# government assistance that encourages them to work but then takes benefits that they need away

# when they attempt to do so.

# Example: “They got us kind of in a catch 22 on SSI. And uhm, I have got to find a way to

# get through that without cutting myself short, anyway. You know? And try get some kind

# of education. I’m not dead, yet. They told me that if I went back to work, because when

# they gave me the SSI award based on… uh I was in liver failure, but it was based off of

# clinical depression... And uhm, so they said that if you go back to work, and you can do

# something with your mind you don't have any reason to be on SSI… And so, you're

# walking a fine line. You gotta really watch it because they're looking to cut people off

# real real bad. And when you get off, you’re going to have a hard time getting back on

# now. That’s the catch 22…If you get if you get if they raise you up some way, they take it

# back another. Like if they raise up my SSI, they pull back some on food stamps, whatever

# that difference is. Yeah, you never can get ahead, except for $1 or two. [laughs]. That's

# why I gotta do something to break out of the cycle. I'm being controlled under, in this

# type of housing and I don't like it” (woman living in a HUD apartment).

# 

# 145

# Finally, women discussed perspective as being a key component of their position in life.

# There was a general sentiment across the groups of women of making the most of what you have

# and being grateful for what you have. They were often grateful for the bare minimum in terms of

# housing accommodations and their ability to make ends meet. This reflects neoliberal beliefs that

# people get what they deserve in life based on the effort they put into it. While this reflects

# neoliberalism, it also in a sense, offered a valued sense of autonomy to these women. While their

# situation in life is challenging on a daily basis, they relish that they can still control how they feel

# about it, their outlook in life, and the narrative they spin for others about their situation.

# Example: “Some people are born to money somewhere, some aren’t. Some are victims of

# crime, some aren’t. It’s just the way it is. It’s how you, it’s how you handle that. What

# you make of it. So, I wouldn’t change anything” (woman living in a HUD apartment).

# Conclusion

# Taking the results above, the experiences in daily life start to provide a picture of life

# among women living and working in precarious settings. The first four themes: bureaucracy,

# safety/violence, mistreatment, and space issues, help us understand that day-to-day living among

# these women is nothing short of difficult. Attempting to understand and meet bureaucracy

# demands across every front of their life just to meet their basic needs, while also navigating

# safety, violence, and mistreatment, vividly illustrates the gaps in our infrastructure that have

# fundamentally failed these women.

# 

# 146

# Discussion

# Participants described their workplace and housing experiences of mistreatment in terms

# of five themes: bureaucracy, safety/violence, space issues, and mistreatment, and neoliberal

# beliefs. By analyzing these interviews, we aimed to learn about the lives of women living and

# working in precarious situations. We further sought to capture the spontaneous expression of

# neoliberal beliefs among these women.

# While we had originally expected there to be some differences in the experiences of these

# women based on the relative precarity of their housing and work, the results showed that there

# was overlap between our categories of precarity in housing (HUD vs. motel) and work (informal

# vs. formal) themselves. Most women who participated in our interviews, regardless of their

# current housing or workplace situations, had experience with both more and less precarious

# housing and work (e.g., a woman currently living in a motel would mention that she had Section

# 8 previously or a woman living in a HUD apartment currently might mention having been

# homeless or living in a motel in the past). Further, most women, regardless of their current work

# or housing setting discussed difficulties in navigating bureaucracy, experiences and fears of

# safety/violence, experiences of mistreatment, and issues related to their space; importantly, there

# was much overlap in the types of experiences they talked about. Finally, while these women

# expressed few differences between precarity of housing and work experiences, they often

# expressed the ever-present precarity of their lives, feeling often on the edge of sliding down or

# moving up in terms of housing and workplace security.

# 

# 147

# Neoliberal beliefs were present among women but there were no systematic differences

# in who endorsed these beliefs. Further, most frequently, women expressed neoliberal beliefs

# while critiquing themselves and their own position in life. Apart from the neoliberal beliefs

# expressed by these women, neoliberalism as a structural power was evident in all the other

# themes that reflected their day-to-day life with housing and work. Further, many of these themes

# were related to and influenced one another, often in the realm of gender-based mistreatment and

# violence.

# Finally, in the texture of these women’s day-to-day life, the accounts that were coded in

# our research are less easily separated than might appear in our discussion here. Specifically,

# experiences reflected in our individual themes both happened simultaneously and were

# overlapping and often affected each other in their lived experience. Further, as discussed below,

# themes that we defined were sometimes catalysts for one another. For example, in the results, I

# outlined an example of a woman who lost her housing due to housing bureaucracy that affected

# her experience where someone in her apartment attempted to rape her and then went on to affect

# her later re-application for an apartment in another government funded complex years later.

# Bureaucracy

# Within the theme of bureaucracy, women commented on barriers to successfully

# navigating bureaucratic demands across type of housing and type of work. Women discussed

# bureaucracy at the federal and local levels as barriers to accessing and maintaining stable

# housing. Women who currently lived in motels mentioned the stringent rules for applying for

# government funded housing including strict income cutoffs, and long waitlists and lotteries to

# 

# 148

# even get on a waitlist for Section 8. Women who had secured government subsidized housing

# often reflected on these same issues as reasons they felt stuck in their current living situation.

# They might like to move but there were few available places that accept their housing vouchers,

# and they were reluctant to risk the housing they were able to secure and have to navigate difficult

# housing bureaucracy again, if they had to reapply.

# Many of the policies mentioned by women in our interviews reflected the view that some

# women deserve economic support, and others do not. If women meet the arbitrary criteria of

# deservingness, they are then placed on a waitlist for the Section 8 housing lottery where their fate

# is up to chance, despite the undercurrent of blame toward them for their situation in life (Bullock,

# 1999; Bullock, Williams & Limbert, 2003; Feagin, 1972; Lott & Bullock, 2001). As discussed in

# the introduction of the dissertation, personal responsibility and individual effort as espoused by

# neoliberal ideology directly contrasts with the lottery-like economic outcomes of lived

# experience where people are less likely to be economically mobile than to repeat the economic

# situation of their families (Bourdieu, 1986; Case & Deaton, 2020; Harvey, 2005).

# The bureaucracy on the federal level adds to a sense of scarcity among these women.

# They are in direct competition with one another for basic resources that are seen as limited and

# finite, including housing. The obstacles presented by housing bureaucracy create large barriers to

# accessing resources that should be readily available for anyone facing housing insecurity.

# However, under neoliberalism, individualism is prized, systemic inequality is discounted, and

# competition for “finite” resources is promoted; thus, the actual overabundance of economic

# resources pooled among those historically privileged by colonial legacies is viewed as earned

# 

# 149

# and justified (Harvey, 2005; Segalo & Fine, 2020; Son Hing, 2013). The combination of these

# ideas drives these women’s experiences navigating and appealing to the federal and local

# bureaucratic demands as “needy enough” to deserve aid. Further, the promotion of these

# resources as “finite,” despite the gross and unequal distribution of generational wealth, is what

# maintains these women’s precarity in terms of housing and discourages them from fighting

# against this system. The myth of these limited resources maintains their fear of failing to meet

# one of their most basic needs-- housing-- and thus falsely engineers an economic world where

# perceptions of deservingness and individualism are central.

# While many of the women critique the lack of housing available for people in their

# situations (e.g., that everyone should have access to housing if needed), some endorse a scarcity

# mindset of limited government resources as one reason why it is so challenging to obtain

# government-funded housing (e.g., there isn’t enough to go around for everyone). Further,

# regardless of their perspective on housing scarcity, most of the women blamed themselves for

# their situation in life regarding housing in terms consistent with neoliberal ideology. Specifically,

# women believed they should have worked harder, they should have continued their education,

# they should have waited to have children, and in general, they should have made better choices.

# This finding fits research documenting that people generally believe individual control is central

# in economic outcomes, even among those most oppressed by systemic economic inequality

# (Bullock, 2013; Feagin, 1972; Jost & Banaji, 1994; Jost, et al., 2015; Larrain, 1983; Liu, et al.,

# 2011; Marx & Engles, 1998; Young, 2004).

# 

# 150

# In addition to bureaucracy at the federal level, women across housing type discussed

# bureaucracy on the more local level (e.g., management at their housing units) in dealing with

# demands and rules in their current housing situation. The bureaucracy at this level seemed to

# work in combination with bureaucracy at the federal government level to maintain fears about

# sustaining stable housing even among women living in subsidized housing who had been able to

# successfully navigate the federal demands to secure that housing. Women expressed concerns

# about being evicted for things they couldn’t control, getting written up for violating rules

# governing the housing, and the unequal application of building policies to residents. While the

# fundamental goal of these rules and policies within their housing is likely not intentionally tied to

# neoliberalism, notions of deservingness and individualism are reflected in the ever-present threat

# of housing insecurity that looms in write ups, evictions, and more (Harvey, 2005; Son Hing,

# 2013). To maintain the centrality of deservingness in decisions about economic aid and to justify

# actions that make it challenging for some to access these resources, there must always be those

# deemed undeserving (Bullock, 1999; Bullock & Lott, 2010b; Bullock, et al., 2003; Feagin, 1972;

# Lott & Bullock, 2001; Weiner, 1995; Williams, 2009).

# A similar pattern was expressed in experiences within women’s workplaces. Women

# were anxious about keeping their jobs, based on constant concerns about being written up or

# penalized for things they did not control. This fear in both primary realms of life is integral to

# maintaining cheap and exploited labor that capitalism, as it currently exists, requires. Since

# African Americans achieved increased rights post-slavery, these “strategies of terror” have been

# used as mechanisms for maintaining an exploited class of cheap laborers (Bruyneel, 2020; Davis,

# 

# 151

# 1981). The deep investment in neoliberal ideology and ideas about deservingness among people

# in the U.S. produces constant questioning of the adequacy of people’s productivity and hard

# work, as well as people’s deservingness of “free” housing or other “free” government support

# (Harvey, 2005; Son Hing, 2013). The precarity that is produced by these ideas in both

# employment and housing maintains a class of people that is utterly desperate for the basic

# necessities of life. They are seen and portrayed as failures in a system that assumes everyone can

# be successful, with those who “chose” not to be constantly critiqued and—particularly

# poignantly—many internalize that critique. This process reinforces neoliberal ideology and

# supports capitalist exploitation (Harvey, 2005; Son Hing, 2013). Focus on individualism is

# integral to successfully avoiding assessment of systemic-level influence on these life outcomes

# (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey, 2005; Perez & Slater, 2019; Son Hing, 2013).

# Safety/Violence

# While we know that low-income women are disproportionately likely to experience

# gender-based mistreatment and are less likely to be seen as legitimate victims compared to

# women coming from more economically resourced backgrounds, structural attributions that aid

# in perpetuating these experiences are often overlooked (Fessler, 2018; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982;

# LaFree, et al., 1985; MacKinnon, 1979; Maryland Coalition Against Sexual Assault [Maryland

# Coalition Against Sexual Assault MCASA], n.d.).We expected women living in more precarious

# housing situations to discuss experiences of gender-based mistreatment more frequently. While

# this was not the case, their concerns, and experiences both overlapped and differed from those in

# less precarious housing in important ways. Crucially, regardless of securing more stable housing

# 

# 152

# (HUD housing), women across housing type describe safety fears and experiences of violence

# that relate to their housing situation.

# Women in both types of housing discussed experiences and fears about sexual assault and

# sexual harassment, fears of theft, fears about drug use among people living near them, and fears

# of housing management. This supports previous research that documents the importance of

# economic precarity in women’s experiences of mistreatment (Bay-Cheng & Bruns, 2016;

# Bullock, et al., 2020; Edin & Schaefer, 2015; MacKinnon, 1979; Maryland Coalition Against

# Sexual Assault [MCASA]). Similarly, women also commonly discussed fears about reporting

# experiences of violence to someone in authority because they feared interactions with the police

# or didn’t believe that anything useful would come from reporting; this has previously been

# shown to be especially true among unhoused and recently unhoused women (Bullock, et al.,

# 2020).

# While there were many overlapping fears and experiences of violence and safety, women

# also reflected on some experiences and fears that were more particular to the housing

# arrangements as well. Women living in HUD housing at the time of our interview reported

# concerns and experiences that focused on interpersonal factors that were concerned with

# strategies of self-protection from others. Women living in motels also discussed some

# interpersonal factors; they focused on fears of others with less emphasis on strategies for self-

# protection. Additionally, the women living in motels outlined fears and experiences of violence

# that focused on basic survival concerns and on a generally stressful and violent living

# environment.

# 

# 153

# While neoliberal policy affecting housing and employment among low-income women

# contributed to experiences of violence, the experiences and fear of violence that were a product

# of neoliberal policy also sometimes led back to women’s precarity of housing and precarity of

# employment. Neoliberal bureaucracy related to housing and work both were mentioned as

# contributors that directly affected some women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment and

# likewise, affected their housing and work precarity in a circular way. Specifically, one woman

# discussed how she faced homelessness for almost two years after building management at her

# apartment let the man who attempted to rape her back onto her floor to live. Given the scarcity of

# housing resources among these women, this woman had to choose either to continue to live on a

# floor near a man who tried to rape her or to risk this housing to protect herself. She chose the

# latter and this directly led to her homelessness. Another woman discussed how she became

# unemployed as a direct result of reporting an experience of sexual harassment in her workplace,

# because management decided to let her go instead of the man who harassed her because he had

# worked there longer. Similarly, a woman who was sexually harassed at work was forced to leave

# her job after reporting her experience to management. Previous research shows that women

# working in service positions are significantly more likely to experience and tolerate experiences

# of gender-based mistreatment at work based on the necessity of their jobs and the precarity of

# low-wage work (Edin & Schaefer, 2015; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982; Messing, 2014).

# Given that low-income women are less likely to be believed in reporting experiences of

# gender-based mistreatment, face negative consequences related to housing and work when

# reporting these experiences, and are then blamed for their lack of employment or housing,

# 

# 154

# neoliberalism is present in creating these women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment in

# the context of housing and work. These experiences outline the complex challenges that women

# face in navigating their own protection from houselessness and unemployment and avoiding

# gender-based mistreatment and violence.

# Mistreatment

# Women living and working in these precarious situations reported mistreatment as a

# standard aspect of daily life as they encounter others with whom they live and work. They

# discussed experiences of identity-based discrimination, sexual harassment, gender harassment

# and more from bosses, colleagues, and customer at work, and managers and residents in their

# homes.

# Resulting from these experiences, a range of consequences was described. Specifically,

# women talked about avoiding building resources (e.g., free food pantries), being fired, being

# written up, being threatened with eviction, and more. Among women who discussed the potential

# of reporting these experiences to someone in management in their homes, to someone in

# management at work, or to an outside entity (e.g., the police), almost none of them thought their

# experiences would be taken seriously or appropriately handled by any of these authorities.

# Further, they feared losing their housing or employment, as was the case for a few women who

# did report these experiences to someone.

# What is clear from these women’s discussions of mistreatment is that these experiences

# do not stand out as singular incidents, but rather appear to be an integral part of daily living.

# 

# 155

# Further, there are few repercussions for those responsible for their mistreatment, and the women

# are well aware of this fact.

# Space Issues

# While there was much overlap in women’s general concerns about their living spaces--

# including complaints about noise and not having enough space-- the difference between women

# in HUD apartments vs. motels stemmed from the degree to which they could control these

# issues. Specifically, while women in the HUD apartments sometimes mentioned they didn’t have

# enough space to cook an intricate meal or to have multiple projects going on at once in their

# apartment, women living in motels discussed experiences living in one small room with a family

# of five and not having the capacity to cook in their homes at all, due to a lack of kitchen or even

# a microwave to heat meals. For women in HUD apartments, the most basic needs related to their

# space were generally met, but they had desires for changes that would enhance their

# environment. Women living in motels generally did not have their basic needs met when it came

# to their living space.

# While women living in HUD apartments wished to change some aspects of their space to

# enhance their overall living conditions, they were generally satisfied with their housing

# accommodations. Their satisfaction seemed to mostly stem from their fears of losing this housing

# and from the expression that there were limited options available for obtaining similarly

# government-funded housing. Neoliberal beliefs influencing the amount of government funded

# housing options available to these women and fears of returning to being houseless or living in

# motels seems to contribute to the general satisfaction with these women’s housing despite the

# 

# 156

# many problems related to space and problems that contribute to experiences of mistreatment and

# violence. Among women living in motels, their desire to obtain government funded apartments

# left them in a seemingly constant state of hope for this housing. Neoliberal policy that has

# contributed to the scarcity and competition of government funded housing among these women

# have implicated both groups of women. Women in the HUD apartments felt complicit in their

# current housing situations despite the many issues due to the limited availability of housing for

# them. Women in motels aspired for a housing voucher to obtain this government funded housing.

# The day-to-day focus for these women was rightfully concerned with getting and

# maintaining the basic necessity of housing. Given the constraints of attaining government funded

# housing based on neoliberal policy among these women, again, the connection between

# capitalism and neoliberalism is clear. Specifically, the strategic set up of scarcity of low-income

# housing as a result of neoliberal policy has drawn these women’s focus away from the fact that

# the overall housing available to them is qualitatively and quantitatively poor. While they are very

# likely aware of this, and some even mention it, their focus remains on attaining and maintaining

# this scarce resource. As discussed previously, the unique and crucial importance of neoliberalism

# in turning attention away from structural inequalities and making people believe they don’t exist

# is necessary to maintaining capitalist exploitation among the very groups most implicated by this

# system (Arfken, 2018, p. 685; Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Brown, 2003; Harvey, 2005; Perez &

# Salter, 2019; Son Hing, 2013).

# 

# 157

# Neoliberal Beliefs

# Regardless of the type of housing or type of work women discussed, neoliberal beliefs

# were central in their understanding of the world and their position in life. They valued work as

# key to their self-value, they believed other people were deserving of things but not them, they

# blamed themselves based on their education level, health, lack of a “career,” and criminal

# background. The valuing of work and their deep desire to return to work (despite many with

# health issues), to pursue a career, and to obtain higher levels of education has been noted in

# previous research by (Hancock, 2004). Like the women in Hancock’s study, the women in our

# study also expressed many hopes and desires related to work and education; at the same time,

# health issues and bureaucratic barriers often prevented them from reaching those goals.

# In addition to neoliberal beliefs, many of the women interviewed recognized some

# element that was outside of their control when it came to their life circumstances. However, even

# when mentioning these, they often returned to blaming themselves for their position in life.

# These women’s responses show that neoliberal beliefs and a critique of bureaucratic systems can

# exist simultaneously. The women recognized that in some instances these systems work against

# them and their goals in life, but they also believed that they could have done more to avoid being

# dependent on the system in the first place. Perhaps the absence of a structural critique that

# absolves these women of responsibility is missing from their own life because of the impact

# neoliberalism has on the relationships they have with other women around them. Neoliberal

# beliefs created among the women a fear of one another rather than a sense of community that one

# could imagine would be important among individuals with few resources. Brown (2003)

# 

# 158

# suggests that a key component and strategy of neoliberalism is reconfiguring all human

# experience into a capitalist equation of “scarcity, supply and demand, and moral value-

# neutrality” (p.5). Crucial to maintaining the myths of individual agency in success in life is

# creating separation between struggling people. The fear instilled through limited and scare

# resources that these women described is created by and maintains the illusion of neoliberal

# individual success and deservingness. Not only are these women facing demands, barriers, and

# obstacles in navigating bureaucracy at every level of life, they have constant fears regarding their

# safety, they experience violence and mistreatment in their housing and work contexts, and they

# are also extremely isolated in these experiences from other women facing similar demands in

# life.

# Conclusion

# Apart from individual participant comments that reflected neoliberal beliefs directly,

# these beliefs were a present undercurrent influencing experiences that participants reflected on in

# all other themes (bureaucracy, safety/violence, mistreatment, and space issues). Further, there

# was often an overlap and trickle down into more nuanced experiences in these women’s lives

# that could be traced back to neoliberal policy in their reflections of bureaucracy. Policies and

# practices in housing and workplace bureaucracy filtered into their direct experiences and

# concerns about safety, violence, mistreatment, and issues with their space. These women’s

# reflections on their daily lives demonstrate that research in areas of marginalized women’s

# mistreatment requires a deeply thoughtful approach to understanding the ways in which policy

# 

# 159

# and other influencers at the structural level implicate their individual experiences in day-to-day

# life.

# 

# 

# 160

# Chapter 4: Overall Dissertation Discussion

# The purpose of this dissertation was to explore the potential influence of neoliberalism on

# perceptions and experiences of gender-based mistreatment. To assess the role of neoliberalism

# on individual-level experience and perception, I attempted to approach this from multiple angles.

# In Study 1, I assessed the role of individual neoliberal beliefs on people’s perceptions of blame

# toward women in experiences of gender-based mistreatment broadly. In Study 2, I took these

# perceptions a step further to try to understand how these judgments might look different toward

# women who are most implicated by stereotypes applicable to gender-based mistreatment and by

# neoliberalism at the structural-level: specifically, racially Black, and White lower-income

# women in experiences of sexual assault. Finally, in Study 3, from the perspective of low-income

# women themselves, I attempted to understand the role of neoliberalism on women’s lived

# experiences attending to the ways in which housing and work precarity as a result of neoliberal

# policy keeps these women disproportionately susceptible to experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment and violence. Across these studies, the findings supported the centrality of

# neoliberal beliefs and neoliberalism as a structural entity landing on people’s perceptions and

# experiences of women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment.

# The first study of my dissertation was meant to extend research documenting the

# importance of neoliberal beliefs in people’s endorsements of gender-based mistreatment myths,

# to understand the role of participant background in the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs, and to

# understand how various social beliefs are related to neoliberal beliefs. In this study, I found

# support that higher participant endorsements of belief in a just world, economic system

# 

# 161

# justification, sexism, racism, and classism all predicted higher endorsements of neoliberal

# beliefs. Further, participants with some more privileged backgrounds (e.g., White, men, and

# White higher-class participants) were significantly more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs.

# Finally, I found that people who endorsed neoliberal beliefs were significantly more likely to

# accept sexual assault, sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility myths.

# The results of this first study broadened the understanding of individual neoliberal beliefs

# to include connections between the endorsement of other forms of systemic oppression that

# previous research has not yet considered. This finding strengthens our insight into the importance

# of neoliberal beliefs in maintaining inequality. A key component of neoliberal ideology is the

# belief that systems of oppression are irrelevant to individual life outcomes (Arfken, 2018; Bay-

# Cheng, et al., 2015; Harvey, 2005; Perez & Salter, 2019; Son Hing, 2013). Previous research has

# demonstrated that those who endorse sexism and belief in a just world are more likely to endorse

# neoliberal beliefs. In the current study, this was also true of classism, racism, and economic

# system justification. Therefore, despite the lack of acknowledgment of structural level privilege

# and oppression, the current study extends and demonstrates the importance of these beliefs

# among people who readily accept neoliberal ideology. They don’t believe that structural

# oppression limits individual success and yet they are the ones most likely to endorse systemic-

# level ideologies that directly contribute to oppression (e.g., racism, sexism, and classism).

# Additionally, this first study helped to provide some evidence of the importance of

# individual background in the likelihood of endorsing neoliberal beliefs. I had originally proposed

# that women, People of Color, and individuals from lower-income backgrounds would be more

# 

# 162

# likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs, and I found some support for this. The literature is mixed in

# terms of support for structural level attributions for life circumstances. Bay-Cheng and

# colleagues (2015) found that individuals who identified as politically conservative were more

# likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs. Other research has found inconsistent results related to the

# centrality of these structural attributions among individuals considering their social position.

# Some researchers have found that lower-income and Black individuals were more likely to make

# structural attributions for life outcomes, while others have shown that Black, low-income

# individuals are less likely to make them (Bullock, 1999; Feagin, 1972; Young, 2004). My

# research builds on this literature considering the importance of social position in the likelihood of

# neoliberal belief endorsement. Here I found that participants who identified as White (compared

# to Black), men (compared to women), and White conservatives (compared to White Democrats)

# were more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs. I additionally found that among White

# individuals, as social class increases, endorsement of neoliberal beliefs increases, whereas among

# Black individuals, as social class increases, neoliberal belief endorsement decreases. My finding

# that men, White participants, and White higher classed individuals were more likely to endorse

# neoliberal beliefs helps demonstrate that endorsement of these structural level attributions are

# somewhat motivated by social position related to privilege. More research is needed to further

# understand the ways that neoliberal belief endorsement is predicted by social position and how

# that might interact with other beliefs and experiences.

# Finally, in this study, I extended previous research showing a connection between

# neoliberal beliefs endorsement and people’s perceptions of women’s gender-based mistreatment

# 

# 163

# to include judgments about sexual harassment and gender-based incivility (Bay-Cheng, et al.,

# 2015). Given the centrality of personal responsibility in life outcomes in neoliberal beliefs and

# the overlap with judgments in blame attributions toward women for experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment, I expected that there would be a relation between these ideologies. Indeed, I found

# that higher endorsement of neoliberal beliefs significantly predicted higher endorsements of

# sexual assault, sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility myth acceptance. This importantly

# demonstrates the significance of structural level beliefs that don’t fully concern women’s

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment in people’s judgments toward them on an individual

# level.

# In Study 2, I wanted to extend the research from Study 1 to understand how these

# endorsements differently affect people’s perceptions of women’s lived experiences of one type

# of gender-based mistreatment: sexual assault. Further, I attempted to assess how stereotypes

# related to Black women and “undeserving” poor women might influence these findings. Here I

# found support that participants were more likely to blame Black women compared to White

# women, and undeserving poor women compared to deserving poor women for their own sexual

# assault.

# For Black women, this relation was mediated by participants’ belief that they were of less

# value compared to White women. Participant neoliberal belief endorsement strengthened the

# endorsement of these stereotypes leading to greater blame attribution. Specifically, among

# participants who read about the Black woman, among those with the highest levels of neoliberal

# belief endorsement, this relation was stronger. Additionally, in Study 2, for the undeserving poor

# 

# 164

# woman this relation was mediated by participant perceptions that this woman was oversexualized

# compared to the deserving poor woman. Again, participant neoliberal belief endorsement

# strengthened the endorsement of these stereotypes leading to greater blame attribution.

# Specifically, as neoliberal beliefs increased among those who read about the undeserving poor

# woman, this relation got stronger. These findings further support the importance of neoliberal

# beliefs in research on women’s gender-based mistreatment.

# The goal of Study 3 was to understand the role of neoliberal policy in women’s

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment through precarious housing and work. While I

# expected differences in mistreatment to arise related to housing precarity, I found instead that

# much of these women’s experiences were overlapping in ways that made the granularity of day-

# to-day life quite similar in concerns and experiences related to mistreatment. Women largely

# reflected on their concerns related to the instability of their current housing situation regardless

# of their status as “more” or “less” precarious (e.g., those who had secured government funded

# housing and those who hadn’t yet). Their responses to our questions illustrate the importance of

# lives that are often over-looked in psychological literature. Their experiences illuminate so much

# about the importance of structural policy in the continuous reproduction of conditions that make

# them disproportionately susceptible to violence, gender-based mistreatment, and mistreatment

# more generally.

# Importance Across Studies

# We know that the perpetuation of women’s experiences of violence at the hands of men

# is largely influenced by patriarchal power where this violence and the endorsement of men’s

# 

# 165

# enactment of violence against others is widely seen as the norm. However, based on the research

# presented in this dissertation, the story is more complex and has many important actors we

# haven’t fully considered in the literature of women’s gender-based mistreatment.

# Patriarchal power that is integral to the perpetuation of women’s mistreatment is fueled

# by sexism and is built upon a colonialist, slave-owning, capitalist society where certain men

# maintain this power over others in disproportionate ways (Davis, 1981). Given that low-income

# women and Women of Color are disproportionately likely to experience gender-based

# mistreatment compared to other groups of women, the patriarchal power fueling this relation is

# inherently tied to this history of the pooling of power and wealth of this country (Bruyneel, 2020;

# Davis, 1981). Further, these systems are inherently tied to capitalism and the formation and

# maintenance of the unequal and oppressive hoarding of wealth that Karl Marx discussed as the

# expected outcome of a capitalist society (Marx, 2010/1867).

# Neoliberal beliefs have a particular importance in the maintenance of this relationship.

# Given the necessity of neoliberal beliefs in maintaining capitalism and the continued hoarding of

# wealth among those historically and presently privileged by this economic system, the key

# component of disbelief in systemic forms of oppression is strategic in maintaining these goals

# (Arfken, 2018, p. 685; Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Brown, 2003; Harvey, 2005; Perez & Salter,

# 2019; Son Hing, 2013). The assumption is neutral outcomes for individuals that are a result of a

# just and fair system. Contrary to this, as discussed in the introduction, intersectionality theory

# offers an opposing framework to neoliberalism and has been fundamental to the current set of

# studies.

# 

# 166

# Intersectional theory focuses on the ways in which systems of power and oppression

# contribute to qualitative differences in individual experiences and in perceptions of others

# (Collins, 2000; Collins & Bilge, 2016; Crenshaw, 1991; Crenshaw, 1989; hooks, 2000; Lorde,

# 1984; Moradi & Grzank, 2017; Yuval-Davis, 2006). Further, while intersectional theory

# proposes differences in people’s perceptions based on individual group membership implicated

# by these systems of privilege and oppression, a body of research has also demonstrated this

# effect (Bavishi, et al., 2010; Cole, 2009; Ghavami & Peplau, 2012; Lott & Saxon, 2002; Reid,

# 2010; Settles & Buchanan, 2014).

# Findings from the current set of studies further demonstrates the importance of

# positionality of both the perceiver and the perceived in making judgments about other people’s

# experiences. Despite the neutral position in life outcomes that neoliberalism claims, the current

# studies establish that the important implications of intersectional theory seem to apply most to

# those who would deny its very existence. Specifically, in Study 1, individuals who endorsed

# racism, sexism, and classism at higher levels were significantly more likely to endorse neoliberal

# beliefs documenting the salience of unequal perceptions about others based on group

# membership among those who claim that inequality in outcomes don’t exist. In Study 2,

# neoliberal belief endorsement was associated with the endorsement of racist and classist

# stereotypes about Black women and women described as members of the undeserving poor and

# was associated with their higher levels of blame for sexual assault. Again, while these findings

# support that Black women and women stereotyped as members of the undeserving poor are

# blamed more in experiences of sexual assault in general, the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs

# 

# 167

# helps us more fully understand one mechanism driving the differentiation in stereotypes among

# participants.

# Finally, in Study 3, neoliberal beliefs were evident in policy that affected low-income

# women’s housing and workplace experiences of precarity that contributed in direct and indirect

# ways to their experiences of gender-based mistreatment. While Studies 1 and 2 demonstrated the

# centrality of neoliberal beliefs in people’s judgments of blame toward women for gender-based

# mistreatment, the final study in this dissertation was meant to extend this research to demonstrate

# how neoliberal beliefs and neoliberal policy might affect women’s housing and workplace

# precarity, leaving them at risk for disproportionately frequent experiences of gender-based

# mistreatment.

# As outlined above, the importance of including an analysis of neoliberal beliefs in this

# line of research does not stem from its sole ability to explain women’s gender-based

# mistreatment or people’s perceptions of it. Any of the findings from any of the three studies

# presented here would remain constant without the consideration of neoliberal beliefs or

# neoliberalism as a theoretical framework. However, it would be misguided to dismiss the

# importance of neoliberal beliefs here and in research on gender-based mistreatment generally.

# This set of studies clearly exemplifies one additional missing piece of the larger story regarding

# women’s mistreatment and people’s perceptions of it. This picture is more complex and nuanced

# when including neoliberal belief endorsement; then we can see the important role that these

# beliefs play in strengthening the perceptions of and perpetuation of women’s experiences of

# violence and mistreatment.

# 

# 168

# Study 1 demonstrated the importance of neoliberal beliefs in people’s perceptions of

# forms of gender-based mistreatment (sexual harassment and gender-based incivility) in addition

# to sexual assault. Study 2 directly built from this first study to understand how neoliberal beliefs

# might be important to people’s perceptions of the experiences of sexual assault among women

# who are marginalized by race (Black or White) and by class (deserving or undeserving poor). I

# argued, and found that neoliberal beliefs predicted stronger endorsements of stereotypes of these

# women as oversexualized and of less value overall, leading to greater blame for their own

# mistreatment. While Study 1 showed that endorsement of neoliberal beliefs related to more

# acceptance of gender-based mistreatment myth acceptance, Study 2 demonstrated that neoliberal

# beliefs strengthened patterns of blame toward Black women and women stereotyped as members

# of the undeserving poor specifically, for experiences of sexual assault. Therefore, while

# neoliberal beliefs are important to women’s experiences of gender-based mistreatment generally,

# they further strengthen the relationship of blame toward marginalized women who are

# disproportionately more likely to experience these forms of mistreatment and to be dismissed

# when they report these experiences in their lifetime (Cortina et al., 1998; Fessler, 2018; Foley et

# al., 1995; Gruber & Bjorn, 1982; Kane, 2020; LaFree, et al., 1985; MacKinnon, 1979; Maryland

# Coalition Against Sexual Assault [Maryland Coalition Against Sexual Assault MCASA], n.d.).

# Findings from this set of studies illuminate an important addition to the gender-based

# mistreatment literature. Moving forward, neoliberal beliefs and neoliberal policy needs to remain

# a key assessment in the implications of women’s gender-based mistreatment experiences and

# people’s perceptions of those experiences. Of particular importance in future research is the

# 

# 169

# analysis of how individual positionality affects endorsement of neoliberal beliefs, given the

# somewhat contested findings of previous research and of the current studies presented here.

# Specifically, previous literature outlines the importance of positionality in the likelihood of

# making structural attributions for outcomes in life or for specifically endorsing neoliberal beliefs

# in inconsistent ways (Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Bullock, 1999; Feagin, 1972; Young, 2004). Bay-

# Cheng and colleagues (2015) found that conservative identifying participants were more likely to

# endorse neoliberal beliefs. Bullock (1999) and Feagin (1972) similarly found low-socioeconomic

# status and African American individuals to be more likely to make structural attributions for

# blame whereas, but Young (2004) found that these structural attributions were less likely among

# low-income Black men.

# In the current studies, I found that conservative individuals were more likely to endorse

# neoliberal beliefs in Study 1. Additionally, men (compared to women), White conservatives

# (compared to White Democrats), White higher-SES (compared to White lower-SES), Black

# lower-SES (compared to Black higher-SES) individuals were all more likely to endorse

# neoliberal beliefs. Further, in Study 3, I found that most of the women in our sample made

# comments about their experiences in life that reflected neoliberal belief endorsement. These

# women were all precarious in terms of social class standing. While this small sample offered

# limited ability to look at potential differences based racial identity, it seemed that women made

# comments reflective of neoliberal beliefs regardless of race.

# While Study 2 supports variations in neoliberal belief endorsements based on both race

# and social class position, Study 3 shows that poor women with precarious housing and jobs also

# 

# 170

# express neoliberal beliefs. While most women in Study 3 made comments reflecting neoliberal

# beliefs, I didn’t measure strength of these endorsements as I did in Study 2. Neoliberal beliefs

# clearly are salient among these low-income women, but the frequency and strength of these

# endorsements may vary depending on other factors, as Study 2 demonstrated. The importance of

# agency implied by these beliefs may be one reason that even these women faced with severe

# structural challenges nevertheless express them (Feagin, 1972; Jost & Banaji, 1994; Larrain,

# 1983; Liu, et al., 2011; Marx & Engels, 1998). Despite that fact, among White women, increases

# in social class status were associated with more endorsement of these beliefs, perhaps

# demonstrating the importance of maintaining clear boundaries between poor White individuals

# and middle- and upper-class White individuals (Bérubé & Bérubé, 1997; Crockett, 2017;

# Hartigan, 1997; Liu, et al., 2011).

# Further, despite surface-level differences between these findings, these studies were

# assessed using very different samples in very different ways (quantitative online survey versus

# qualitative interviews). We did not name neoliberalism or neoliberal beliefs in the interviews nor

# ask about components of neoliberalism like we did in the surveys. Rather, women spontaneously

# expressed neoliberal beliefs reflective of their own and other people’s experiences. The survey

# findings that reflected differences in endorsements of neoliberal beliefs by race and class do not

# discount the likelihood that those who were less likely to endorse these beliefs may still also

# endorse neoliberal beliefs overall just with less consistency.

# Taking this large and inconsistent body of findings from past and current research into

# account, we need to study more representative samples to make clearer remarks about the role of

# 

# 171

# positionality in neoliberal belief endorsement. However, what does seem clear is the importance

# of an intersectional analysis in the endorsement of neoliberal beliefs moving forward in future

# research and attending to the ways in which individual positionality within a web of power and

# oppression produces different levels of neoliberal belief endorsement (Crenshaw, 1991;

# Crenshaw, 1989). For instance, while there are some general findings that men and politically

# conservative individuals are more likely to endorse neoliberal beliefs, more nuance in these

# endorsements is provided through an analysis that attends to the multiple layers of positionality

# offered by overlapping situatedness within systems of power and oppression (Bay-Cheng, et al.,

# 2015).

# Moving forward into future research directions, there are many avenues to pursue in this

# line of research. Below I outline some of the potential directions I intend to pursue this work

# following my dissertation.

# Future Research Directions

# There are a few specific areas I intend to follow directly from the findings presented in

# this dissertation. I have the goal of extending my research both in more formal institutional

# settings (e.g., workplaces and higher education) and those alongside formal institutions (e.g.,

# people’s experiences interacting with formal institutions but not necessarily recruited through

# these institutions/organizations).

# First, given the important contribution of the gender-based incivility scale, I would like to

# conduct research to further validate this scale and define sub-scales aimed at measuring

# experiences of incivility among women in the workplace that are particularly gender-based in

# 

# 172

# nature. Further, using this scale in future research, I would like to attempt to understand how

# experiences of gender-based incivility among women might relate to other forms of

# discrimination among women in the workplace. Specifically, I would like to assess a potential

# relation between classism, racism, and sexism with gender-based incivility. Given that incivility

# is categorized as mundane behavior that often systemically negatively impacts the experiences of

# marginalized individuals in the workplace, I’d like to continue to explore how these more

# “mundane” experiences might be related to other forms of mistreatment in the workplace as well.

# Second, extending findings from my third dissertation study, I would like to conduct a

# broad study capturing experiences of gender-based mistreatment among low-wage working

# women in a more systemic way (e.g., through quantitative online surveys and qualitative open-

# ended survey questions in online surveys). Within this line of research, I would like to document

# the experiences and frequencies of mistreatment among women in low-wage work and consider

# the role of racism, classism, and sexism in predicting these experiences of mistreatment and

# gender-based mistreatment.

# Again, extending the findings and research from my third dissertation study, I would like

# to replicate this study with more diverse populations in terms of racial and ethnic identity and in

# terms of location (urban versus rural, etc.). In an attempt to extend this research to capture more

# diverse experience, I would like to attend to mechanisms of coping among women in these

# situations. One finding from this study suggested the centrality of neoliberalism in relationships

# among low-income women as an important contributor to the fear of forming relationships

# among these women, despite their potential importance in terms of the support they might find in

# 

# 173

# connection. I would like to replicate this study to continue to document experiences and

# perceptions of mistreatment and daily living among low-income women in different settings but,

# I’d also like to extend this to understand what mechanisms these women rely on for coping with

# daily living when they feel apprehensive about forming social relationships with women in

# similar situations as themselves.

# Considering neoliberal beliefs in the context of the workplace, I’d like to explore in

# future research the role of neoliberal beliefs in organizational responses to and experiences of

# workplace mistreatment especially among low-wage workers. This could include assessing

# neoliberal beliefs of employees, and also assessing their training experiences and perceptions of

# gender-based mistreatment, racialized mistreatment, and more in the workplace to explore a

# possible relation between neoliberal belief endorsement and perceptions of and experiences of

# mistreatment in the workplace (especially as it pertains to marginalized groups).

# Finally, given the important theoretical connection between neoliberalism and capitalism,

# in future research, I would like to investigate the overlap between these ideologies in a statistical

# manner to confirm that these systems overlap on an individual and psychological level.

# Systemically we can see the influence and centrality of neoliberalism on the ultimate goals of

# capitalism, however, on an individual level, this relation is currently speculative. This could

# involve measuring participant endorsements of neoliberal beliefs and asking them how likely

# they would be to support various example capitalist policies and then assessing how the

# endorsement of these capitalist policies relate to neoliberal belief endorsement directly.

# Policy Implications

# 

# 174

# While we have many policies regarding racism and sexism in the U.S., there is little

# consideration of the ways in which endorsements of racism, sexism, and classism are influential

# to one another in attempts to protect individuals from gender-based mistreatment.

# First, it is crucial that we bring discussions of neoliberalism and capitalism into policy

# consideration and discussions regarding gender-based mistreatment. As suggested by Angela

# Davis in her 1981 essay Rape, Racism, and the Capitalist Setting, “If the anti-rape movement is

# to avoid the dilemma of Sisyphus, if current activities—ranging from emotional and legal aid to

# defense methods and educational campaign—must be complemented by larger offensive

# measures and situated in a strategic context which envisages the ultimate defeat of monopoly

# capitalism” (Davis, 1981, p. 45). Although researchers are doing important work showing these

# experiences are more frequent among Women of Color and lower-income women and the

# centrality of racism and classism, there needs to be a broader discussion about why these have

# remained catalysts for the exploitation of these groups of women. The absence of understanding

# how both racist and classist ideology are instrumental to the maintenance of a capitalist society

# in discussions of rape, sexual harassment, and gender-based incivility does a disservice to the

# root of their continued disproportionate exploitation.

# In training and education on gender-based mistreatment especially among policy

# stakeholders, the centrality of sexism, racism, classism, and their interconnectedness in the

# perpetuation of violence against women must be included. Given the disproportionate

# experiences of gender-based mistreatment among low-income women and Women of Color

# (both low-income and otherwise), stereotypes about these groups that have been consistently

# 

# 175

# shown to be important to their higher levels of blame attribution must continuously be prioritized

# in training and education (Kiebler & Stewart 2021a; Kiebler & Stewart, 2021b; Kiebler &

# Stewart, 2022; Kiebler & Stewart, 2023; Spencer, 2016). Further, a discussion of within class

# stereotypes and how those lead to differences in blame toward low-income women should be

# included in discussions of the ways that classism is important in people’s perceptions of

# women’s gender-based mistreatment (Kiebler & Stewart, 2023).

# Further, there is considerable work that needs to be done in debunking myths related to

# social class and the myth of neoliberal beliefs more generally. At the national, state, and local

# level of policy, neoliberal beliefs limit opportunity and accessibility to basic necessities among

# low-income people based on neoliberal beliefs that perpetuate the myth of meritocracy where

# hard work is falsely made to be the sole separation between economic success and failure in the

# U.S. (Arfken, 2018, p. 685; Bay-Cheng, et al., 2015; Brown, 2003; Harvey, 2005; Perez &

# Salter, 2019; Son Hing, 2013). Results from all three of the studies point to the necessity of this

# work. In the first two studies, participant results clearly demonstrated the role of stereotypes in

# blame attribution toward women, specifically toward Women of Color and low-income women,

# for their experiences of gender-based mistreatment. In Study 2, I found that people were more

# likely to perceive the woman stereotyped as a member of the undeserving poor as

# oversexualized. Additionally, in Study 2, I found that Women of Color were seen as significantly

# less valuable than White low-income women. If we think about these perceptions toward these

# groups of women, it is unlikely that these stereotypes don’t also affect other aspects of their

# lives. For example, workplace norms of respectability and expectations of presentation and

# 

# 176

# particular ways of communicating with customers are likely to leave women that are stereotyped

# in these ways less likely to find and maintain employment. Further, given the embeddedness of

# neoliberalism in policy at every level of our governance, access to economic and other forms of

# assistance are also likely to be more challenging to secure among women stereotyped as

# “undeserving” of such resources in the first place. More research needs to be conducted in these

# areas to assess the lived experiences of these women across various aspects of their lives, while

# considering the role of neoliberal policy and neoliberal beliefs in outcomes.

# Closing Thoughts

# The current set of studies draws our attention as psychological researchers to the

# importance of the interplay between the individual and the structural factors that implicate

# individual experience, expression, and perception. Prominent and influential systems such as

# neoliberalism and systemic forms of oppression trickle into individual phenomenon. We are

# embedded within these systems and according to the current body of research, they are central in

# experience and perception that we wouldn’t readily see as relevant. Moving forward, we must

# continue to take seriously the importance of interdisciplinary psychological research that attends

# to these systems of power, privilege, and oppression in the study of individual life.

# Appendices

# Appendix A: Study 2 Full Vignettes

# 1. Black woman stereotyped as a member of the “deserving” poor: Keisha is a 27-year-

# old Black woman who works hard at a fast-food restaurant and lives in a decent

# apartment for the money she makes. Keisha has worked hard to obtain a General

# Education Degree (GED) and hopes to apply to be a manager at the restaurant if a spot

# ever opens up. Her current manager and co-workers describe her as a hard-working and

# honest woman. One day, Keisha returned home from work to her apartment and noticed

# her cat Sprinkles is nowhere around. She went outside to look for Sprinkles when Derek,

# whom she had met the previous weekend at a neighborhood barbecue, asked if everything

# was all right. He offered to help her find her cat and after about an hour of looking, they

# found Sprinkles in a neighbor’s yard. Derek whose house was near there, invited her in

# for coffee to celebrate finding Sprinkles. At the end of their coffee and conversation,

# Keisha excused herself and said she needed to get home because she had a big day

# tomorrow. At that point, Derek became insistent that they talk a little longer. After saying

# again that she really should get home, Derek began to push her towards the bedroom and

# onto the bed. Keisha insisted he stop; however, Derek proceeded to have sex with her

# anyway.

# 2. Black woman stereotyped as a member of the “undeserving” poor: Keisha is a 27-

# year-old Black woman who dropped out of high school at age 16 and has been on welfare

# for most of her adult life. Keisha lives in an apartment that is funded by government

# Appendix B: Neoliberal Beliefs Measures

# Neoliberal Beliefs Inventory: (Bay-Cheng, Fitz, Alizaga, & Zucker, 2015)

# 1. Affirmative action is an outdated policy now that people are generally treated as equals.

# 2. Discrimination does not exist today to such a degree that affirmative action policies are

# necessary.

# 3. Affirmative action does not help eradicate discrimination. Instead it exacerbates it by

# promoting people on the basis of minority status instead of merit.

# 4. Affirmative action is a problem because it treats people unequally.

# 5. People who complain about discrimination are often just blaming other people for their

# own problems.

# 6. I think people imagine more barriers, such as discrimination, than actually exist.

# 7. Based on my own experience and the people around me, it’s hard for me to feel sorry for

# people who complain about discrimination.

# 8. People should be allowed to compete to ensure that the best person wins.

# 9. \*Being competitive is not part of human nature.

# 10. Competition is a good way to discover and motivate the best people.

# 11. \*Shielding children from competition prepares them for adulthood.

# 12. Fairness means letting people have equal opportunity, not guaranteeing equal outcome.

# 13. To get ahead in the world, people have to depend on themselves more than anyone else.

# 14. Anybody can get ahead in the world if they learn to play the game.

# 15. Any goal can be achieved with enough hard work and talent.

# 

# 208

# 16. Right now, pretty much all Americans are free to live any kind of life they want.

# 17. When it comes to challenges like discrimination, individuals just have to be tough enough

# to overcome them.

# 18. I’ve benefited from working hard, so there’s no reason others can’t.

# 19. If you’re smart and strong enough, discrimination won’t hold you back.

# 20. A person’s success in life is determined more by their personal efforts than by society.

# 21. Anyone who is willing to work hard can be successful in America.

# 22. A problem with government social programs is that they get in the way of personal

# freedom.

# 23. The government is inefficient, and therefore should not interfere in the private sector.

# 24. \*The government doesn’t often hurt individual ambition when it interferes.

# 25. \*The government has a right to take what I earn and give it to someone else.

# 26. Social programs sponsored by the government provide false incentives and unearned

# rewards.

# Appendix C: Ambivalent Sexism Inventory Measure

# Ambivalent Sexism Inventory Measure (Glick & Fiske, 1996)

# Hostile Sexism

# 1. Women exaggerate problems at work.

# 2. Women are too easily offended.

# 3. Most women interpret innocent remarks as sexist.

# 4. When women lose fairly, they claim discrimination.

# 5. Women seek special favors under guise of equality.

# 6. \*Feminists are making reasonable demands.

# 7. \*Feminists are not seeking more power than men.

# 8. Women seek power by gaining control over men.

# 9. \*Few women tease men sexually.

# 10. Once a man commits, she puts him on a tight leash.

# 11. Women fail to appreciate all men do for them.

# Benevolent Sexism

# Protective Paternalism

# 12. A good woman should be set on a pedestal.

# 13. Women should be cherished and protected by men.

# 14. Men should sacrifice to provide for women.

# 15. In a disaster, women need not be rescued first.

# 2. Irish, Italian, Jewish, and many other minorities overcame prejudice and worked their

# 9. \*Poverty is caused by being taken advantage of by the rich.

# Appendix F: Economic System Justification

# Economic system justification scale (Jost & Thompson, 2000).

# 1. If people work hard, they almost always get what they want.
